records.Title: Gospels of Mac Durnan
records.Contents: Old Irish scholium

records.Title: Book of Deer
records.Contents: Middle Irish notitiae

records.Title: Airbertach mac Coisse (fl. 982; †1016), Rochuala crecha is tír thair
records.Beginning lines: Rochuala crecha is tír thair eter sretha síl Ádaim.
records.Contents: A Middle Irish poem (23 st.) on the conquest of the Midianites by the Israelites (NM 31). It also deals with some of the doings of Joshua (st. 12-14). Though unascribed to Airbertach, his authorship is likely on grounds of style and subject.

records.Title: Airbertach mac Coisse (fl. 982; †1016), Fichi ríg - cia rím as ferr?
records.Beginning lines: Fichi ríg - cia rím as ferr? - rogabsat Hierusalem
records.Contents: A learned Middle Irish poem (61 st.) on the kings of Judah who ruled in Jerusalem from Saul to the destruction of the city, with two additional stanzas on the return of the Jews after the Babylonian capitivity.

records.Title: Glosses on the Psalms from Milan, Bib. Ambrosiana, C. 301 inf.
records.Beginning lines: Multiplicasti magnificantiam tuam … malorum nostrorum disperatio
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Catena on the Psalms, 39:11-151:7
records.Beginning lines: A concilio multa id est toto Israhel praedicabo
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Treatise on the Psalter in Old Irish
records.Beginning lines: Is he titul fil i ndreich in lipuirsi taitnea do menmannaib
records.Contents: This Old Irish commentary is thought to be based on a Latin one, the source of the Latin glosses in MS iii, infra. The Irish text is a general introduction to the Psalms and a commentary on Ps 1:1. It then breaks off. Thus the extent of the original commentary is unknown. It has a close affinity with Pauca problesmata de enigmatibus ex tomis canonicis. A versified summary of its introduction was made by Airbertach mac Cosse in 985 at the monastic school at Ross Ailithir, evidence that the text continued to be studied in the schools.

records.Title: Airbertach mac Coisse (fl. 982; †1016), A Dé dúlig, adat-teoch
records.Beginning lines: A Dé dúlig, adat-teoch - is tú mo rúinid co rath
records.Contents: A Middle Irish poem (50 st.) in four parts, on the Psalter. It draws heavily on Treatise on the Psalter in Old Irish … It reeks of the classroom, and is evidently an elementary textbook for students of the Psalter, who probably committed it to memory. The poet dates his work in st. 37-40. It is marked by modernisation of language, simplification, a strong liturgical and devotional flavour, and a particular interest in the psalms as part of the divine office.

records.Title: On the Maledictory Psalms
records.Beginning lines: Sreb a salmaib suad slán feib ro-horddaig Adamnán
records.Contents: A Middle-Irish poem (13 st.), probably of the eleventh century, in two parts: part 1 ... lists the maledictory psalms (arranged in order of occurrence in the psalter); part 2 … lists the saints (a slection of twenty) to be associated with these psalms. Formal malediction of those who violate clerical property to persons is common in hagiography and in other ecclesiastical documents.

records.Title: Glosses on Amos
records.Contents: Contains six Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Pauca de libris catholicorum scriptorum in evangelia excerpta
records.Beginning lines: Quomodo vocatur evangelium in tribus principalibus linguis?
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses

records.Title: Glosses on the gospels by 'Man', or Manchianus
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses and marginalia

records.Title: Liber questionum in euangeliis
records.Beginning lines: Matheus instituit uirtutum tramite mores et bene vivendi iusto dedit ordine legis
records.Contents: Contains a single Old Irish gloss.

records.Title: Commentarius in Mattheum e codice Vindobonense latino 940
records.Beginning lines: Queritur quod cooperantur circa agnitionem evangelii
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Historica investigatio evangelii secundum Lucam
records.Beginning lines: Quoniam quidem multi conati sunt. Prochemium est hoc
records.Contents: Contains a few Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Glossae Libri Ardmachani
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Pauca ex commentario beati Hilarii et sancti Hieronimi et beati Augustini et aliorum eruditorum virorum expositionibus in epistulas beati Pauli apostoli excerpta
records.Beginning lines: Paulus Ebreo sermone temptatio dicitur
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Commentarius in epistulas catholicas Scotti anonymi
records.Beginning lines: Septem tubae quae fuerunt cum populo Israel quando obsessa est Hiericho
records.Contents: Contains two Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Glossae in epistulam II Petri (1:1 - 2:13)
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Saltair na Rann - verse
records.Roman dates: s. x(2), c. AD 988, ut fertur
records.Beginning lines: Mo rí-se rí nime náir, cen úabur, cen immarbáig
records.Contents: A Middle Irish verse account of bible history, from the creation to the Crucifixion, with additional pieces to the end of days, drawing on the bible but even more on apocrypha … It contains 7788 lines in 1947 stanzas ...The whole may have been intended as a teaching text in the schools. Parts are of very considerable literary merit, others are much less polished. Dating evidence ... indicating that the text was written c. AD 988, is later and disputed.

records.Title: Scél Saltrach na rann al. Saltair na rann: prose version
records.Beginning lines: Do-rigne Dia immorra in rigthech uachtarach do shlog amra archaingel hi filet .x. cutruma in domain (recension 1, from MS i); Abhram mac Nara meic Nachoir iss é cétna fírén tánic i ndomun iar ndílend (recension 2)
records.Contents: As Thurneysen proved (infra), the prose version derives from the verse. The author of the prose has abbreviated (the last 27 poems are ignored), has sometimes misunderstood, and omitted incidents, and has drawn on materials not used in the verse … The first section treats of Creation, the Fall of Lucifer, the Fall of Adam, the story of Adam and Eve. The second ... treats of biblical history. According to Dillon's stemma (infra, p. 4) recension 2 is the earlier (c. AD 1100).

records.Title: Adam Octipartitus
records.Beginning lines: Is fisigh cidh dia ndernad Adhamh .i. do uii rannaibh (MS i); Is hedh inso immorro na secht rain dia ndernadh Ádham (MS ii); Abrom cid dia ndernadh Ádhomh (MS iii)
records.Contents: On the eight cosmic elements from which Adam was made …

records.Title: Cenn ard Ádaim al. Elements of Adam
records.Beginning lines: Cenn ard Ádaim, étrocht rád
records.Contents: On the lands from which Adam's body was made … This short poem appears as an interpolation in the poem on the psalter of Airbertach mac Cosse (†1016), fer légind and superior of Ross Ailithir (Ó Néill, infra).
records.info:: The copy in MS Rawlinson B 502 occurs as part of a poem on the Psalter (beg. A Dé dúlig, atat-teoch) and is directly followed by an additional quatrain with an ascription to Airbertach mac Coisse (d. 1016), saying that he translated the poem from Latin into Irish.

records.Title: Gnímradha in ṡesadh laí láin al. The works of the sixth day
records.Beginning lines: Gnimradha in ṡesadh lai lain aisneidfet insin deaghdail
records.Contents: A didactic poem (63 st.) 'on the complete sixth day in proper order' (as the poet promises). Based on apocrypha and a wide range of speculative learning, it recounts the varieties of humanity, the materials of the human body, the consequences of the Fall ...

records.Title: Eve's Lament
records.Beginning lines: Mé Éba ben Ádaim uill
records.Contents: Eve's lament, poignant and brief (4 st.), for her part in the Fall and its consequences.
records.info:: 11th century (Murphy)

records.Title: Athair cáich coimsid nime
records.Beginning lines: Athair cáích coimsid nime in rí uasal ainglide
records.Contents: A verse narrative (58 quatrains, with some variation in the MSS) of Creation, the Fall, the birth of Cain and Abel, the years of the patriarchs, the descendants of the sons of Noah, Nimrod's Tower, and the origin of the languages of mankind … The poem draws on a wide range of apocrypha, available in the Irish schools in the eleventh century and before, and is thus a useful point of reference. These sources remain to be studied.

records.Title: Cain and Abel
records.Beginning lines: Cáin didiu ro-formdig re hAibel co ndechaig spirat mallachtnach ina chride
records.Contents: Cain, born before his fallen parents had done penance for their sin, was accursed. Abel, born after their penance, was pure, and God prevailed on his descendants to have no relationships with the offspring of Cain. Ambia, daughter of Cain, part woman, part fish, was impregnanted by a trout and gave birth to 22 children, two hudge, whence the Fomuir or Fomorians; and the rest tiny, whence the leprechauns. This quaint narrative is a cross between a biblical 'leading case' and an origin legend.

records.Title: Dá brón flatha nime al. The two sorrows of the kingdom of Heaven al. Enoch and Elijah.
records.Beginning lines: Cid ara n-apart brón i nnim? Ní ansa. Eli & Enoc ro gadatar in Coimdid ara mbrith 'na corpaib dochum nime.
records.Contents: Enoch and Elijah passed in their mortal bodies to heaven. There they await their return to earth to do battle with Antichrist and be martyred by him. This text represents Elijah as preaching to the just in Paradise on the terrors of Doomsday. It is indebted to a Latin text.

records.Title: Soloman and the power of women
records.Beginning lines: Baí rí amra de Grecaib, Salemon a ainm
records.Contents: A comic and shortened version of 1 Esdras 3-4. At a royal fest, the king's boon companions try to determine, drunkenly, which is the greatest power in the world: wine, the king's power, or women. The queen smartly resolves the issue.

records.Title: Procept na Machaabdai in so al. Teachings of the Maccabees
records.Beginning lines: Caithigid co calma, cobsaigther & cómnertaigther bar cride, a uli doíne
records.Contents: A homily on the martyrdom of the seven sons of Macchabaeus and their mother, for 1 August, the feast of the Maccabees in the Irish church. It begins as an exposition of Ps 30:25, but quickly turns to the heroic martyrdom of the Maccabees as an inspiring example of fearless obedience to God's commands.

records.Title: How Samson slew the Gesteda
records.Beginning lines: Ro boí rí amra fir Geistedaib .i. Cainnill a ainm & do-siacht teidm n-aduathmar a n-aimsir in rig.
records.Contents: CODECS: Late Middle Irish tale in which Jewish traditions about Samson are combined with Greek traditions about the Trojans. Ferann na nGeisteda, the homeland of the pagan Gesteda in the tale, has been identified as a reference to the Land of Goshen in Egypt.

records.Title: Sgél ar Dáibíd mac Iesse al. King David and the Beggar
records.Beginning lines: Dia cascc is and no dailed Dauid mac Iesse, a dechmada di bochtaib & aidilcnechaib in Coimded.
records.Contents: A short tale, in two different but hitherto unstudied recensions, of king David's almsgiving and Solomon's judgement … In fact, this is an aetiological tale, in bibical terms, that makes the prescribed division of goods and of inheritance in early medieval Ireland the jdugement of Solomon viz., one-third to the church, one-third to the lord, and one-third to the family ... The aetiology is lost in the later version (MSS v-vii).

records.Title: Tales of King David
records.Beginning lines: (1) Dauid mac hIsse rí is ferr tarraid talam inti Dauid; (2) Dá mac amra la Dauid .i. Solam & Aibisilón. In tí Abisilón esaide dealb duine as deach taraill talmain; (3) Do-ber Abisilón idna catha dia athair; (4) Na bíd Dauid fut ind shamlaí oc breith na h-énbreithi
records.Contents: (i) 'David and Goliath' … (ii) 'David and Absalon' … (iii) 'Absalson's death' …. (iv) 'David and Solomon' …

records.Title: King Constantine of Greece and Solomon's wife
records.Beginning lines: Mochean do tęcht a lębair 'ga tá in ęgna domhębair
records.Contents: A long late medieval poem (104 st.) on Constantine's sucessful courtship of one of Solomon's wives, her deception of her husband, and her elopment … The fanciful attribution to Cormac ceolach mac Cuilennáin (last stanza) may hdie the poet's identity and his purposed. Unedited.

records.Title: The Irish Sex aetates mundi
records.Beginning lines: Panechte incipit .i. tintúd Duiblitrech huí hUathgaile forsin Pandecht Cirine tria Góedeilg in so sís (title)
records.Contents: An Irish translation and reworking by Dublittir ua hÚathgaile (fl. c. 1082 x c. 1116), fer léiginnd of Killeshin, of a postulated Latin original (no longer extant). Three recensions have plausibly been proposed. The stema codicum is disputed. The text deals with the periodisation of history, the six ages of the world, from creation to the Last Judgement, and is based on the Vulgate, Jerome on Genesis, Hiberno-Latin biblical commentaries, Auraicept na nÉces, and other sources.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Dublittir ua hÚathgaile (fl. c. 1082 x c. 1116),

records.Title: Poem on Sex Aetates Mundi
records.Beginning lines: Sé bliadna coicait malle ar sé cétaib ar míle
records.Contents: A brief summary (7 st.) of the peroidisation of Sex aetates mundi, dated internally to 1126, and representative, in style and content, of pedagogical texts of the early twelfth-century monastic schools.

records.Title: Euangelia infantiae (Liber Flavus Fergusiorum)
records.Beginning lines: Iacob mac Ioseb gaba arna oileamhain a ngrádhuib & a n-eagailsib Dé is sé ro sgríb (prologus); Et do bi immorro fer saidbir sona soceineóil oirmidneach don cinad Israelde & do Síl Dabid (text)

records.Title: Euangelia infantiae (Leabhar Breach &c)
records.Beginning lines: Ar it trí soscéla légthar & chantar i n-eclaisib na crístaide adaig notlac (prologue); Tánic didiu Ióseph & Muire ó Nazareth Galile co Bethil Iúda hi cumma cáich & a muinnter (text)
records.Contents: This lengthy text, embedded in the collection of associated texts known as the 'Gospel History', narrates the Nativity, the coming of the Magi, the slaughter of the Innocents, the flight into Egypt, the miracle of the palm, the death of a murderous Herod afflicted by foul diseases, the subsequent history of Israel, and the slaying of Zacharias, father of John the Baptist.

records.Title: Euangelia infantiae al. Infancy gospel of Ps-Thomas
records.Beginning lines: Imbu macán cóic mbliadnae Ísu mac Dé bí
records.Contents: A devotional poem (48 st.) based on the apocryphon … originally composed in Greek … He sees his text through an Irish lens - légend (st. 23), suí rechto (st. 34) are terms of art in early medieval Irish schools and ro scríb abbgitir dó 'he had written an alphabet for him', is what St Patrick does, repeatedly, in Irish hagiography.
records.info:: c.700? According to Carney, this poem and the short one that follows (Maire máthair in maic bic) “seem somewhat older than those of Blathmac, and a seventh- rather than an eighth-century date may perhaps be thought of”.

records.Title: Caesarian tax and the birth of Christ
records.Beginning lines: Ochtauin Auguist ba hairdrig in domain in tan ro génair Críst isin dara bliadain .xl. a flaithiusa
records.Contents: This is part of the 'Gospel History'. Chronological and computistic calculations, in the Irish style, of the circumstances of Christ's birth and life, and reflections on the nature of the rule and the taxation of Augustus.

records.Title: Seventeen wonders of the night of Christ's birth
records.Beginning lines: Do secht n-ingantaib déc in domain in adaig ro génir Crist indister budesta (prose recension); In n-aidchi geini Crist cain seacht n-inganta dég domain (verse recension)
records.Contents: … Only some of these wonders can be traced in earlier exegetical works of Irish origin. Robin Flower … thought that these wonders might have been inspired by a passage in Orosius.

records.Title: Gospel of James son of Alphaeus
records.Contents: The gospel in the mass of the Circumcision in this liturgical fragment of putative Irish origin, is from an otherwise unknown Gospel of James.

records.Title: Names and appearance of the Magi
records.Beginning lines: Amal boí Iosep ann & se i ndorus in tigi ina shessum i n-aroili la n-and (MS i); Nomina et habitus et munera magorum (MS iii)
records.Contents: A later witness, derived from a very old Latin text, to an early and keen Irish exegetical interest in the Magi …

records.Title: Lament of the mothers of the Innocents
records.Beginning lines: Cid ima ndelige mo mac grádach frim?
records.Contents: Poignant dramatic lyrics, the voices of four mothers, bewailing their children who are about to be slaughtered. This text occurs in Infancy narrative of the Lebhar Breac & related manuscripts (123).

records.Title: Abgar legend
records.Beginning lines: Ocus is é in Taha descipul sin ro chuir Tomas apstal co hEuagair rí thíre Armęnia & na tíre fri sruth (MS i); Iar cur Eoin isin carcair amar adubhramar romhaind bhaí Críst ic forcedul gu cuala cach uli é (MS ii)
records.Contents: An apocryphal legend, first found in Eusebius (1.13.6-18) about correspondence between Abgar, prince of Edessa, and Christ. It was known in Ireland by the eighth century. The Irish text is a late and free Middle- Irish rendering of Rufinus' Latin translation of Eusebius, and forms part of the 'Gospel History' in MSS i-ii (see also 1360).

records.Title: Clanna Israël uli al. Beheading of John the Baptist by Mug Roith
records.Beginning lines: Clanna Israël uli scaílset fón mbith mbarrbuidi
records.Contents: A long poem (43 st.) attributed to Flann Fína mac Gossa (evidently a pseudonym of the cleric-poet), on the killing of St John the Baptist. The gospel narrative (Mt 14:1-12; Mk 6:17-29) has been changed, apocryphal matter added, and the executioner unnamed in the gospels, is here the Irish druid. Mug Ruith, ancestor in the genealogies of the Munster dynasty Fir Maige Féne, reputed discipline of Simon Magus in medieval Irish legend. Hence the Irish geelings of guilt (st. 40-2) over the death of St John.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Flann Fína mac Gossa (evidently a pseudonym of the cleric-poet)
records.Location of the narrative: St John the Baptist; Irish druid. Mug Ruith, ancestor of the Munster dynasty Fir Maige Féne

records.Title: Abstalón adba na ríg al. Beheading of John the Baptist
records.Beginning lines: Abstalón adba na ríg baile i ndernad in mórgním
records.Contents: A poem (27 st.) on the killing of St John the Baptist … Apocryphal matter grreatly supplements the gospel narrative. None could be found to execute John but the Irish druid Mug Ruith.
records.Location of the narrative: St John the Baptist; Irish druid Mug Ruith

records.Title: Passion of John the Baptist (prose)
records.Beginning lines: Bui aroile fer angid etróccar i nIerusalem

records.Title: Stair Nicoméid al. Irish Gospel of Nicodemus al. Páis in Choimdead & scéla a chrochta
records.Beginning lines: Isin nómad bliadain déc do flaithius Tibir Chesair ind impir Rómánaich & airdríg na n-uili domain
records.Contents: A translation of the Latin apocrypha Gesta Pilati and Descensus Christi ad inferos, themselves renderings of Greek originals. The Gospel of Nicodemus, as the conjoined texts were known, was very popular in the medieval West. The Irish translation(s) belong to the eleventh century but their relationship with the Latin versions is unclear. A critical edition is needed.

records.Title: Woods of Christ's cross
records.Beginning lines: Setrus & cipresus & palma & oliua .i. as iad so anmann na ceithre crann (prose); Ceithre fedha fáth gin gheis i croich Mic Dé dia fhégmais (verse)
records.Contents: The prose and verse reflect different traditions: cedar, cypress, palm and olive according to the prose; cedar, cypress, pine and birch according to the verse. The last may be a mistranslation of buxus. A Latin version of the list occurs in Collectanea Ps=Bedae.

records.Title: The Mythical Tree
records.Beginning lines: Crand ingnad indistear isin leigend a uachtar uas fhirmamaint & a ichtar i talmain
records.Contents: A mystical tree, its upper parts in the firmament whence it grows, its lower parts and roots in the earth, music of all kinds in its middle, and shining

records.Title: The Finding of the True Cross
records.Beginning lines: Amail fo-frith crand croiche Críst i n-aimsir Dabid meic Iese ar tús
records.Contents: This scholastic if devout text usually occurs in the MSS as a prelude to the story of Fierabras, and is a version of the Latin text in AASS, Maii, i, p.450, a text of which also occurs in Dublin, TCL, 667 olim F. 5. 3, p. 66b; s. xv (c. AD 1454); origin a Franciscan House in Co. Clare.

records.Title: Dígal fola Críst
records.Beginning lines: Da bliadhain .xl. Uero batar na hIudaide a morforpairt cruid & bíd & clainni
records.Contents: Part of the 'Gospel History' … This unedited text tells of the persecution of the Christians after the Crucifixion, the dispersal of the apostles, the ominous signs that presaged the catastrophe, and finally the destruction of Jerusalem by Titus. Its dating awaits its edition and that of the larger 'History' to which it belongs.

records.Title: Páis Longinuis al. Betha Loinginuis al. Acta Longini al. Passion of Longinus
records.Beginning lines: Dia mbuí Críst hi croich la hIudaigib dodeochaid oen dona míledu
records.Contents: An Irish rendering of Acta Longini (itself perhaps of the tenth century), in the form of a resounding sermon against paganism and its diabolical nature. A version of the story was known to the Irish martyrologies at least as early as the beginning of the ninth century ...

records.Title: The finding of the body of St Stephen
records.Beginning lines: Ísu Críst mac Dé bíi sláníccid in uli domuin (homily); Césad Stephain insin anuas: do faillsiugud a chuirp in so sís (text)
records.Contents: The body of the proto-martyr Stephen was found in Palestine in the early fifth century and one Lucianus composed a narrative of the find and the revelation of the grave of Gamaliel. The Greek text was translated into Latin … and the Irish text is an adaptation of the Latin. It is preceded by an introductory homily, mostly biblical in origin, that stresses the value of christian prophecy. This text is rather more a tract on the verification of relics than an apocryphon.

records.Title: Idolatry and the mission of the apostles
records.Beginning lines: Ídail ó rohairgid-som ro hairged cach olc amlaid
records.Contents: A poem (24st.) on the nature of idolatry (idols are occupied by lying demons), its overthrow, the mission of the apostles, and the regions in which they laboured.
records.info:: 11th century Boyle

records.Title: Origins of the apostles
records.Beginning lines: Petor co treib Iuda áin Aindrias co treib Isacháir
records.Contents: A short poem (4 st.) on the Israelite tribes to which the apostles belonged.

records.Title: Airecc na n-aspal amal ro gairmit dochum n-irse al. The calling of the apostles
records.Beginning lines: Fecht n-oęn do Críst iarna baitsed amail Simeóin oc imdecht fri toeb mara na Galilee
records.Contents: A detailed scholastic description of Christ's calling of the apostles (including St Paul), with canonical and many apocryphal details of their lives, including genealogy, tribal affiliations, and etymological speculations.

records.Title: Páis Aindrias al. Passion of Andrew
records.Beginning lines: Dia mboí ingreim mór forsna Crístaigib isin cathraig dianad ainm Patrais
records.Contents: Much of the text is a debate on the Redemption between Andrew and the pro-consul Aegeates. The Irish appears to be a somewhat condensed and simplified from the Latin original, but how exactly it relates to its source has yet to be established.

records.Title: Páis Partolóin al. Passion of Bartholomew
records.Beginning lines: Luid Partholón apstal do forcetual isin India
records.Contents: This apocryphon derives from the Latin text of the martyrdom of Bartholomew in the so-called Ps-Abdias … perhaps a Frankish compilation of the late sixth century or the seventh. The Irish text is a full translation of the apocryphon, and appears close to it (apart, notably, from a more grisly description of Bartholomew's end), but its exact relationship to its source remains to be clarified.

records.Title: Páis Iacóib apstail al. Passion of James son of Zebedee
records.Beginning lines: Luid Iacop mór mac Zepedei .i. bráthair Eoin apstail
records.Contents: The acta and passion of James as in the so-called Ps-Abdias … perhaps a Frankish compilation of the late sixth century or the seventh.

records.Title: Páis Petair & Póil al. Acts of Peter and Paul
records.Beginning lines: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur &c .i. is conaich in tíí fuilnges martra & ingreim (exordium); Iarsinni trá do-dechaid Pól co Róimh táncatar na hIúdaide chuca & is ed ro ráidset fris (text)
records.Contents: This apocryphon, presented in the form of a homily for the feast of SS Peter and Paul, is an Irish rendering of Ps-Marcellus … a text probably put together in the sixth century or somewhat earlier. There are two recensions, the long and the short, and the Irish text appears close to the first ...

records.Title: Miraculous recovery of the head of St Paul
records.Beginning lines: Dia mbaí Pól apstal a cuibreach ag Ner Segsair isin Róimh
records.Contents: The account of the beheading of St Paul and the recovery of his head, as in the Irish Páis Petair & Póil. This circulated as a separate devotional anecdote, and had a medieval and modern readership.

records.Title: Visio sancti Pauli: Irish translations
records.Beginning lines: Don domnach andso .i. la arna togha le Dia he & is and is mo forbfailtigit aingil & árcaingil (translation I); Vissio Pauli de penis inferni per Dei licentiam .i. aisling Poil do phianaib ifrinn do thoil Dia annsa domnach (translation 2)
records.Contents: Though there are minor differences, the two translations are Irish renderings of recension IV of Visio sancti Pauli, very close to the variant that is Ps-Bedan Homilia C in PL 94, 501-2.

records.Title: Acallam in chuirp & inna hanme al. On the bringing forth of the soul
records.Beginning lines: Domine, quis habitabit in tabernaculo tuo aut quis requiescet in monte sancto tuo?
records.Contents: The text opens with a statement of theme, attributed to Augustine (but not found in his works) … The soul before it leaves the body, at the point of death, is conducted in this context. The Latin, which may be extracted from a Hiberno-Latin original, is simple and direct, but the bombastic Irish text sags under its load of repetitions and useless adjectives.

records.Title: The two deaths
records.Beginning lines: Is coir a fhis tra conid foichlidhi do cach æn in dál derb
records.Contents: An Irish eschaton about the moment of death that conflates an anecdote from verba seniorum (a Latin version of Apophthegmata patrum) with a Latin sermon … known as the 'Three utterances' of the sinful and the sinless souls, and the answers they get from demon and angel. It is not clear whether this is a rendering into Irish of an existing Latin text or an Irish compilation from both sources. The first is more likely, but there appears to be no extant Latin text of this kind.

records.Title: Páis Philip apstail al. Passion of Philip the apostle
records.Beginning lines: Bui Pilip apstal dá fhichit bliadan oc sermóin & oc procept isin Scethia
records.Contents: The apocryphal acta of Philip the apostle, his preaching in Scythia, his torture, mutilation and crucifixion at Hieropolis. The Irish text differs totally from the Acta Philippi …, and evidently draws on other sources.

records.Title: In tenga bithnua al. The ever-new tongue
records.Beginning lines: Airdri domain as treisi cach righ, is airdiu cumhachtai, as foechru cach ndracon (recension 1); Airdrigh in domain as treisi na cach righ cumachtach, & is feochra na gach dreacan (recension 2); Do chruthaigh Dia neamh agus talamh air ttúis (recension 3)
records.Contents: … the voice of the apostle Philip descends, and reveals the mysteries and wonders of the cosmos and the creation of the universe … This eloquent and imaginative text, as much cosmology as apocryphon, has a long, complex, and uncertain prehistory.
records.info:: “probably composed in the ninth century” (Carey);(1) “may safely be ascribed to the tenth or eleventh century, when Old Irish was merging into the Early-Middle Irish of the Book of the Dun [Cow] and the Book of Leinster” (Stokes).

records.Title: Transitus Mariae al. Dormitio Mariae al. Timna Muire
records.Beginning lines: Araili uair & aimsir da raebi naemmáthair in Coimdeg ac sirgabail a hirnaithi (MS i); Post passionem Domini anno XVI uenit Dominus ad Mariam habens uirgam palme in manu sua (MS v)
records.Contents: This is the Irish version of an uninspired apocryphon on the death of the Virgin and her Assumption, soul and body, into heaven … The Irish text is important for the reconstruction of the history of the apocryphon and it appears to be related to the fifth-century Syriac Obsequies of the Virgin. All the versions below (Irish and Latin) belong to the same family.

records.Title: Fís Adomnáin al. Vision of Adomnán
records.Beginning lines: Is uasal & is adamraigthe in Coimdiu na ndúla & is mor & is machdaigthe a nert (MS i); Magnus dominus noster et magna virtus ejus et sapientiae ejus non est numerus. Is uasal & is adamra in Coimdiu (MS ii)
records.Contents: A remarkably colourful and imaginative presentation of the joys of heaven and the fearsome landscape and dreadful punishments of hell, derived from scripture and the apocrypha. It is closely linked to social and ecclesiastical reform, and in effect, a social commentary.

records.Title: Second Vision of Adomnán al. Visio quam uidit Adamnanus
records.Beginning lines: Vae, uae, uae uiris Hiberniae insolae mandat Domini (praefatio); Is ead inso tra forus & dliged anmchairdesa fer nErenn fria lesugud a corp & a n-anmann (text)
records.Contents: This vernacular text (with a brief Latin opening) purports to be the words of an angel of the Lord, spoken in a vision to Adomnán. It belongs to the panic of 1096, induced when (with other chronological conjunctions) the feast of the Decollation of St John fell on a Friday ... In effect, this is a sermon that sets out the penance for their sins, and the prayers, and good works required, with the advocacy of St Patrick, to avert the heavenly fire, pestilence, and calamity that their evil deeds deserve. It then becomes an eloquent homily, citing many Old Testament examples of the efficacy of fasting and prayer. Much of this can be read as clericalist social commentary.
records.info:: "O'Curry writes, fairly enough, that this Vision was written shortly before 1096, a leap year in which the Decollation of John the Baptist fell on a Friday" (Stokes).

records.Title: Airdena inna cóic lá ndéc ria mbráth al. Signs of the fifteen days before Doomsday
records.Beginning lines: Hieronimus in Annalibus Ebreorum clarat de signis quindecim dierum diem iudicii praecedentium (title); Is iat airdena an cóiced lá déc ria mBrath .i. na huili muir & uisci do thógháil do dreich an talman (text)
records.Contents: This legend grew in the Insular lands, and passed to continental European literature, Latin and vernacular. Evidence for its cultivation among the Irish occurs in Poems of Blathmac … Collectanea Ps-Bedae … Saltair na rann … and elsewhere … This rhetorical text is meant rather to inspire fear and horror in a wicked world, to terrify the sinners (listed §30) with images of an angry deity, his struction of the world, and the exquisitely cruel punishments of hell, rather than to convey the mercy of God and the ineffable rewards of the virtuous.

records.Title: Conception and characteristics of Antichrist
records.Beginning lines: Ceithre coimperta caema uaisle cuibde comshaera
records.Contents: A late Middle Irish poem (28 st.) on conceptions, natural and supernatural (st. 1-15) and specifically on the birth, appearance, and powers of Antichrist. He is the incestuous son of a bishop in Jerusalem who lay with his daughter on Good Friday, in church, at the instigation of the devil.
records.info:: (very) late Middle Irish (Ó Cuív)

records.Title: Tale of Antichrist
records.Beginning lines: Ancrist immorro duine eside genfes i nderiud domain
records.Contents: A brief prose outline of the story of Antichrist (173)

records.Title: Bráth ni ba beg a brisim al. On the day of Judgement
records.Beginning lines: Bráth ni ba beg a brisim in lá loiscfes in domun
records.Contents: A poem (24 st.) on the Judgement that draws heavily on the signs of Doomsday (171). Those condemned to hell - red-mouthed judges, the lewd, the crooked, satirists, hard-faced contentious clerics, the envious, the kin-slayers, venal impious superiors, loose women - reflect Irish social concerns. The poet ends with a long prayer ... for divine mercy.

records.Title: The seven journeys of the soul
records.Beginning lines: Cétna laithi tairiraith anma doraig a císu (text A); Anum ó téid as a corp do fidir anba do olc (text B); Secht n-aisdir do-ghní an anuim tar éis an chuirp (text C)
records.Contents: The matter is the ancient belief that the soul spends seven days between death and Judgement … Text A is a poem of 9 st., signed conceitedly by its author, Móel Móedóc mac Diarmata, probably the scholar-bishop of Leinster and abbot of Glenn Uissen (parish of Killeshin, barony of Slievemargy, Queen's Co.) slain at the battle of Cenn Fuait in 917. Text B (9 st.) covers the same ground. Text C is a single short paragraph. These texts, precious evidence for this apocryphon, are without any literary merit.

records.Title: Scéla laí brátha al. Tidings of Doomsday
records.Beginning lines: Dia do bennachad na n-éstidi uli tabrad cach óen díb fó leith a menmain
records.Contents: A vivid homily on the day of Judgement …

records.Title: Scéla na hEsérgi al. Tidings of the Resurrection
records.Beginning lines: Tabrad cách dia airi co ticfa bráth is anside bias esergi dona hulib daínib tri erfuacra meic De
records.Contents: A Middle-Irish sermon on the Resurrection.

records.Title: The seven heavens
records.Beginning lines: Is andsam trá lasin n-anmain iar comgnáis & comattrib na colla cona súan & cona sádaile (MS i); Nuimir na seacht neimhe ata go ruigi in rightheadh ann so (MS iii)
records.Contents: Belief in many heavens (usually seven and sometimes named) is ancient and common in the apocrypha. There are Irish accounts of how the souls of the good and wicked ascend through the seven heavens, notably in Fis Adomnáin …

records.Title: On Christ and the apostles
records.Beginning lines: Críst rocrochad - coem ar chend - i ndorus Ierusalem
records.Contents: A poem (27 st.) based on the apocrypha, principally on the apostles, their appearance, and the manner of their deaths … shares some details with Collectanea Ps-Bedae (33).

records.Title: Molaisse and his sister
records.Beginning lines: Bui siur Mo Lassi Lethglinni oc legud i fail Mo Lasse
records.Contents: The tale of the release of a nun, sister of St Molaisse, from the pains of hell (to which her brother had consigned her for her sins of the flesh), through the assiduous singing of the psalm Beati immaculati in uia (Ps 118) by her monk-lover. This may be a exemplum from an Old-Irish serum.

records.Title: Bishop Cairpre Crom and king Máel Sechnaill
records.Beginning lines: Epscop uasal ro bui a Cluain Meic Nois, Coirpri Crom at-bertha fris
records.Contents: The fire-blackened soul of Máel Sechnaill mac Máel Ruanaid, king of Ireland (r. 846-62) appeared to bishop Cairpre Crom (†904) of Clonmacnoise, as he prayed. The king was in hell for his sins, and for having a negligent and lowly priest-confessor, now in hell too. The bishop and his twelve priests pray and fast for king and confessor ... In a year, both are in heaven. This mercenary clericalist text, using the conventions of afterlife apocrypha, promotes prayers for the dead - the more exalted the cleric, the better the prayers - and, in this matter, seeks for Clonmacnoise the lucrative patronage of the kings of Ireland.
records.Location of the narrative: Máel Sechnaill mac Máel Ruanaid, king of Ireland (r. 846-62); Cairpre Crom (†904) of Clonmacnoise

records.Title: A soul loosed from Hell by prayer
records.Beginning lines: I n-araile domnach do ṡenóir nóémh a ǽnur co faccaidh in duini cirdubh (prose); Bendacht arin n-irnaithe mochin do neoch nod n-aile (verse)
records.Contents: A Middle-Irish poem (8 st.), with a short prose introduction, on the efficacy of prayers for the dead. A pitch-black soul appears to a holy elder on Sunday and asks him to say his requiem and pray for him. The soul grows whiter and whiter and on the third Sunday announces to the elder that he is freed from Hell, and he utters a poem in praise of the prayers for the dead that release souls from infernal torment.

records.Title: Two clerical students and the afterlife
records.Beginning lines: Días macclerech ro batar i commaid oc légund
records.Contents: Two clerical students make a pact that whoever dies first will visit the second to tell him of the land beyond the grave.

records.Title: Wonder tale of Cairpre Crom and the hereafter
records.Beginning lines: Rígféndid cróda aindseirc ro boí i Connachta diarbo comainm Cairpre
records.Contents: When the brigand Cairpre Crom, ancestor of the kings of Uí Maine, awakened, he and his band had left their bodies, and were invisible to all, except to St Brendan of Birr who restored them to their bodies. Cairpre Crom was killed and beheaded shortly after he had made his confession to St Ciarán of Clonmacnoise. Head and body were miraculously rejoined at Clonmacnoise, and St Ciarán raised him from the dead ... This crass tale, promoting the merits of confession and the claims of the churches to royal gifts, is clothed in the conventions of the apocrypha.
records.Location of the narrative: Cairpre Crom, ancestor of the kings of Uí Maine; St Brendan of Birr; St Ciarán of Clonmacnoise

records.Title: St Brendan and the fear of death
records.Contents: St Brendan, leaving his body in the care of the bishop Moinenn, went to hell to liberate his mother. He suceeded and, returning wearily to his body, sighed. Moinenn asked him whether he feared death. He did, he replied eloquently, listing the terrors of the afterlife and the dread of the Judgement.
records.Location of the narrative: St Brendan; bishop Moinenn

records.Title: Old-Irish homily
records.Beginning lines: Ad-tluchammar buidi do Día uilechumachtach do Choimdid nime & talman
records.Contents: A learned if brief homily, directed to a community of religious, on the great benefits a merciful God has conferred on humanity, even on sinners … Here one sees the influence of the apocrypha. The homilist's use of legal language (techt maige & taige, beódil, marbdil) is noteworthy.
records.info:: CODECS: 8th century?

records.Title: Homily on the deadly sins
records.Beginning lines: Conæmdetar sruithe Érenn a ríaglaib na screptræ pennatóir dílgid frepthæ cech pecthæ ó biuc co mmór (MS i); Vana gloria .i. innocbáil uaibhrech us edh ainm in .uii. ndúailchi (MS ii); Luxoria tra hissed ainm in cétna dualchi mharbus anmain duine (MS iii)
records.Contents: This homily is abstracted from the Old-Irish penitential.

records.Title: Gloria Deo principio al. Homily on God
records.Beginning lines: Gloria Deo principio .i. glóir do Dia & do crích cen dered

records.Title: Homily on the Life of the Virgin
records.Beginning lines: TERRA DEDIT FRUCTUM SUUM .i. do-rat in talam a torud
records.Contents: The homily opens with learned exegesis of Terra dedit fructum suum (Ps 67:6) and, drawing on the apocrypha and especially the infancy gospels, presents a detailed and eloquent life and death of the Virgin … There are two versions, the second an abridgement of the first.

records.Title: The Greek king who never smiled
records.Beginning lines: Rí irisech ro boí do Grécaib, mór a thabartche & a dearc
records.Contents: A masterly exemplum from a sermon. The devout and charitable king never smiled since he succeeded his father. This puzzled his bishop and his sons. He did not smile because he feared the sword of vengeance of the Lord that hung over him should he do wrong - a matter he conveyed to all most dramatically.

records.Title: Leabhar Breac Irish-Latin Homiliarium
records.Contents: An invaluable collection of homilies, passions and apocrypha, most of c. AD 1100, but some are clearly later. A full and proper edition of the texts, both Latin and Irish, with a study of the sources, is badly needed.

records.Title: A Latin and Middle-Irish homily on alms giving
records.Beginning lines: Cum ergo facies elimossinam &c. In tan didiu do-géna almsain náchas commaíd
records.Contents: A bilingual homily on almsgiving, based on Mt 6:2 which serves to provide its eleven themes … This is a sharp and learned homily firmly based on a Hiberno-Latin biblical commentary and directed to a religious community who alms do not match its means and, what is worse, are all too public and self-serving. The Latin text is fuller in MS i, the Middle Irish is better transmitted in MS ii which, however, omits nearly all the Latin.

records.Title: Cambridge Iuvencus
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Cassiodorus (485/90-580), Expositio Psalmorum (Commentary on the Psalms)
records.Contents: Fifteen Old-Irish marginalia and an Old-Irish gloss.

records.Title: Isidore of Seville, c. 560-636
records.Contents: Contains Old-Irish glosses dated to AD 655 by Ó Cróinin.

records.Title: Gregory the Great, c. 540-604, Regula pastoralis
records.Contents: Seven Old-Irish glosses.

records.Title: Gregory the Great, c. 540-604, Homiliae in Ezechielem prophetam
records.Contents: An Old-Irish marginal.

records.Title: The Patrician Documents
records.Contents: Contains Old-Irish names and an Irish word.

records.Title: Adomnán (†704), Vita Columbae and its derivatives
records.Beginning lines: Beati nostri patroni Christo sufragante uitam discipturus (praefatio I); Vir erat uitae uenerabilis et beatae memoriae monasteriorum pater et fundator (praefatio 2); De uirtutum miraculis bruis narratio. Vir itaque uenerandus qualia uirtutum (text)
records.Contents: Contains names of Irish persons and places.

records.Title: Vita S. Fintani (Findani)
records.Beginning lines: Cum Deus omnipotens electos suos quos ad vitam ante mundi constitutionem predistinavit aeternam (praefatio); Findanus cum recludi voluisset et instantibus precibus pro hoc Domini voluntatem laboraret (text)
records.Contents: Contains Old-Irish glosses.

records.Title: Vita Tripartita of St Patrick
records.Beginning lines: Populus qui sedebat in tenebris uidit lucem magnam in popul dessid i ndorchaib (praefatio); Pátraic didiu di Bretnaib Ail Cluaide a bunadus. Calpurnd ainm a athar, huasalsacart hé (text)
records.Contents: The Vita Tripartita is the fuller and even more politically adept version of Patrick's Life, based principally on the extended Patriciana in the Book of Armagh … Its date is disputed. Mulchrone puts it in the reign of Finguine Cenn Gécáin, king of Munster (r. 895-902). Thurneysen agreed. Herbet thought it 'completed by the end of the tenth century'. Jackson, on foot of a painstaking linguistic analysis (1986) took it to be a recension of the later part of the tenth century, superficially re-edited in the eleventh. Vita Tripartita appears rather to be a text is Irish and Latin first compiled (mainly from inherited materials), in the mid ninth century, and successively edited and interpolated. An important part of that editing is the progressive translation of much of the Latin into Middle Irish. Thus the strata of the text must be dated from their content rather than from the language.

records.Title: Pátraicc Macha mártai Gaidil glaine ríagla
records.Beginning lines: Pátraicc Macha mártai Gaídil
records.Contents: An Old-Irish poem (13 st.) on St Patrick. It is a brief account of the acta of the glorified Patrick of later hagiography written in the interest of Armagh.
records.info:: The poem was described as Old Irish by Kuno Meyer, but more recently (2104), Caoimhín Ó Dónaill has argued that the poem was composed in the Middle Irish period, probably in the late tenth century. Ó Dónaill gives a linguistic analysis and also points to historical elements that preclude a much earlier date.

records.Title: Bethu Brigte al. Old-Irish Life of Brigit
records.Beginning lines: … miracula uulgata sunt. Laæ n-and i suidiu luid in Broicsech

records.Title: Lives of Saints from the Book of Lismore
records.Beginning lines: Populus qui sedebat in tenibris uidit lucem magnam .i. in pobul deissidh i ndorchaibh atconnairc soilse
records.Contents: Nine Middle-Irish Lives: SS Patrick, Columba, Brigit, Senán, Finnén, Finnchua, Brénainn, Ciarán of Clonmacnoise, Mo Chua of Balla.

records.Title: Martyrology of Tallaght
records.Beginning lines: Uiii kl. Ianuarii. Nauitatas Domini nostri Iesu Christi
records.Contents: A recension of the Martyrologium Hieronymianum that originated perhaps in Péronne or Luxeuil. It was transmitted to Iona where compilation may have begun as early as the time of Adomnán (†704). The enchanced martyrology was passed to Tallaght where the main text received its present form in the first third of the ninth century. There are additions as late as the beginning of the tenth century. There are additions as late as the beginning of the tenth century. Its exact date is disputed ...

records.Title: Martyrology of Óengus al. Féilire Óengusso
records.Beginning lines: Sén a Christ mo labrai a choimmdiu secht nime (prologue); Re síl dálach doíne toíded in rí remain (text); Ón calaind co araili ro fersan ar ṅ-íarair (epilogue)
records.Contents: An Old-Irish verse calendar of the saints by a master poet, writing at Tallaght. The prologue and the epilogue are outstanding. The main text is a foreshortened versified martyrology dependent on matter in its predecessor, the Martyrology of Tallaght and other records. Its exact date is disputed.

records.Title: Martyrology of Gorman al. Féilire Uí Ghormáin
records.Beginning lines: Is he inad i ndernad in felerese Cnoc na nApstol i Ilughmhudh (preface); For kalaind aird Enair fo recht Isu ergna (text)
records.Contents: A vernacular verse calendar compiled in 1166 x 1174, by Maol Mhuire Ó Gormáin, otherwise known as Marianus Gorman, abbot of the Augustinian House of Cnoc na nApstal al. Cnoc na Sengán (SS Peter and Paul, Knock, near the town of Louth).
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Maol Mhuire Ó Gormáin, otherwise known as Marianus Gorman, abbot of the Augustinian House of Cnoc na nApstal

records.Title: Karlsruhe Martyrology
records.Beginning lines: Kl. Feb. sanctae Brigitae
records.Contents: Fragmentary martyology. On the right margin, f. 17 a third scribe adds: bás Muirchatho maicc Maíle Dúin hi Cluain Maccu Nóis á Imda Chiaráin 'The death of Murchad son of Máel Dúin in … St Ciarán Bed'. Murchad, king of Cenél Éogain, deposed in 823, died in religious retirement in Clonmacnoise.

records.Title: Drummond Missal & Martyrology
records.Beginning lines: Octavas Dominicae natiuitatis in hoc die celebratur. Hoc quoque die circumcisio Domini
records.Contents: Old Irish marginalia.

records.Title: Cuimmín of Condere, Poem on the saints of Ireland
records.Beginning lines: Carais Pattraic phuirt Macha
records.Contents: The full text of the poem consists of 37 st. It is attributed to Cuimmín of Condere (†659), bishop of Nóendruim (Nendrum, Co. Down), but this is a devotional work of the twelfth century.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cuimmín of Condere (†659), bishop of Nóendruim (Nendrum, Co. Down)

records.Title: Liber Hymnorum
records.Contents: Irish hymns and glosses.

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - (i) 'Abbas probatus' al. Ymnus Lasriani .i. Molaisse Daminse
The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - (ii) Admuinemmar nóebPátraic al. Oratio Ninini al. Ninian's prayer
records.Beginning lines: Ad-muinemmar nóebPátraic prímapstal hÉrenn
records.Contents: CODECS: Early Irish prayer which invokes St Patrick and was composed, according to the prose attribution, by either Niníne the poet (éces) or Fíacc of Sleibte (Sletty, Co. Laois).
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Niníne the poet (éces) or Fíacc of Sleibte (Sletty, Co. Laois) ??

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - (vi) Ateoch ríg n-amra n-aingel al. Hymnus S. Sanctani al. Sanctán's Hymn
records.Beginning lines: Ateoch ríg n-amra n-aingel uair ised ainm as tressom

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - Atomriug inniu al. Lorica S. Patricii
records.Beginning lines: Atom-riug inniu niurt trén togairm Trínóit
records.info:: 8th century (Binchy).

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - Brigit bé bithmaith al Hymnus S. Ultani in laudem S. Brigidae al. Ultan's Hymn
records.Beginning lines: Brigit bé bithmaith breó órde oíblech

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - (xvi) Génair Pátraic i nNemthur al. Hymnus S. Fiechi in laudem S. Patricii al. Fiacc's Hymn
records.Beginning lines: Génair Pátraic i nNemthur iss ed ad-fét hi scélaib
records.Contents: CODECS: Old Irish hymn attributed to Patrick’s pupil Fíacc of Sléibte (Sletty, Co. Laois).
records.info:: The poem is usually dated to (c.) the eighth century (Grosjean 1950, Binchy 1962), with Grosjean arguing for some ninth-century interpolations. Ó Riain (1997) allows for the possibility that it may have been composed as late as the 9th century.

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - (xvii) In spirut nóeb immun by Máel Ísu Úa Brolchán (†1086)
records.Beginning lines: In Spirut nóeb immun, innunn ocus ocunn
records.info:: 10th or 11th century (Murphy)

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - (xxi) Ní car Brigit buadach bith al. Hymnus S. Broccani in laudem S. Bridigdae al. Broccán's Hymn
records.Beginning lines: Ní car Brigit buadach bith síasair suide éoin i n-ailt

records.Title: The Latin & Irish Hymns in Liber Hymnorum - (xxiv) Sén Dé al. Humnus Colmani moccu Chluasaig
records.Beginning lines: Sén Dé don-fé for-don-té Macc Muire ron-feladar
records.Contents: CODECS: Early Irish verse hymn ascribed to one Colmán mac Uí Cluasaig, lector in Cork. The first divison (ll. 1-38) is regarded as the original poem, which appears to be an adaptation of a Latin prayer. The next divison (ll. 39-47), itself perhaps of mixed origin, serves as an appendix. The final one, almost certainly a later addition, invokes the chief patron saints of Ireland (Brigit, Patrick and Columba).
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Colmán mac Uí Cluasaig, lector in Cork
records.info:: Stokes (1903): “The indications in the hymn itself point to the early part of the ninth century. A superior limit may be found in the mention of Joseph, the husband of Mary, who seems not to be commemorated in Irish liturgies before about 800 A.D. An inferior limit may be found in the treatment of final vowels. As the rhyme shews, there is yet e.g. no confusion between final ‑ae and final ‑a, a confusion well established for the middle of the ninth century by the St Gall glosses on Priscian. The language of the hymn strongly resembles that of the Félire Óengusso, which belongs to about 800 A.D. The most striking departure from Old-Irish usage is the use of anacht (l. 22) for the relative anachte.”

records.Title: Fragmentum Placentinum
records.Contents: A single sheet of parchment, being a fragment of a sacramentary (with two rubrics in Old Irish), now apparently lost, and containing parts of three masses headed 'Missae cotidianae' and 'Ordo missae sanctae Mariae'.

records.Title: Vernacular Tract on the Canonical Hours
records.Beginning lines: Cid ara ndéntar celebrad isna tráthaib sech na tráthaib ele (prose); Tánic teirt dénam tarbai co rrísam in rígadbai (verse)
records.Contents: A lengthy tract on the hours in the form of a later prose introduction (MS ii only) and an earlier poem (41 st.). The short prose tract in MS iii, identical in incipit with the prose in MS ii, may be an extract from the text. The verse may belong to the early eleventh century, the prose to the early twelfth. In MS ii this tract is followed by a Latin tract on the liturgy. This is a list of the important events, in the Old Testament and the New that happened at each of the hours.

records.Title: Vernacular Tract on the Consecration of a Church
records.Beginning lines: Incipit coisecrad eclasi indso. Líne andso dorigensat hécnaide eolcha um cháirechtair toraind n-eclaisi
records.Contents: A remarkably detailed tract on the consecration of a church that belongs to the peroid before the beginning of the Hildebrandine reform in Ireland. It refers again and again to the libar escuip, the Latin pontifical, and the text appears to be a skilled translation of a Latin original.
records.info:: Stokes: “the composition of the tractate may safely be placed in the eleventh, when Old-Irish was passing into Early-Middle-Irish”.

records.Title: Vernacular Tract on the Mass
records.Beginning lines: De figuris et spiritualibus sensibus oblationis sacrificii ordinis. Figuir ta inchollaigthi Crist o chompert coa chesad

records.Title: Vernacular Tract on the Liturgical Colours
records.Beginning lines: Ceist, cia lasa tucait na datha éxamla isin cochull n-oiffrind hi tús?
records.Contents: A tract on the colours of the mass vestments - yellow, blue, white, green, brown, red, black and purple - their purported Mosaic origin, and their mystical and moral symbolism.

records.Title: Middle Irish Verse Ordinal
Turin Irish liturgical texts
Milan Commentary on the Psalms
records.Beginning lines: Oculos suos statuerunt. Merito in terra oculos declinant
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses

records.Title: Second Epistle of Peter (1-2.13)
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Charisius, Ars grammatica; Servius, De centum metris
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses on f. 33

records.Title: Milan Glossary fragment

records.Title: Cellán of Péronne (†706) - Epistula ad Aldhelmum
records.Beginning lines: Domino lectricibus ditato studiis mellifluisque ornato lucubratiunculis
records.Contents: Cellán of Péronne (†706) - A scathing and scintillating letter from Cellán, writing from Picardy, to Aldhelm (c. 639-709), who had unwisely chosen to cross swords with his former mentors, the Irish literati. It is elegantly parodic of Aldhelm's works … It impugns his Latinity and style, and conveys subtly and stylishly that Aldhelm is mollis. The bilingual puns (Latin/Old Irish) at the end of the greeting, in tota et tuta trinitate, reveal this more explicitly, if cryptically. Aldhelm, educated by the Irishman Máeldub at Malmesbury and probably at Iona, knew Irish enough to suffer the barbs. The letter shows how close, how gossipy, how acrimonious, was the scholarly elite in Ireland, England and Francia.
records.info:: Manuscript, Oxford, Magdalen College Lib., 127, f. 79v no date given.

records.Title: Sedulis Scottus (fl. 840-860): Munich Glossary al. Liber Glossarum al. Glossarium Salmonis

records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Text and glosses in the same hand.

records.Title: Donatus Ortigraphus, Ars Grammatica

records.Title: Tracts on Latin declension, in the vernacular or glossed in the vernacular
records.Beginning lines: 1) Prima declinacio quot literas terminales habet? 2) Cúig coitchind tiaghuid in es
records.Contents: Latin Grammatical Tracts - The first text is a Latin prose text, with some 1100 glosses in the vernacular. The second text, a poem of 60 st. in Middle Irish and possibly dating to the eleventh century, treats of the gender and declension of Latin nouns, drawing directly on Priscian, V-VII. It shows that the scientific study of Latin grammar continued in Ireland into the eleventh century and later.

records.Contents: Hiberno-Latin writers and texts - Laicend mac Baíth Bannaig (†661), Dublin, RIA 23 P16 '… with abundant interlinear glosses in late Old Irish/Middle Irish of c. AD 1000'

records.Title: De locis sanctis
records.Beginning lines: Arculfus sanctus episcopus gente Gallus diuersorum longe remotorum peritus
records.Contents: Hiberno-Latin writers and texts - Adomnán of Iona (†704). There's single word glosses in some of the manuscripts.

records.Title: Scholia on the Bucolica and Georgica of Vergil
records.Contents: Hiberno-Latin writers and texts - Adomnán of Iona (†704). These Virgil scholia, two series of extracts from Iunius Philargyrius with Old-Irish glosses and an anonymous Georgicorum brevis expositio with many additions, are associated with the school of Iona.  There is a direct reference in the text to Adomnán: 'De Mevio uero nihil reperi, ut Adamnanus ait'. He may have been one of the teacher-compilers of these texts.

records.Title: Prouerbia Grecorum
records.Beginning lines: Incipiunt Prouerbia Grecorum. Hec uero de Grecorum prudentia quasi lapides preciosas multicolores (praef.); Sapiens sapientem adiuuat stultus stulti sententiam exornat (text)
records.Contents: Hiberno-Latin writers and texts - Early Anonymous Medieval Latin Texts. It has links with the Hibernensis (585) and with Sedulius Scottus' Collectaneum miscellaneum (436) in which collection it is preserved.  Old Irish glosses

records.Title: Old-Irish Penitential
records.Beginning lines: Incipit de luxoria. Luxoria tra hissed ainm inna dualcha tanaisi marbas anmain duini
records.Contents: The text of the Old-Irish Penitential, the lone vernacular representatives of the genre, is acephalous in MS I; MSS ii-iv contain a homily based on the Penitential that largely supplies that defect.

records.Title: Old-Irish Table of Penitential Commutations
records.Beginning lines: Arra tessairgne anma a iffurn .i. coic pater
records.Contents: Arr(a)e … In religious terms, it means the replacement of penance by a shorter and more severe discipline and, more generally, the substition of one religious duty for another … The Old-Irish texts lists about 35 such commutations.

records.Title: Cáin Adomnán al. Law of Adomnán
records.Beginning lines: Cóic amsira ria ngein Críst .i. ó Ádam co dílinn (praefatio); Iss ead inso forus cána Adomnáin for hÉirinn & Albain: soíre ecalsi Dé cona muintir (text §34)
records.Contents: CODECS: Old Irish legal-ecclesiastical text originating in a law which was promulgated at the 697 Synod of Birr (Co. Offaly) and was apparently drafted by Adomnán, abbot of Iona. The law sought to exempt women, children, clergy and other non-combatants from combat in warfare.

records.Title: Ríaguil Phátraic al. Rule of Patrick
records.Beginning lines: Fortá anmanda fer nÉrenn a timna Pátraic. Prímepscop cecha túaithe accu fri hoirned a n-óessa gráid fri coisecrad a n-eclas
records.Contents: An important vernacular canon-law text on the duties of bishops and priests, pastoral care, the administration of the sacraments, the maintenance of the clergy, and the rules governing the income of the church from the faithful. This text is not 'Cáin Phátraic'.
records.info:: “The ascription to St Patrick is manifestly false, but taken with the Rule’s appeal to the ‘Testament of Patrick’ (timna Pátraic) and assertion of an authority extending to all Ireland, it points to Armagh as its place of composition” Westley Follett,  Céli Dé in Ireland  (2006): 142–143.

records.Title: Cáin Domnaig
records.Beginning lines: Soíre Domnaig ó tráth espartai Dia Sathairn co fuine maitne Die Luain
records.Contents: An Old-Irish sabbatarian tract, not later than the first half of the eighth century and very probably earlier, drafted in the technical language of Irish vernacular law, and therefore by a professional clerical jurist. It sets out the rules for the observance of Sunday, what is permitted and forbidden, the sanctions and fines for breaking the law, and the legal provisions and conditions attending their application ... There is a single citation in the glosses to the vernacular law tract Gúbretha Caratniad.

records.Title: Epistil Ísu
records.Beginning lines: Intinscana epistil int Slánícceda ar Coimded-ne Ísu Críst di laithiu domnaig
records.Contents: A letter, purporting to have fallen from heaven, ordering, under threat of dire penalties, the strict observance of Sunday. Of unknown provenance, the first evidence for its existence belong to the late sixth century. It may have reached Ireland by the ninth, or perhaps earlier. The metrical version is much later than the prose.

records.Title: Monastery of Tallaght al. Tallaght Memoir
records.Beginning lines: Athlaoch bói hi comaidecht meic bethad. As-bert nicon feddur cid fil do sírgabail na bíaide
records.Contents: This Old-Irish text … is an important collection of memoranda on the religious teachings of the leading figures among the Céli Dé, Mael Ruain of Tallaght (†792) and Mael Díthruib of Terryglass (†841) … Most of the text was written in the lifetime of Mael Díthruib.
records.Location of the narrative: Mael Ruain of Tallaght (†792); Mael Díthruib of Terryglass (†841)

records.Title: Rule of the Céli Dé
records.Beginning lines: Biait prointige & Magnificat fair & Ego uero & reliqua hi sessam chanar (MS i); Bíaid phrainntighe na sesamh do candaois sa phrointhigh namá & gabháil éccnairce na marbh na sesamh beos (MS ii)
records.Contents: A composite text containing materials of different dates and, as Gwynn … supposed, it is based on a Middle-Irish version of the Tallaght Memoir al. Monastery of Tallaght … but the textual problems that attend the document remain unresolved.
records.info:: “originally written perhaps in the ninth century” (Gwynn)

records.Title: Rules of Dochutu al. Metrical Rule of the Céli Dé
records.Beginning lines: Is é ascnam na flatha is uasal in bríg serc Dé ón uli anmain ó chridi ó gním
records.Contents: This text is connected neither with St Carthach al. Mochutu of Rathen and Lismore nor with Fothud na Canóine (†819). It is the work of Dochutu (†838), bishop and anchorite of Slane. It prescribes for bishops … abbots … priests … confessors, monks, céli Dé, clerifical students, the refectory, fasting, diet; kings ... husbandmen ... It is a clericalist prescription for the good ordering of a christian society. A critical edition is required.

records.Title: Óentu Máel Ruain
records.Contents: The evidence for a 'Union of Mael Ruain' (i.e. an association of churches by rule) is a short list of thirteen names entitled Lucht oentad Mael Ruain … This is followed by the same in verse in exactly the same order, attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), king of Munster ... and a poem, inc. 'Cethrur ar ḟichet nosfail' (12st., the last a late addition) al. Oentu Fedelmid, listing 24 clerics and, by implication, their churches ... Both are retrospective documents that seek to attach certain Munster churches to the distinguished reputation of Tallaght and the Céli Dé. ˙
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), king of Munster (verse attributed)
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Cuilennáin (+908)
records.info:: “unlikely to be earlier than the second half of the ninth century” Westley Follett Céli Dé in Ireland  (2006): 137

records.Title: Rule ascribed to St Ailbe
records.Roman dates: "Old Irish" with few "Middle Irish forms" - Joseph O'Neill
records.Beginning lines: Apair dam fri mac Sáráin is trom int aire gebes
records.Contents: This Old-Irish verse text (56 st.) is not the rule of St Ailbe of Emly. It is in the form of advice to Éogan mac Sáráin, said to be of Cluain Cóeláin (Martyrology of Donegal, 15 March) but the martyrology entry is dependent on the poem. Cluain  Cóeláin may perhaps be Clonkeelan, parish of Drummully, barony of Dartree, Co. Monaghan, but this is uncertain. The poem urges the monastic virtues ... The monastery shall have a just and fair abbot ...
records.Location of the narrative: Éogan mac Sáráin
records.Characters in the narrative: Cluain Cóeláin, perhaps Clonkeelan, parish of Drummully, barony of Dartree, Co. Monaghan????
records.info:: “The language of the Rule is Old Irish, though it contains a few Middle-Irish forms, such as gebes v. 1, geba v. 10, and the monosyllabic cóir v. 31 a, which are all fixed by the rhyme; the Middle-Irish plural mugada in 39 a is such a late form that it seems to point to some corruption in the text” OʼNeill, Joseph, “The rule of Ailbe of Emly”, Ériu 3 (1907) 93

records.Title: Metrical Rule ascribed to St Comgall al. Rule of the Lord
records.Beginning lines: Comae ríaguil in Choimded is and ní fogbae báegul
records.Contents: Only MS ii has the ascription, in the hand of Míchél Ó Cléirigh, to St Comgall of Bangor. The language is Old Irish but much later than Comgall with whom it has no evident connection. This is not a monastic rule but a poem (29 st.) of pious exhortation to monastic virtue as understood in early medieval Irish religious communities ...

records.Title: Rule ascribed to St Colum Cille (Columba)
records.Beginning lines: Bith i nn-uathad i lluc fo leith i fail prímchathrach
records.Contents: A text of the eighth or ninth centuries. In no sense a monastic rule, it contains sententious statements on personal sanctification for one who is 'alone in a place apart, near a major church', close to, but not of, the community - very likely a senior cleric (or a small group of such persons) in retirement from high office ...

records.Title: Rule ascribed to St Ciarán
records.Beginning lines: Ma asbera a dheoraidh armpá heólach a riaghlaibh
records.Contents: A short Old-Irish metrical rule (16 st.) or rather an instruction to monks. Only its title attaches it to St Ciarán. The text of the codex unicus is defective. The poem (16 st.) is in the form of an address, by a confessor to an abbot or a monk on monastic discipline, and especially on keeping holy for the Sabbath.

records.Title: Ríagal na Manach Líáth al. Metrical Rule of the Grey Monks
records.Beginning lines: Corann liath lethet baisi rolas oc losgud drisi
records.Contents: Not a rule, but a sarcastic poem (10st.) by a sardonic and lazy monk … He is acerbic about those in orders - they go to hell, while the unordained go to paradise. He is a misogynist: Adam, Samson and Solomon were deluded by women as will anyone who listens to them. But he likes the monastic life of ease.

records.Title: Rule of Cormac
records.Beginning lines: Sámud búan bríathar-ísel fó húar mad mé foglésed
records.Contents: An Old-Irish religious poem (14st.), in no sense a rule, attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin (+908), king-bishop of Cashel. It opens qith the pleasant singing of the congregation and the religious sentiments are monkish. But the poet, who proposes to 'sidestep kings, and renouce wine and meat' and 'forget the wretched world', is an outsider, and no monk.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cormac mac Cuilennáin (+908), king-bishop of Cashel

records.Title: Southampton Psalter
records.Contents: A complete Gallican psalter, with numerous interlinear glosses in Irish and Latin, one of the finest pre-Invasion illuminated Irish manuscripts;
records.info:: Manuscript Cambridge, St John's College, C. 9 olim 59 al … Origin Ireland, perhaps Armagh; provenance the priory of St Martin, Dover, and donated St John College in 1635.

records.Title: Psalter of St Caimín
records.Contents: A psalter fragment containing 13 of the 22 eight-verse sections of Ps 118, with a highly complex and well organised scholarly mariginal and interlinear commentary and some glosses in Irish. Gallicanum text, with an abbreviated Hebraicum on the top margin. Unpublished as a whole.
records.info:: Dublin, Univ College Lib., OFM, A 1 al. Psaltar of St Caimín; s. xi (ex)/xii (in) … origin Iniscaltra (Inis Celtra), on SW shore of Lough Derg or (according to Henry & Marsh-Micheli) possibly Clonmacnoise; provenance the learned family of Meic Bruaidheadha (Flann and Bernard) of Tearmann Caimín on Iniscaltra; brought to Donegal by Míchél Ó Cléirigh, and to Louvain in 1643.

records.Title: Vatican Psalter
records.Contents: A Gallican Psalter, without Jerome's diacriticals, with characteristic Irish spellings, and probably not meant for liturgical use. It is very fragmentary … Unpublished and little studied.
records.info:: Manuscript Rome BAV lat. 12910 al, Vatican Psalter … origin Ireland; provenance Chiesa di S. Angelo in Spata in Viterbo, according to a modern pencilled note on a fly-leaf.

records.Title: Harley Gospels
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Gospels of Mael Brigte
records.Contents: CODECS: Twelfth-century Irish gospelbook written at Armagh by Máel Brigte úa Máel Úanaig, including an interlinear and marginal commentary on parts of the Gospels (glosses and some notes), with four Irish poems and a number of single-quatrain verses, a scribal colophon, and two portraits of Evangelist symbols (Mark and Luke).
records.Location of the narrative: Armagh

records.Title: Corpus Gospels
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish glosses.
records.Location of the narrative: Bangor or Armagh

records.Title: Drummond Missal & Martyrology
records.Contents: Contains Old Irish entries.
records.Location of the narrative: Glendalough

records.Title: Lambeth Commentary
records.Beginning lines: Securitas nascitur et in amore celestium gaudiorum
records.Contents: Commentary on the Sermon on the Mount, a part of an earlier work, in Latin and Irish, drawing on Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose and Gregory the Great, copied in the tenth century …

records.Title: Calcidius' Timaeus and Extracts of Eriugena's Periphyseon
records.Beginning lines: uereor tamen ne .i. nad necma ut sunt uagi palantesque (Calcidius glosses)
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Boethius, De institutione arithmetica: Leiden Fragment
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses.

records.Title: Boethius, De institutione arithmetica: Dublin Fragment
records.Contents: An Old Irish note.

records.Title: Boethius, De consolatione philosophiae, Verba Iohannis Scoti, Metrica
records.Contents: A teaching collection … Manuscript Florence, Bib. Medicea Laurenziana, Pluteus 79.19 … origin perhaps Glendalough …. Boethius, De consolatione, full text with abundant glosses, about 5000 in Latin and 28 Irish glosses (ff. 4ri to the end).
records.Location of the narrative: Glendalough ?

records.Title: Clemens Scottus, Ars grammatica; De abaco
records.Contents: Old Irish notes
records.Location of the narrative: Glendalough

records.Title: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job
records.Contents: Manuscript Oxford, Bodleian Lib., Laud Misc 460 … Contents: … with one obscure gloss and many marginalia in Irish ...
records.Location of the narrative: Armagh

records.Title: Annals of Ulster al. Annála Uladh
records.Beginning lines: … die dominica hi Seimniu occisus est o Crimtund Nia Nar uel a Gallis ut alii dicunt
records.Contents: The text of these annals down to c. AD740 is based on a chronicle compiled mainly in Iona. Contemporary recording begins about the middle of the sixth century. A copy of the Iona annals passed to Ireland c. AD 740 but there is no scholarly consensus about what happened next. It is likely that annal-writing continued in Brega, with the addition of some records from Armagh, down to 911. From AD1014, the Annals of Ulster and the Annals of Loch Cé have a common core, mostly derived from Armagh; in the second half of the twelfth century, from annals compiled mostly at Derry; and from c 1190 to 1220, particularly from Derry. After about 1225 the records ... become scant ... The early-medieval portion is remarkable for the fidelity with which its scribes preserve Old-Irish, even archaic forms, but this conservatism does not extend to chronology.

records.Title: Annals of Tigernach
records.Contents: An acephalous, lacunose, and imperfect text of a representative of the Clonmacnoise group of annals that preserves historical annals for AD 489-766. 974-1003, 1018-1178 (and breaks off  in mid-entry).

records.Title: Chronicon Scottorum al. Chonicum Scottorum
records.Contents: A text of the Clonmacnoise group of annals, containing annals from AM 1599 to AD 1135. There is a lacuna, AD 723-804 (part). Scribe Dubhaltach Mac Fir Bhisigh, imitating the writing of his exemplar. Further annals, of unknown provenance, occupying the four last pages and in two different hands, refer to the years 1141-50 ... These are in the ordinary hand of Mac Fir Bhisigh and that of his unidenfitied amanuensis.

records.Title: Annals of Roscrea
records.Contents: This is a text made by Brendan O'Connor, a scribe, copying in haste and incompletely, from a mutilated exemplar, a Liber annalium (given to him by Fínghin Mac Carthaigh al. Florenance MacCarthy) and called 'Historia D. Cantwelig'. The present title is that of O'Connor and there is nothing in the text to suggest a Roscrea origin ... This is a fragmentary series of annals from the Flood to AD995 with lacunae ... and gaps ...

records.Title: Annals of Inisfallen
records.Contents: The transmission of these annals is uncertain. Mac Niocaill, suggests that while the earliest stratum may be associated with Emly, the annals may have been continued at Tomgraney, transcribed at Killahoe after the mid eleventh century, and continued at Lismore from about the year 1119. The MS passed to a West-Munster monastery, most likely Inisfallen, in 1130x1159. There are lacunae ... That much of the later part of these annals is in phonetic spellings lends them an additional linguistic interest ... A translation of portion of these annals (1173 [=1174] to 1281) by Dubhaltach Mór Mac Fir Bhisigh, made for Ware, occurs in London, BL., Additional 4799 ...

records.Title: Egerton Annals al. Mionannála
records.Beginning lines: … lá dana do Shuibhne Mhenn ina ghilla óg ina thig féin ro buí acá rád re a mhnaí
records.Contents: Acephalous and imperfect extracts from annals, AD 615 to 710, interspersed with sagas that occur elsewhere in varying recensions … These annals are related to Fragmentary Annals of Ireland and both texts may utlimately derive, at least in part, from annals kept at the monastery of Cloneagh.

records.Title: Annals from the Book of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Incipit do fhlaithesaib & amseraib hErend iar cretim. Loegaire mac Néill .xxx. Annos regnum Hiberniae post aduentum Patricii tenuit
records.Contents: Brief annals, organised by reigns of kings of Ireland, without other chronological criteria, from the reign of the supposed fifth-cenutry Lóegaire mac Néill to the accession of Ruaidrí Ó Conchobair, king of Ireland, in 1166. It contains a noable entry on the synod of Kells-Mellifont: 'Senad Cenannsa ubi Iohannes Cardinalis praesidens interfuit. Millessimo c. mo. l. mo secundo celebratum fuit istud nobile concilium'. Later hands bring the text down to the death of Ruaidrí Ó Conchobair in Cong in 1189.

records.Title: Short Annals from Armagh province al. Annála Gearra as proibhinse Ard Macha
records.Beginning lines: Laogaire mac Neill iar feiss Teamra annis .uii. & mensibus .uii. & diebus .uii. Uixit
records.Contents: Brief annals, preceded by a saga extract on the reign of Lóegaire … from the early ninth century to AD 1134… Instead he dated events by the interval of years between them, but dates can usually be established from other sources. The work was porbably compiled at Armagh. It has an entry on the death of Edward the Confessor (5 January 1066) and the battles of Stamford Bridge (25 September 1066) and Hastings (14 October 1066).

records.Title: Annals of Ireland (1170-1201)
records.Contents: Short unpublished annals for the peroid 1170-1201.

records.Title: Dominican Chronicle of Trim ???
records.Contents: Unpublished annals, AD 432-1260, entries for 33 years, of which 25 are virtually identical with the Annals of Multyfarnham (733)

records.Title: Gilla Mo Dutu Ó Casaide - Verse Banshenchas al. Ádam óenathair na ndóene
records.Beginning lines: Ádam óenathair na ndóene duine ro delb Dia na ndám
records.Contents: The verse Banshenchas was composed at the church of Devenish in 1147 by Gilla Mo Dutu Ó Caiside who came from the church of Ardbracken, Co. Meath. It treats the women of the Old Testament §§1-11, those of pagan Irish pre-history (§§12-101), and those of the historical peroid to c. AD1030 (§§102-80). His principal concern is the women associated with those kings accounted kings of Ireland. It appears that the scribe of MS i dropped the names that brought the poem down to Ó Casaide's own time ... he draws on historical material no longer extant.

records.Title: Prose Banshenchas
records.Beginning lines: Eua bean Ádaim is í side céd-bean in beatha: .l. mac & .l. ingean aici fri hÁdam
records.Contents: The Prose Banshenchas derives from the Metrical Banshenchas, a long poem written in 1147 by Gilla Mo Dutu Ó Casaide of the church of Devenish on Lough Erne. However, the material is greatly elaborated and extended in the various versions of this prose recension. The text is an invaluable if somewhat neglected source for Irish royal and aristocratic marriages, and thus for social and political history, especially in the elventh and twelfth centuries.

records.Title: Progeny of Cianóc (Banshenchas)
records.Beginning lines: Cianócc inghean Chíocharáin ben éinfhfir 'na fhír pósta (verse); Brugaid cétach comrumach baí isin leth iartharaig do Connachtaib (prose)
records.Contents: A narrative in prose and verse (17st.) about the offspring of Cianóc, wife of Crechán mac Angaile, born through the intercession of St Cairell. She is mother of (i) Osnat, whose daughter Bébinn, was wife of Cennétig and mother of Brian Bóraime, king of Ireland, and of seven of his brothers; and wife of Máel Sechnaill, king of Corcu Modruad and mother of his sons Lochlann (†1015)(a quo Uí Lochlainn) and Conchobar †1003 (a quo Uí Chonchobair); and (ii) Creise, who married Tadc Mór (†956), mac Cathail (†925) and thus was ancestress of the Uí Chonchobair kings of Connacht, Uí Mael Ruanaid and Ui Thaidc in Teglaig. This is an explicit attempt to link important dynasties of Munster and Connacht to the Ui Briain dynasty, through matrilateral kinship.
records.Location of the narrative: offspring of Cianóc, wife of Crechán mac Angaile; Munster dynasties

records.Title: Turin, Biblioteca nazionale, F. IV. 1, fasc. 7 (Cummian on Mark)

records.Title: Karlsruhe Bede al. Reichenau Bede
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses

records.Title: Karlsruhe Augustine
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses

records.Title: Carinthia Kloster S. Pauli, Stiftsbibliothek., 26b/1 (Codex Sancti Pauli)
records.Contents: Five Old Irish poems: i) Adgúisiu fid nallabrach, ii) Messe ocus Pangur Bán, iii) M'airiuclán hi Tuaim Inbir, iv) Is én immoniada sás, v) Aed oll fri andud nane

records.Title: Vienna Bede
records.Contents: Interlinear and marginal notes and glosses - Old Irish

records.Title: Berline Augustine
records.Contents: Old Irish glosses

records.Title: Amra Coluim Chille
records.Beginning lines: Ní díscéoil dúe Néill ní uchtot óenmaige
records.Contents: There are serious difficulties in dating this text, a panegyric of Columba al. Colum Cille composed shortly after his death (but, evidently with much later reworking), modelled on Latin panegyric and written in a vernacular Kunstprosa.
records.Location of the narrative: Colum Cille

records.Title: Verse Fragments of Colmán mac Léníni
