records.Beginning lines: (1) Luin oc elaib ungi oc dírnaib; (2) Dún maic Daim doë ós roí; (3a) Ó ba maic cléib caindlech ser; (3b) Indlith dún drúb iar már; (4) Ní séim anim i n-anmib áne; (5) Ní fordiuchtror for duain indlis; (6) Ropo thánaise triuin crapscuil
records.Contents: Seven fragments of the verse of Colmán mac Léníne, poet and later a monastic founder, who ided c. AD 602 … The verse is in polished stanzaic form, based on syllable count, with rhyme and binding alliteration. The implication of the date, proposed by Thurneysen ... and Carney ... is that the written transmission of vernacular poetry goes back to the sixth century.
records.Location of the narrative: Colmán mac Léníne

records.Title: Leinster Genealogical Poems
records.Beginning lines: (1) Móen óen ó ba nóed; (2) Nuadu Necht ní dámair anfhlaith; (3) Énna, Labraid luad cáich; (4) Ní dír dermait dála cach ríg rómdae; (5) Dind Ríg ruad tuaim tenbad; (6) Lug scéith scál find; (7) Mál ad-rualaid iathu marb; (8) Baeth buide bánán dron; (9) Find, Taulcha; (10) Tri meic Ruaid ruirig flaind; (11) Huait a meic húi Moguirni; (12) A Eochaid Airtt Fuath ara-falnathar iath aneoil; (13) Níbu chroíb chrínfedo
records.Contents: This is the earliest Leinster dynastic verse, but of uncertain date. Carney argued that some of the poems belong to the pagan peroid, in his terms before AD 450. Others place them much later. They probably belong to the middle years of the seventh century. Similar verse occurs elsewhere in the genealogies.

records.Title: Apgitir chrábaid of Colmán mac Béognai al. Colmán Elo moccu Sailni (†611)
records.Beginning lines: Ires co ngním, accobar co feidli, féthamle co lléri, castót co n-umli
records.Contents: A tract on monastic piety written c. 600, with great skill and confidence, by Colmán macc Béognai, an alumnus of Iona. Its style is a vernacular form of Kunstprosa, evidently based on such Latin ecclesiastical models as Jerome and Augustine and so elegant and regular in structure that one can confidently eliminate submerged glosses and other faults of transmission.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Colmán mac Béognai al. Colmán Elo moccu Sailni (†611)
records.info:: a mixture of Old Irish and early Middle Irish forms (Hull)

records.Title: Cambrai Homily
records.Beginning lines: Si quis uult post me uenire &c. inscne in so as-ber ar féda IHu fri cach n-oein
records.Contents: An exegetically complex homily, in a code-switching mix of Latin and Early Old Irish, addressed to a learned monastic clerical audience.

records.Title: The caldron of poesy
records.Beginning lines: Moí Coire coir Goiriath gor rond-n-ír Día dom a dúile ndemrib
records.Contents: A text on the philosophy of knowledge, poetic art and language, composed in two different registers of Old Irish. Three caldrons in three different positions represent the different levels of knowledge and art. This understanding of learning is ultimately a borrowing from Classical antiquity.
records.info:: Two different registers of Old Irish

records.Title: Auraicept na nÉces
records.Roman dates: s. vii/viii, but reworked for centuries
records.Beginning lines: As-berat trá augtair na nGoídel combad sí tucait airic in bérla Féne gním n-ingnad n-indligthech for-cháemnacair isin domun
records.Contents: An Old-Irish historicist tract on the foundation of Irish culture - the invention of the Irish language, its alphabet, its letters, and its grammar and the creation of ogam - that became a staple textbook of the medieval schools and that accumulated a vast corpus of gloss and commentary, making it a handbook on grammar, poetics, language, and literature for poets and scholars and their schools. It is deeply indebted to the Irish study of Latin grammar ...
records.info:: The core of the text has been dated to “a fairly early stage of the Old Irish period” (Ahlqvist)

records.Title: In Lebor Ollamon
records.Beginning lines: Incipit do senchaidecht filed a pupall Patraic & bendachais a ngina arna heipridis gai a ndlighiodh senchusa conad ann is-bertatat indso sios. Incipit Lebar Ollamon
records.Contents: A historicist tract on the invention of writing - Hebrew, Syriac, Egyptian, Greek, Latin and Irish (alphabetic and ogam) - and its inventors; the origin of the seventy-two languages of humanity, corresponding to the purported number of nations, and speculations about their relationships. It lists legendary authors, judges and poets, just and truthful because of precocious divine intervention.

records.Title: In Lebor Ogaim
records.Beginning lines: Caide loc & aimsir & persu & fath airic in ogaim? Ní ansa. Loc do Hibernia insola quam nos Scoti habitamus. I n-aimsir Brese meic Elathan rig Erenn do-frith
records.Contents: Here the invention of ogam writing is attributed to the god, Ogma mac Elathan, described as ro-eolach a mbérla & a filidecht 'very learned in language and poetry', thus giving the art of writing a divine origin and high status to the scholars and poets who practised it. The work ... a prescribed text of the medieval schools, is principally occupied with speculations on the origin of ogam and listings of its various categories.
records.Location of the narrative: Ogma mac Elathan

records.Title: The Middle Irish Metrical Tracts al. Mittelirische Verslehren - Text 1
records.Beginning lines: Incipit de corus bard cona bardni .i. cetharda condegar co hæs nuath do airic (Text 1)
records.Contents: The metrical tracts are handbooks of metrics for use in the schools where poets were trained … The first, from the late ninth to tenth centuries, originally contained 44 metrical types … The second, a metrical tract with much illustrative material, also sets out the curriculum of the student poet. It is extant in a much expanded and later form, its core being tenth century. The third, apparently from a different school and perhaps redacted in the mid eleventh century ... The fourth is a poem of 14 st., itself an exemplification of the twelve most important metres of his own day by Cellach Ua Ruanada (+1079), an eminent poet. These tracts cite metrical examples as early as the end of the sixth century and as late as contemporary practice at or near the time of compilation. and are evidence of a long and copious written record.

records.Title: The Middle Irish Metrical Tracts al. Mittelirische Verslehren - Text 2
records.Beginning lines: Ni fili nad fiasar .ui. hernaili deg na filideachta co n-aisneis anma athar Athairne (Text 2)
records.Contents: The metrical tracts are handbooks of metrics for use in the schools where poets were trained … The first, from the late ninth to tenth centuries, originally contained 44 metrical types … The second, a metrical tract with much illustrative material, also sets out the curriculum of the student poet. It is extant in a much expanded and later form, its core being tenth century. The third, apparently from a different school and perhaps redacted in the mid eleventh century ... The fourth is a poem of 14 st., itself an exemplification of the twelve most important metres of his own day by Cellach Ua Ruanada (†1079), an eminent poet. These tracts cite metrical examples as early as the end of the sixth century and as late as contemporary practice at or near the time of compilation. and are evidence of a long and copious written record.

records.Title: The Middle Irish Metrical Tracts al. Mittelirische Verslehren - Text 3
records.Beginning lines: Incipit dona haistib. do aistib in aircetail i coitchinn indso. Cia lin na n-aisti didu? (Text 3)
records.Contents: The metrical tracts are handbooks of metrics for use in the schools where poets were trained … The first, from the late ninth to tenth centuries, originally contained 44 metrical types … The second, a metrical tract with much illustrative material, also sets out the curriculum of the student poet. It is extant in a much expanded and later form, its core being tenth century. The third, apparently from a different school and perhaps redacted in the mid eleventh century ... The fourth is a poem of 14 st., itself an exemplification of the twelve most important metres of his own day by Cellach Ua Ruanada († 1079), an eminent poet. These tracts cite metrical examples as early as the end of the sixth century and as late as contemporary practice at or near the time of compilation. and are evidence of a long and copious written record.

records.Title: The Middle Irish Metrical Tracts al. Mittelirische Verslehren - Text 4
records.Beginning lines: Sluindfet duib dagaisti in dana (Text 4)
records.Contents: The metrical tracts are handbooks of metrics for use in the schools where poets were trained … The first, from the late ninth to tenth centuries, originally contained 44 metrical types … The second, a metrical tract with much illustrative material, also sets out the curriculum of the student poet. It is extant in a much expanded and later form, its core being tenth century. The third, apparently from a different school and perhaps redacted in the mid eleventh century ... The fourth is a poem of 14 st., itself an exemplification of the twelve most important metres of his own day by Cellach Ua Ruanada (†1079), an eminent poet. These tracts cite metrical examples as early as the end of the sixth century and as late as contemporary practice at or near the time of compilation. and are evidence of a long and copious written record.

records.Title: Treḟocal al. Triple utterance
records.Beginning lines: Treḟocal can chlóen can rudrach, can roigair can rofota
records.Contents: A tract on the faults of discourse, some rhetorical, most metrical or grammatical. This text appears to be the work of Cináed ua Con Mind of Ciarraige Luachra, bishop of Lismore and Inis Cathaig († 958). Its contents are incorpated into a commentary on Auraicept na nÉces.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cináed ua Con Mind of Ciarraige Luachra, bishop of Lismore and Inis Cathaig († 958)

records.Title: A mo Choimdiu néll cid do-gén?
records.Beginning lines: A mo Choimdiu néll cid do-gén fri Firu Arddae?
records.Contents: This lengthy, difficult, and allusive scholastic poem (70st.) on the nature of poetry and satire is attributed to Fíngin mac Flainn, fosterson (dalta) of Dubdartach Bérri, sapiens (†867/8, AFM, AI). Fíngin and his foster-father are mentioned amongst the legal authorities of Ireland in a law text, Cró & díbad (Ériu, 1 (1904), 214). Internal references to Fir Ardda, Ard Ruide &c ... indicate that Fir Ardda of Corcu Modruad in Munster are intended.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Fíngin mac Flainn, fosterson (dalta) of Dubdartach Bérri, sapiens (†867/8, AFM, AI).
records.Location of the narrative: Fíngin and his foster-father; Fir Ardda of Corcu Modruad in Munster
records.info:: See Howard Meroney, ‘Studies in early Irish satire’, Journal of Celtic Studies 2 (1958): 62–63 for dating

records.Title: Sét no tíag
records.Beginning lines: Sét no tíag téiti Críst
records.Contents: A short poem (6 st.), seeking heaven's protection for a priest on his pastoral journeys, attributed to Colum Cille. His authorship cannot be ruled out. It is inscribed Coimge Coluim Cille ann sin & a gabail ac loigi & hic ergi & ag dul for sed & is adamra 'This is the protection of Colum Cille and it is to be recited at bed-time, at rising, at going on a journey and it is of marvellous avail'.

records.Title: Tiugraind Béccáin
records.Beginning lines: To-fed andes i ndáil fíadat findál caingel
records.Contents: A poem (25st.) in praise of Columb Cille, 'light of the Connachta, light of Britain … pastor of monks, judge of clerics', who 'abandoned his ancestral posession for the love of learning'. The work is attributed to Béccán mac Luigdech, who may have flourished in the seventh century, a date consonant with its language and its sober style.
records.Location of the narrative: Colum Cille

records.Title: Fo réir Choluimb céin ad-fías
records.Beginning lines: Fo réir Choluimb céin ad-fías find for nimib snáidsium secht
records.Contents: A glossed poem (25 st.) in praise of Columb Cille (here also called Mochummae) - his reputation, his ascetic piety, his scholarship, and his mission to Britain. The poet prays for the great saint's protection. The author is likely to be Béccán mac Luigdech, and the work has much in common - in style, language and thought - with Tiugraind Béccáin.
records.Location of the narrative: Colum Cille
records.info:: See also the poem beg. Doféd andes andáil fíadhat. “Like our poem it has 25 verses, and has so much in common—linguistically, stylistically and metrically—that their ascription to the same author [Bécán] could well be correct” (Kelly).

records.Title: Poems of Blathmac mac Con Brettan
records.Beginning lines: Tair cucum a Maire boíd do choíniuth frit do rochoím (poem 1); A Maire a grian ar clainde a mba moí mo chélmaine (poem 2)
records.Contents: Two lengthy poems headed Blathmac mac Con Brettan maic Conguso do  Feraib Rois do-rigne a ndúthracht-sa do Mairi & da Mac 'Blathmac mac Con Brettan maic Congusa of Fir Rois made this devout offering to Mary and her Son' … Carney's dating of the poem depends wholly on the historicity of the opening ascription in the codex unicus. Blathmac's father, Cú Bretrtan died in 740; his brother Donn Bó was killed in battle in 759. Therefore, he flourished c. 750-770 and, accordingly, Carney ... dates the poems to 750x770. But the poems may be much earlier, indeed as early as AD 700, even if the ascription is correct.
records.Location of the narrative: Blathmac mac Con Brettan

records.Title: Muire máthair in maic bic al. A poem on the Virgin Mary
records.Beginning lines: Muire máthair in maic bic génair i n-aidchi Notlaic
records.Contents: A short poem (8 st.) that asserts the nobility of Mary's lineage … and her deep learning and knowledge of the law and the prophets.
records.info:: c.700? According to Carney, this poem and the longer one that precedes it (Imbu maccán cóic blíadnae) “seem somewhat older than those of Blathmac, and a seventh- rather than an eighth-century date may perhaps be thought of.”.

records.Title: A maccucán sruith in tíag
records.Beginning lines: A maccucán sruith in tíag nod-gaibi fort muin
records.Contents: A poem (19 st.) attributed to Adomnán (†703). It may be his. On the surface a list of the relics of Christ, the Virgin, and of the saints in the satchel of a clerical student. In fact, the poem tells the student that all the holy things needed for salvation and for protection against the perils of this life are in his satchel, viz. the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the Lives of Martin, the Desert Fathers, and the early Irish saints.

records.Title: Fort ḟoísam, a Muire
records.Beginning lines: Fort ḟoísam, a Muire, dom-aisilbim uile
records.Contents: A short poem (5 st.), represented as Columb Cille's prayer-poem to the Virgin, beseeching her protection against disease and plague. Meyer connects it with the pestilentia magna in Hibernia insola, reported by the annals for the year 806.
records.Location of the narrative: Columb Cille

records.Title: Columb cáid cumachtach
records.Beginning lines: Columb cáid cumachtach a clétib clithnime
records.Contents: A prayer, expressed with powerful emotion, to Columb Cille, beseeching the saint to protect the poet from the deadly spiritual and physical threats that surround him, and he prays that his soul may pass into the saint's hands at his death. This poem is cited int he metrical tracts (Thurneysen, Mittelirische Verslehren ... 56 §106
records.info:: “gehört zweifellos der spät-altirischen Zeit an und [because of a citation in Sanas Cormaic] ist gewiss älter als das Jahr 900” (Pokorny).

records.Title: Guidim mac Feidelmid
records.Beginning lines: Guidim mac Feidelmid fri ithge n-ardḟlatha
records.Contents: A poem (9 st.), attributed to St Cainnech in praise of, and in prayer to, Columb Cille 'of the illustrious seed of Éremón of the storied island of the Scots'. The poet praises his noble birth, his sanctity, his scholarship, and his mission to Britain, and there are clear intertextual echos of the earlier Columban verse, for example, Fo réir Choluimb céin ad-fías.
records.Location of the narrative: Columb Cille

records.Title: Amra Senáin
records.Beginning lines: Senán soer sídathair sílem soáilche
records.Contents: A poem of 16 st., by the learned king-bishop, Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), in praise of St Senán, founder of the church of Inis Cathaig, in the Shannon esturary.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), king-bishop of Cashel
records.Location of the narrative: St Senán, founder of the church of Inis Cathaig, in the Shannon esturary.

records.Title: Uga Corbmaic meic Cuilennáin al. The choice of Cormac mac Cuilennáin
records.Beginning lines: In rogho so a Ríg na rún íar comso clúm ocus ceol
records.Contents: A poem of penitence (29 st.), seeking the mercy of Christ. The poet will abandon, as pilgrim, the pleasures of a royal life to win salvation, and to be forgiven by a Christ who forgave Peter for denying Him and who brought the good thief with Him to Heaven. Excerpts from this poem are cited as examples in the metrical tracts.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), king-bishop of Cashel
records.info:: Early Irish religious poem (29qq) attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin. What appears to be a full copy of text is attested in a single manuscript, while fragments of it also turn up as citations elsewhere.

records.Title: Monastic verse attributed to Manchán Léith
records.Beginning lines: (1) Dúthracar a Maic Dé bí; (2) Nech at-cobra dul for nemh at-cosna in flaith
records.Contents: Attributed to the monastic founder Manchán (†665) of Liath Mancháin (parish Lemanaghan, barony of Garrycastle, King's Co.), but much later, probably tenth-century. The first item is a lyric poem (11 st.) setting out the ideal monastery … The second item, 'Anmchairdes Mancháin Léith' (28 st.), probably from the same pen, prescribes the spiritual exercises ... and the virtues of the monk ...
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Manchán (†665) of Liath Mancháin (parish Lemanaghan, barony of Garrycastle, King's Co.)

records.Title: An Chrínóc
records.Beginning lines: A Chrínóc, cubaid do cheól cenco bat fíróc at fíal
records.Contents: Meyer took the poem to be about spiritual marriage, but Carney has argued convincingly that it is a sustained metaphor. The Crínóc is the psalter of the monk's youth, used in time by four others … As Ó Broin points out … the conceit is inspired by Horace, Epistulae, i 20. It playfully and pointedly contrasts the fortunes of the psalter and Horace's book. The poem has been ascribed to Máel Ísu Ó Brolcháin (†1086).

records.Title: Moling Poems
records.Beginning lines: Tainic rath forettarsa orm o righ na ruaime
records.Contents: A collection of 24 poems of varying length and theme put in the mouth of St. Moling, founder-abbot of the church of Tech Moling, parish of St Mullins, Co. Carlow.
records.Location of the narrative: St. Moling, founder-abbot of the church of Tech Moling, parish of St Mullins, Co. Carlow.

records.Title: Airbertach mac Coisse (fl. 982; †1016), Ro fessa i curp domuin dúir al. Geography of Ross Ailithir
records.Beginning lines: Ro fessa i curp domuin dúir cóic cressa caíne comthúir
records.Contents: A poem of 66 st. (67 st. in MS ii) on world geography, clearly a textbook for the schools and versified to be memorised. It is the compilatory work of Airbertach mac Cosse, fer légind (head of school) and superior of Ros Ailithir. It derives largely from Isidore of Seville and is based indirectly on late classical sources, scripture, Josephus, and the Fathers. It provides the essential geographical background to sacred studies.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Airbertach mac Coisse (fl. 982; †1016) of Ros Ailithir

records.Title: Airbertach mac Coisse (fl. 982; +1016), Fichi ríg - cia rím as ferr?
records.Beginning lines: Fichi ríg - cia rím as ferr? - rogabsat Hierusalem
records.Contents: A learned poem (61 st.) on the kings of Judah who ruled in Jerusalem from Saul to the destruction of the city, with two additional stanzas on the return of the Jews after the Babylonian captivity. It is based on Paralipomenon I-II (Chronicles), not Kings. The last two stanzas derive from Esdras.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Airbertach mac Coisse (fl. 982; †1016) of Ros Ailithir

records.Title: Úasalepscop Éirenn Aed al. Poem in praise of Aed Ua Forréidh
records.Beginning lines: Uasalepscop Éirenn Aéd ra-lég léigenn gonid lór
records.Contents: A professional praise poem (33 st.) for which the poet seeks a drinking-horn in payment … lauding Áed Ua Forréid (†1056), bishop of Armagh, written a little before 1046. Among the Armagh hierarchy other than the bishop the poem mentions the youthful abbot, Amalgaid mac Máel Muire (sed. 1020-49); the oeconomus Echnartach Mac Cernaig; the learned head of school, Máel Pátraic Ua Bileóice (†1046); Duiligén son of Gilla Críst, like his father, 'noble priest of Armagh' (†1053); Mac Gilla Ciaráin, superior of the guest house ... Among clerics added at the end, not of the Armagh community, are Ua Ruadrach, superior of Termonfeckin (†1053) and the learned Flann Mainistrech, 'the magic mead-scholar who imbibes ale', poet and head of school at Monasterboice (†1056). The poem offers a brilliant and unconsciously revealing image of eleventh-century church grandees.
records.Location of the narrative: Áed Ua Forréid (†1056), bishop of Armagh; Amalgaid mac Máel Muire (sed. 1020-49); Echnartach Mac Cernaig; Máel Pátraic Ua Bileóice (†1046);  Duiligén son of Gilla Críst (†1053); Mac Gilla Ciaráin,; Ua Ruadrach, superior of Termonfeckin (†1053) and the learned Flann Mainistrech poet and head of school at Monasterboice (†1056).
records.info:: 1032 x 1042/46. Gerard Murphy accepts that the poem was composed to be recited in Áed’s presence and identifies a number of religious men who are mentioned in the poem. On these historical grounds, he suggests a date between 1032, the year in which Áed took office as bishop of Armagh, and 1046, when Úa Bíleóige, lector of Armagh (1041–1046), died, and probably before 1042, the year in which Eochagán, superior of Slane, died.(1) Benjamin Hudson notes that the stanza on Dubthach Albanach (beg. Dubthach duine dligthech dúr) also occurs in the A-version of the Annals of Ulster (TCD 1282, f. 45c, top margin) and suggests that it is older than the poem as a whole. Benjamin T. Hudson, The Prophecy of Berchán: Irish and Scottish high-kings in the early Middle Ages (1996): 121

records.Title: Treatise of Échtgus Ó Cuanáin of Ros Cré on the Eucharist
records.Beginning lines: A dhuine nach creit iar coir in fleidh caite 'con altoir
records.Contents: Not a monastic rule but a learned metrical treatise (86 st.) on the Eucharist, written c. 1050 x 1150. The strict verse form assures the integrity of the text. It is explicitly written to educate clergy and laity on the orthodox theology of the Eucharist, in the context of contemporary controversies.

records.Title: Colcu ua Duinechda (†796), Scúap chrábaid al. Besom of devotion
records.Beginning lines: Ateoch frit a Ísu noíb do cethri suiscélaige (litany 1); A Ísu nóeb a chara cóem, a rétlai maidinda (litany 2)
records.Contents: These appear to be two litanies of Jesus, together known as Scúap chrábaid. Meyer regards the attribution to Colcu as well founded.
records.info:: “The language is unmistakeably Old-Irish, and may well be that of the latter half of the eighth century” (Meyer).

records.Title: De confessione al. A litany of confession
records.Beginning lines: Omne malum feci coram te crimina nosti (praef); A Athair, a Meic, a Spirut Noím dilguid dam (text)
records.Contents: A litany divided into sections by the rubrics. The penitent confesses to God … and to saints … his sins are many and vast … he begs forgiveness for every sin … and with great eloquence he seeks pardon for every ill-will he has 'harboured against God or man'.

records.Title: Litany of the Saviour
records.Beginning lines: A Slánícidh in ciniuda daona, a fhírliaig cecha tedma
records.Contents: In the words of Plummer 'a beautiful and genuine outpouring of simple piety'. If iter fedbaib 'amongst widows' is a sound reading, it may have been composed by or for a community of holy widows.

records.Title: Prayer to the Virgin and all the saints
records.Beginning lines: Impide Maire & Eoin macáin & Eoin Babtaist co n-uilib naomaib an domain
records.Contents: The prayer of a community of nuns that they keep custos oculorum, that they be not distracted by idle songs and dainties, and that as brides of Christ they faithfully keep their virginity spotless.

records.Title: Litany of the Virgin
records.Beginning lines: A Muire mór, a Muire is mó dona Muirib, a romor na mban
records.Contents: The Virgin is invoked under many titles, among them 'Cedar of Lebanon, cypress of Zion, crimson rose of the land of Jacob'. The second part changes from litany to eloquent prayers. This text may have belonged to a female religious house.

records.Title: Litany of the Irish saints I
records.Roman dates: s. xi/xii, edition of early materials
records.Beginning lines: Secht noeb-epscoip déc ar secht cétaib di áes raith in Chomded i Corcaig Moir
records.Contents: The litany opens with an inflated count (717) of the holy bishops of Cork, associated with its patron, SS Finnbarr and Nessán. A second section refers to the 150 bishops and 300 priests ordained by St Patrick, but the text quickly returns to the 150 bishops of Ailén Arda Nemid (Great Island in Cork Harbour) and the 350 bishops and 350 priests of Loch Irce, a local church claimed as a foundation of St Finnbarr - more than enough evidence that this text was redacted in Cork. It is, however, based on much earlier materials. Some of these, as Plummer points out ... are likely to originate in Cell Achaid Dromma Fota (Killeigh, King's Co.).
records.Place text was written: Cell Achaid Dromma Fota (Killeigh, King's Co.); Cork
records.Location of the narrative: SS Finnbarr and Nessán; St Patrick
records.Characters in the narrative: Ailén Arda Nemid (Great Island in Cork Harbour)

records.Title: Two Litanies of irish saints
records.Beginning lines: Trí choícait curach di ailithrib Rómán gabsat hÉrinn (1); Secht nóeb-epscoip Dromma Urchailli, secht nóeb-epscoip Cilli Derce Daim (2)
records.Contents: This document is, in fact, a text of two separate litanies, one following the other without a break … Both texts are learned and antiquarian as well as devotional. Litany 1 is of pilgrim saints: foreign saints … who came to Ireland; Irish saints who went abroad (Columba, Brendan, Ibar, Abbán, Ailbe, Donnán of Eigg), or who moved to Ireland ... The latest datable saint mentioned is Colmán Find, anchorite  (†776) and its author is familiar with Navigatio S. Bredani and Vita S. Brendano. This litany belongs to the late eighth century, and is based on earlier materials, and may originate in Lismore. Litany 2 invokes only bishops in groups of seven ... There are 32 sections ... There is no evidence that this is later than the eighth century and, given its many references to foundations called domnach and to the plagues, it may be as early as the seventh century.
records.Location of the narrative: Columba, Brendan, Ibar, Abbán, Ailbe, Donnán of Eigg; Colmán Find, anchorite (†776)
records.info:: Sanderlin suggests that the text was written at Lismore, Co. Waterford.

records.Title: Litany of the Trinity
records.Beginning lines: Mugrón comarba Coluim Cille hec verba composuit de Trinitate (praef.); Airchis dún a Dé Athair uilicumachtaig, a Dé na slóg (text)
records.Contents: Attributed (MS i) to Mugrón (†980), head of the Columban monasteries in Ireland and Scotland, to whom some other religious pieces are ascribed.

records.Title: Máel Ísu Ua Brolcháin (†1086), Hymn to St Michael the Archangel
records.Beginning lines: A aingil, beir a Michíl mórfhertaig
records.Contents: Máel Ísu Ua Brolcháin who died at Lismore in 1087 was the best-known religious poet of his time.
records.info:: 11th century

records.Title: A Litany of Virgin Saints
records.Beginning lines: Nam-churim ar commairge Maire ogi ingini
records.Contents: This is a remarkable litany of the Virgin Mary and of exclusively Irish female virgin saints, of whom twenty-eight are named. Then the Trinity, the prophets, the apostles, saint-monks, martyrs, widows, virgins and angels (none named) are invoked for protection from the evils of this life and the next. This is likely to be the work of a female religious, perhaps of Kildare.

records.Title: Metrical Litany of the Virgin Mary al. Invocation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
records.Beginning lines: A Muire mín maithingin tabair fortacht dún
records.Contents: An elegant poem of invocation (16 st.) to the Virgin rather than a litany.

records.Title: Litany of Creation al. A poem of intercession
records.Beginning lines: Ateoch frit in dechmad gradh i talmain trebruid
records.Contents: A poem of invocation that divides, in style and theme, into two related parts. The first … invokes Crist, St Michael and the angels … In the second part … 'his 'besom of devotion', he prays to be in 'God's ranks' and he entreats His boundless mercy to help him in all his battles and conflicts.

records.Title: Cormac's Glossary
records.Beginning lines: Adam .i. homo uel terrigena (short recension); Adam (.i. terra robrum) i.e. hommo uel terrigena, on talmuidecht, uel truncus .i. tamhan (long recension)
records.Contents: A scholarly glossary of scarce and arcane words, many legal. There are two recensions … The work is attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin, king-bishop of Cashel (†908), but it has been added to by later scholars.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), king-bishop of Cashel

records.Title: Loman
records.Contents: An independent text of the later part of the additional entries to Cormac's Glossary in the Yellow Book of Lecan.
records.info:: Medieval Irish glossary, with headwords under L–U, based on a long version of Sanas Cormaic.

records.Title: O'Davoren's Glossary
records.Beginning lines: Abgiter .i. tinscetal uel bunaidh, ut est cetheora aibgitre gaisi .i. cethre bunaidh na hamainnsi
records.Contents: An invaluable glossary, especially for law and legal terms, copied in 1569 by Domhnall Ó Duibh Dhá Bhoireann (MS i), and named for that scholar-scribe. It contains extensive and important citations (s. vii/viii, and later) from legal texts (some otherwise lost) and particularly from Bretha nemed toísech, Bretha nemed dédenach, Senchas már, Caldron of poesy. It draws on other glossaries, e.g. from Trinity medieval glossary or else shares a source with it; and from glossed extracts from the Vita Tripartita in Dublin TCL, 1337 olim H. 3.18 pp. 520-528.

records.Title: O'Mulconry's Glossary al. Descriptio de origine Scoticae linguae
records.Beginning lines: Incipit discreptio de origine Scoticae linguae quam congregauerunt religiosi uiri
records.Contents: A glossary of 874 entries. It claims that the Irish language derives from Greek. The earliest stratum may date to s. vii(2)/vii(1) (MacNeill infra). Two strata: one rich in Latin, Greek and Hebrew etymologies, and with some classical mythology; one treating of difficult Irish words. There are later additions.
records.info:: The earliest stratum of the text may date back to the second half of the 7th or first half of the 8th century (Mac Neill). Whitley Stokes dates certain late features of the text to the 13th or 14th century.

records.Title: Irsan'
records.Contents: A short glossary text, distantly related to O'Mulconry's Glossary.
records.info:: Medieval Irish glossary (A–S) related to O’Mulconry’s glossary.

records.Title: Dúil Laithne
records.Beginning lines: Dairtinne .i. duine. Troicit .i. corp
records.Contents: A glossary of 291 strange and unusual lexical items, uniquely preserved in a copy made by Dubhaltach Mór Mac Fir Bhisigh, but not compiled by him. There are two kinds: words that occur in other glossaries, and ordinary words that have been deformed, usually by expansion. Like material occurs in the commentary on Amra Coluim Chille and in Auricept na nÉces, but its purpose is not clear to scholars.

records.Title: Dúil Dromma Cetta
records.Contents: Dúil Dromma Cetta may contain materials from the ninth century, and perhaps much earlier, but the occurrence of ucing .i. cabhlach, ut est ucing la sesur for muir (CIH 627.35) dates the glossary to the peroid after the arrival of the Vikings, if the text is sound.

records.Title: A Breithe Neime Dedhinach so
records.Contents: A brief non-alphabetised legal glossary (39 lemmata) from Bretha Nemed.

records.Title: Trinity medieval glossary
records.Beginning lines: Adhart quasi adharth adha in bhais ar is ar bás atrímter codlad
records.Contents: A partly alphabetised glossary of 318 items, drawn from many sources, including other glossaries - Tochmarc Emire, Táin bó Cúailnge, Tochmarc Étaíne, Tecosca Cormaic, Cath Maige Tuired, Vita Tripartita, Mesca Ulad, Fled Bricrenn, the dindshenchas poem 'Carman', and the larger glossaries. This work cannot be dated properly until the sources are more thoroughly investigated and later additions identified.

records.Title: Tulchuba briathar
records.Beginning lines: Fer ar fechtaib fer .i. fer aba nó locha
records.Contents: A fragment of a glossary … described by Hull as 'a collection of Irish poetical expressions with their accompanying explanations'.

records.Title: Traigshruth Firchertne al. Bríatharogam
records.Beginning lines: Feochas foltchain .i. cos feoidhe bán lais & is álaind a barr
records.Contents: Three very brief closely related glossaries, principally concered with ogam and trees, plants and natural phenomena: Briatharogam Moraind meic Maín (25 entries): Briatharogam Meic in Óicc (24 entries); Briatharogam Con Caulaind (21 entries) … The title 'Traigshruth Firchertne', occurs at p. 314 (Calder, 312, line 6127), but the text has nothing to do with these glossaries.

records.Title: Cóir Anmann
records.Beginning lines: Art Ænfhear cid dia n-abar. Ní ansa. Ar ni baí mac fa dheoid ag Conn acht eisium (short recension); Mumu, cánas rohainmnighidh? Ní ansa. a nomine aliicuius reigis (long recension); Fothardha .i. fuath n-arta no fuath na ndea (third recension)
records.Contents: A handbook of etymological, aetiological, and narrative explanations of personal names and epithets, dealing mainly with the personae of Irish mythology and early medieval Irish literature … The short recension is arranged in a loosely alphabetical sequence, the long one in a largely genealogical order, opening with a very lengthy Munster Éoganacht section (§§1-57). The third recension is a drastically shortened derivative of the short one. The short recension belongs to the eleventh century and to the Uí Néill area as references to eight early heroic Uí Néill kings and to the great Uí Néill victory at Leth Cam (AD 827) indicate. The second recension belongs to the twelfth century and was redachted at Cork, as pointed references to the eponyms of its eccleiastical rulers (Mac Brócc and Mac Iair, §§46-8) show. It may have been begun in the reign of Cormac Mac Carthaig, king of Munster (r. 1124-38), but was re-worked, as such texts often are. Dál Cais, dynastic rivals of Éoganacht, are excluded from the Munster section and occur only briefly elsewhere (§§167-9). The text relies heavily on an annotated Éoganacht king list of which there are copies in ... Rawl. B502 (x. ii(1)) and Book of Leinster.
records.Place text was written: The short recension:  Uí Néill area as references to eight early heroic Uí Néill kings and to the great Uí Néill victory at Leth Cam (AD 827). The second recension: Cork.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Néill; Éoganacht; Dál Cais; eccleiastical rulers Mac Brócc and Mac Iair; Cormac Mac Carthaig, king of Munster (r. 1124-38)
records.info:: Late Middle Irish (Arbuthnot)

records.Title: Ligi Guill i mMaig Raigni
records.Beginning lines: Ligi Guill i mMaig Raigni airechtas fair ní n-aidle
records.Contents: A long … poem … It lists the killings of men and women by Goll, enemy of Finn, and by his kin, Clann Morna: seventy of the eighty-six stanzas record … the killing of one or many persons. It is probably a crib, to be committed to memory by student poets, a teaching tool got up when the literature on Finn began to be taught in the schools.
records.Location of the narrative: Goll, enemy of Finn, and by his kin, Clann Morna

records.Title: Audacht Moraind
records.Beginning lines: Incipit auriccept Moraind no teccosca Moraind for Ferdach Find Fechtnach (recension A); Incipit audacht Morainn maic Moín do Fheradach Fhinn Fhectnach (recension B)
records.Contents: The oldest vernacular speculum principis, artistically presented in the rhetoric of ancient tradition as the exhortation of the sage jurist Morand (al. Morann) to a prehistoric king. This is an exquisitely executed synthesis of inherited values and the Irish christian ethical teaching on kingship. Though expressed in traditional and apparently ancient terms, the language of Latin christianity is inescapably present in such borrowings as mortlaith (mortalitas), grád (gradus), bendacht (benedictio). Its ideal king is a christian one, though clothed in the language of apparent inherited and timeless wisdom.

records.Title: Bríathra Flainn Fina maic Ossu
records.Beginning lines: Ad-cotai socell saidbres
records.Contents: Collections of maxims ... Of the three recensions of this text, two (N and Y) are associated in title, with Flann Fína al. Aldrith son of Oswiu, king of Northumbria (r. c. 685-705), the third (L) with Fíthal, a legendary poet-judge. There is significant overlapped between the recensions and between these and other wisdom texts. Recension L innovates: it appears to be a fresh work of conflation and editing. In any case, the original text is not recoverable from the surviving witness.
records.Location of the narrative: Flann Fína al. Aldrith son of Oswiu, king of Northumbria (r. c. 685-705); Fíthal, a legendary poet-judge.

records.Title: Senbríathra Fíthail al. Ancient sayings of Fíthal
records.Beginning lines: Tossach augrai athchosan. Tossach éthig arlicud
records.Contents: Collections of maxims … This is the third recensions (L) of a wisdom text, of which two other recensions (N and Y) are associated with Flann Fína. Fíthal is a legendary poet-judge. Recension L appears to be a fresh work of conflation and editing. There is significant overlap between the recensions and between these and other texts. The original text is not recoverable from the surviving witnesses. For late metrical version, 10 st. s. x/xi see Yocum
records.info:: “ninth century” (Meyer)

records.Title: Tecosca Cormaic al. Instructions of king Cormac
records.Beginning lines: A uí Chuind, a Chormaic, ol. Carpre, cid is dech do ríg?
records.Contents: This is a courtly text, prescribing good behaviour at court and on social occassions at which kings, lords, and one's betters are present … It has a large legal content. It is very concerned about justice as the key to peace at all social levels and about the appropriate maintenance of the class structure ... a pithy speculum principis ...
records.info:: “I think there can be no doubt that Tecosca Cormaic in the form in which it has come down to us was compiled during the Old-Irish period of the language and so far as I can judge, not later than the first half of the ninth century. The later forms of the infixed pronouns which Strachan has pointed out [...], such as -das- or -dos-, do not appear in our text” (Meyer).(1)/ "so far as I can judge, not later than the first half of the ninth century" (Meyer).(2)

records.Title: Trecheng Breth Féni al. Triads of Ireland
records.Beginning lines: Cenn hÉrenn Ard Macha. Ordan hÉrenn Clúain Maic Nóis
records.Contents: An Old-Irish wisdom text, mostly in triads, that covers many and varied topics, especially law.

records.Title: Aibidil Luigne maic Éremóin al. Aibidil Cuigni maic hEmoin
records.Beginning lines: Cach breitheam a báegal. Cach crích a coindealg
records.Contents: A collection of legal maxims and saws in three sections. The first (78 items) is a medley of legal maxims from the earliest stratum of the vernacular laws, some not extant elsewhere and all beginning with the formulaic Cach. The second (68 items) consists mostly of dicta on personal and psychological characteristics. The third (11 items) is a series of sententiae, all beginning with measam 'the worst of (...)'.

records.Title: Advice to Doindin mac Nin
records.Beginning lines: Mo cosc duit, a Doidhin
records.Contents: A legal tract on sureties, rather than a wisdom text. Sections 1-8 … detrive from Bretha nemed dédenach.

records.Title: Bríatharthecosc Con Culainn al. Instructions of Cú Chulainn
records.Beginning lines: Nírbat taerrechtach debtha déne dóergairce
records.Contents: A short speculum principis that occurs as an interpolation of 40 lines embeded in the saga Serglige Con Culainn. It is represented as Cú Chulainn's instructions to his foster-son, Lugaid Reóderg, who is about to be enkinged.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn; Lugaid Reóderg

records.Title: Tecosc Cúscraid al. Instructions to Cúscraid Menn Macha
records.Beginning lines: Artotroi a Chuscraid coemainigh comheirig fri set soerathar
records.Contents: Embedded in the tale Cath Airtig, it is spoken by Conall Cernach, as advice to Cúscraid Menn Macha when he was proclaimed king of Ulaid. The text occurs only in MS i. It is heavily glossed and much of it is obscure.
records.Location of the narrative: Conall Cernach; Cúscraid Menn Macha

records.Title: Metrical maxims
records.Beginning lines: In rannán do-gníat-som sanchán a n-iathaib Íli
records.Contents: An Old and Middle Irish collection of seventeen metrical saws and sententious social observations.

records.Title: On capital punishment
records.Beginning lines: Ro chuala la nech legas libru
records.Contents: A short early medieval Irish poem of advice to kings, fathered on St Moling and thus claiming his authority. It unrelentingly urges kings to use capital punishment … The clerical poet takes as example Moínach (†662), a suitably obscure king of Cashel …
records.Location of the narrative: St Moling; Moínach (†662), a suitably obscure king of Cashel

records.Title: Cert cech ríg co réil
records.Beginning lines: Cert cech ríg co réil do chlannaib Néill náir
records.Contents: A wide-ranging speculum principis (72 st.), attributed in MS i to Fothad Canóine, and purporting to be counsel to Áed Oirdnide (†819), king of Ailech. The language is much later. It is addressed to one or other of the three eleventh-century kings of Ailech who bore the name Áed ... This is an important text for ideas concerning royal rule and church-state relations in the eleventh century. The text and the relationships between the MSS need to be critically investigated.
records.Location of the narrative: Áed Oirdnide (†819), king of Ailech.

records.Title: Dia mbad messe bad rí réil
records.Beginning lines: Dia mbad messe bad rí réil nocho chingfinn céim dar cert
records.Contents: A poem of advice to a king (36st. In MS I; other MSS vary). The work of many hands, this is a loosely structured collection of conventional proverbial sayings about kingship, hereditary succession to offices and trades and other matters.
records.info:: "From stanzas 6 and 7 it is evident that in origin the poem had some connection with Cashel."

records.Title: Mairg thochras fri cléirchib cell
records.Beginning lines: Mairg thochras fri cléirchib cell mairg nos-triallann tenn fri tenn
records.Contents: A cautionary clerical poem set, for effect, in the context of the conflict of Diarmait mac Cerbaill with the saints (Aided Diarmata), warning kings to respect the church and its clergy and indicating the evils that offences against them. The unstranslated poem, In rígan ecnaid óg fial, fathered on Flann Fíne al. king Aldrith of Northumbria has a like theme.
records.Location of the narrative: Diarmait mac Cerbaill with the saints (Aided Diarmata)

records.Title: Becc mac Dé profetauit al. Baile Bicc meic Dé inso
records.Beginning lines: Is maírg thairgeubhai a hairisne a luc tíre na nGaídhel
records.Contents: A dire prophetic list of evils that will befall Ireland. It opens, strikingly, with 'the son suceeding his father in Armagh, a plump pathic ruling Iona, the overthrow of Bangor'. Evils are of two kinds, those attached to individual churches or kingdoms (Clonmacnoise, Kildare, Lismore, Leinster, Cashel) and such general woes as evil kingship, intemperate weather, darkness in the sun, the moon bloody, rough seas, loss of crops, disease and social disorder (including too many churches). The prophecy closes with 'the banishment of angels, the opening of hell, the closing of the kingdom of heaven'.

records.Title: Fursu Cráibthech profetauit al. Baile Fursa Chráibthig
records.Beginning lines: Mairg taircébai ind aimsir a mbía særbrath cin chæmgníma
records.Contents: A prose prophecy that is merely a list of moral and social evils …

records.Title: Trédhe nach fuilingeand rígh réil
records.Beginning lines: Trédhe nach fuilingeand rígh réil sámhadh Pádraig gan a rér
records.Contents: A long poem (72 st.), 'signed' by Bec mac Dé (st. 72), no doubt a pseudonym for the author-editor. It is clearly a composite of different texts. St. 5 appears to refer to a shocking event, the rape of the abbess of Kildare, ordered by Diarmait Mac Murchada, king of Leinster, in 1132 ... The poem opens with a long section (st. 1-17) on the evils that attend wrongs perpetrated ona  long list of major churches. St. 14-16 (on mischiefs that befall Birr, Clonfert, Lismore, Armagh, Cork, Aran, and Clonmacnoise) and st. 29-31 (on social and economic evils) draw directly on Becc mac Dé profetauit (923) ... The remainder of the poem is poorly structured, and deals with many and varied ill-deeds and vices. It ends with Antichrist and the world's end.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: 'signed' by Bec mac Dé (st. 72), no doubt a pseudonym for the author-editor
records.Location of the narrative: Diarmait Mac Murchada, king of Leinster
records.info:: According to Eleanor Knott, the poem as preserved in RIA MS D ii 1 is a composite work: “In attempting to determine the date of our poem we have to take into account that it is not so much a composition as a compilation, in which at least two documents, assignable on linguistic and other grounds to the early part of the eleventh century, are freely utilized (see Notes).” She observes that the latest datable reference may be from 1136. “The general tone of the verses throughout is suitable to the eleventh and twelfth centuries, a period in which war and pestilence caused widespread damage, moral and physical, throughout Ireland. Apart from the two doubtful references mentioned above I see no reason to date the poem much later than 1150”.

records.Title: Comaillfithir d'Éirinn
records.Beginning lines: Comaillfithir d'Éirinn ídail dara hora
records.Contents: A list (15 st.), in the form of a prophecy signed by one Eochu Éce (st. 15), of the moral and social evils in store for Ireland - …

records.Title: Vision of Laisrén
records.Beginning lines: Feachtas luid Laisrén for slatrad o muintir Cluana do glanad Chulana Cain
records.Contents: St Laisrén, sleeping in church, was awakened by angels, and saw the church open to the heavens, his soul floating above him, and the angels bearing it aloft. Then he saw black and horrible demons contending for the soul with the angelic host, and charging it with its misdeeds (and here the demon cites scripture ofr his purpose). Then the angel shows Laisrén the pit of hell, and reveals to him the horrible sufferings of the damned. Here the text breaks off imperfect.
records.Location of the narrative: St Laisrén

records.Title: Scúab a Fánait al. Broom of Fánad
records.Beginning lines: Is a n-aimsir didu Fhlaind Chinaid ticc in Roth Rámach (prose); A Dhé máir co gaba mu dá eráil (verse); Is i ndighail marbtha Eoin Bautist immorro tic in Scuab a Fanait do erglanadh Erenn (MS v); Colum Cille dixit de Scopa: In Scóp a Fánait, cia tairgébha i nhÉire? (MS vii)
records.Contents: Semi-religious, semi-folkloric prophetic legends, differing in textual form, about the threatened disasters of AD 1096: 'In vengeance for the killing of St John the Baptist comes the Broom from Fánad to cleanse Ireland towards the end of the world, as Ailerán the Wise and Colum Cille foretold' (MS iii). This is mingled with material derived from Aislinge Óengus and the dindshenchas of Loch Bél Drecon (MSS i-ii). The Roth Rámach 'Paddled Wheel' derives from legends about the druid Mug Ruith, legendary executioner of St John. Much of this material recurs in the annotations to the Martyrology of Óengus (ad 29 August)
records.Location of the narrative: Fánad

records.Title: Acallam na senórach
records.Beginning lines: Ar tabhuirtt chatha Chomuir & chatha Gabra & chatha Ollurbha & ar ṅdithugud na Féindi (recension 1); Feacht n-óen do-rala Oissin & Cailti i nDún Clithair oc Sliab Crott. Is í sin aimsir tháinic Patraicc dochum nÉrenn (recension 2); … ionnus gurbho so-fhaircsona soilleas ... gleannta, foithre, & fásoighe (recension 3)
records.Contents: A lengthy frame-tale of the osetensible lore of the ancient warrior band (fian) of Finn, presented as the stories of Caílte (or Oisín) who, having outlived their peers, tell their tales to St. Patrick and his clerics, as he journeyed on his mission throughout Ireland ... It is the earliest and the longest text of the Irish chivalry and it reveals much of the values and aspirations, if not the realities, of twelfth-century Irish aristocratic society ...

records.Title: Aided Bresail meic Diarmata
records.Beginning lines: Feacht do-ringni Bresal mac Diarmata meic Cerbaill fleid móir dia athair
records.Contents: Partly a tale of violent kings, artistically placed in the early historic peroid, but much more an exemplum on the rights of the church and the powers of the saints by which even great kings are humbled.
records.Characters in the narrative: Diarmait mac Cerbaill, his son Bresal; St Béccán

records.Title: Aided Cheit meic Mágach al. Orgain Bélcon (Bélcon) Breifne
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia tá aided Ceit maic Mágach? Ní ansa. Luid Cet fecht ann a crích nUlad (recension 1); Ba tréinfhear an Ceat so & fa biodhbha biothfhoglaidh (recension 2)
records.Contents: A gory tale of the killing of Cet mac Mágach by Conall Cernach - both are described as 'the two hounds of slaughter who ruined Ireland between them' - and the subequent kiling of Bélchú Bréifne and his three sons by Conall Cernach, each side having planned treachery against the other. The tae existed in some form as early as the late tenth century. Recension 2 is an Early Modern Irish re-telling.
records.Characters in the narrative: Cet mac Mágach; Conall Cernach; Bélchú Bréifne

records.Title: Aided Cheltchair maic Uithechair
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia tá aided Cheltchair maic Uthechair? Ní ansa. Fer amra ro buí de Ultaib
records.Contents: Blaí Brugaid, compelled by his geis, sleeps reluctantly with the wanton wife of the warrior Celtchar mac Uithechair, who exacts revenge by killing Blaí as he stood, at a board game, between king Conchobar and Cú Chulainn …
records.Location of the narrative: Ulster
records.Characters in the narrative: Blaí Brugaid; Celtchar mac Uithechair; king Conchobar; Cú Chulainn

records.Title: Aided Chon Culainn (A) al. Brislech Mór Maige Muirthemni
records.Beginning lines: ... Ro fhoghluinnsett na mic druighecht & coimlecht & aidmilliudh
records.Contents: Ulster Cycle, The slaying of the Ulster hero Cú Chulainn, Conall Cernach’s revenge, Cú Chulainn’s ‘phantom speech’ (síabur-chobra) delivered after his death and a lament by Emer.
records.Location of the narrative: Ulster; Emain Macha
records.info:: Pokorny (1921) dated the text to the mid-8th century or even earlier, which would make it one of the earliest Irish sagas to survive.(1) Kimpton (2009), in a more recent, more detailed analysis, concludes that “instances of early Old Irish features [...], occurring in both poetic and prose portions of the text, suggest an original date of composition for the tale in the early eighth century”, while the simultaneous appearance of Middle Irish verbal forms suggest to her that the “LL text presents a late ninth- or early tenth-century reworking of an early eighth-century composition, with later scribal modernizations”.

records.Title: Aided Chon Roí
records.Beginning lines: A mbátar Ulaid i nEmuin, con-acatar Fer Equencaill dóib dar Magh nEmna (recension 1); Cissí tucaid ar ro marbsad Ulaid Coin Raí mac Dáiri? (recension 2); Ni hadha dom anmuin apairt romnett (Amra Con Rói); At-chíu dá choin ac congail (Brinna Ferchertne); Coimétar lip cend an rígh a Érna co n-imatt ngnímh
records.Contents: Aided Chon Roí and Amrae Con Roí are the two larger and more significant works in a cluster of narrative texts, verse, and fragments about the Munster hero Cú Roí mac Dáire.
records.Location of the narrative: Munster
records.info:: The poem beg. Coimétar lip cend an rígh a Érina co n-imatt ngnímh (s.xii). Egerton 88 (poorly transmitted, usual orthography and abbreviation), Recension 1 considered the earliest version, Recension 3 is a later expansion of it.

records.Title: Aided Chonchobair al. Death of Conchobar
records.Beginning lines: Baí mesca mór for Ulto fecht n-and i nEmain Macha (version A); Baí Conchobar mac Nessa fechtus n-ann. Ad-fét dó Altus crochad Críst (version B); Budh dáil mór la hUlltu a Muigh Muirthuimni (version C); Ceat mac Mádach rotheilg in cloich .i. inchind Miscedhra (version D); Ba hapruinn nan dáil cu Artrig n-arnac (retoriric)
records.Contents: A tale made of two conjoined narratives of the deaths of Conchobar mac Nessa, king of Ulaid. In the first, Cet mac Mátach of Connachta fatally wounded Conchobar with the brain-ball of Mess Gegra … In the second, the wounded Conchobar survives, is cured by his physician but, since removing the missile is fatal, he must lead a placid life ...
records.Location of the narrative: Ulster
records.Characters in the narrative: Cet mac Mágach; king Conchobar; Mess Gegra
records.info:: Version 1 is corrupt and is then followed by version 3 which is a later, expanded version. Version 2: prose fragment and the poem beg. Atchíu dá choin ac congail (q.v)

records.Title: Aided Chrimthainn meic Fidaig & trí mac Echach Muigmedóin .i. Brian, Ailill, Fiachra
records.Beginning lines: Rí uasal airmitnech ro gab righi nErenn fecht n-aill .i. Eochu Muigmedón mac Muiredaig Thirigh. Bai baincheli a dingbala lais .i. Moingfhind ingen Fidaig
records.Contents: This dynastic tale sets out the pecking order amongst the royal lineages of Connacht. In effect the real historical situation is realised as an aetiological narrative that explains the political realities as the result of a primary contest between the sibling eponyms in which Brion, ancestor of Uí Briúin, triumphs. It belongs to the reign of the greatest Uí Briúin king, Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair (1106-56), king of Connacht and king of Ireland, and is a historicist genealogical justification of his political claims. The tedious verse summary, 'Maicne Echach and a nglé' (in both MSS), recurs as a separate item in Dublin, TCL, 1339 olim H. 2.18 al. Book of Leinster ,,, s, xii(2) (post AD 1151xc, 1189), where it was attributed to Flann mac Lonáín.
records.Location of the narrative: Connacht
records.Characters in the narrative: sons of Eochaid Mugmedón i.e. Brían, Fíachra, Ailill and their sons.
records.info:: Ó Corráin (1986) has posited that the tale was composed in the 12th century, during the reign of Toirdelbach Úa Conchobair (r. 1106-d. 1156), whose royal claims it seems to favour over those of rival dynasties. He argues that it is one of a number of texts that form “part of the work-book of the scholars attached to Tairrdelbach Ua Conchobair” (p. 146). Dillon, in an earlier work, suggests that the prose “belongs perhaps to the eleventh century”, while the poems quoted are “earlier in language than the prose” (Dillon 1946: 30).

records.Title: Aided Chuanach meic Ailchíni al. Mór Muman 7 Aided Chuanach meic Ailchíni
records.Beginning lines: Áed Bennáin rí Irlóchra. Da mac déc lais & téora ingena. Senfhocul leó: Ní amail for-ácail Áed Bennáin a maccu.
records.Contents: A poorly transmistted Old-Irish dynastic tale, part historicist, part myth, of relationships  between the rival Éoganacht lineages of Munster and between their subordinate kingdoms. The characters of the tale belong to the seventh century. The mysterious Mór Muman, daughter of king Áed Bennán (+619/621) , is both a historical and a sovereignty figure, and has been the subject of much speculation by students of mythology.
records.Location of the narrative: Munster
records.Characters in the narrative: Mór Muman, daughter of king Áed Bennán (+612/621); Cuana mac Ailchine
records.info:: The poetry is Old Irish. The prose is Middle Irish. Entire text, single version.

records.Title: Aided Chuind Chétchathaig
records.Beginning lines: Eochaid Bélbuidi mac Feidlimid Rechtmair bráthair Cuind
records.Contents: His troublesome brother, Eochaid Bélbuide, fled Conn and took refuge in Ulaid, but Conn's agents surprised and killed him alone on Sliab Breg. This crime outraged the kings of Ulaid, who wanted Conn's life for the deed, but they made peace reluctantly. Not so king Tibraide, who exiled himself in Scotland for fear of Conn. He returned, disguised himself and his men as veiled women, and slew Conn when he was alone near Tara.
records.Location of the narrative: Sliab Breg
records.Characters in the narrative: Conn Cétchathach; Eochaid Bélbuide; king Tibraide

records.Title: Aided Derbḟorgaill
records.Beginning lines: Derb Fhorgaill ingen ríg Lochlainne ro charastar Coin Culaind ara urscélaib
records.Contents: A dramatic tale of the violent death of Derbḟorgaill, daughter of the king of Lochlainn and her hero-husband, Lugaid Ríab nDerg, companion of Cú Chulainn, whom Derbḟorgaill loved. This much misunderstood tale treats of subtly of sexual and social concerns. Its author, probably a cleric, had specialist medical knowledge.
records.Characters in the narrative: Derbḟorgaill, daughter of king of Lochlainn; Lugaid Ríab nDerg; Cú Chulainn

records.Title: Aided Diarmata meic Fergusa Cerrbéoil al. Aided Diarmata meic Cerbaill
records.Beginning lines: Dia mbúi Diarmait mac Fergusa Cerrbeoil for loingius ó Thuathal Maelgarb for Loch Ríb & for Sinainn
records.Contents: A subtle discourse on the relationship between king and church, cast as a tale of conflict in the Age of the Saints between the great clerical founders and heads of churches (Ciarán, Rúadán of Lothra &c.) and the king of Tara, Diarmait mac Cerbaill (+565), common ancestor of the two great branches of the Southern Uí Néill (Clann Cholmáin and Síl nÁeda Sláine), and thus representative of the kings of Ireland. This was written in Clonmacnoise, in the first half of the twelfth century ... The second recension looks like work-in-progress on the writer's desk ...the second recension of the tale is poorly constructed.

records.Title: Aided Echach meic Maireda (verse)
records.Beginning lines: Fó Loch Echach adba dam ard in sceng dron dringed draig (poem 1); Muirgein in gein co mbuadaib ingen Echach imualaig (poem 2)
records.Contents: A wonder tale in three parts (of different date, prose, and verse), folkloric and hagiographical, of the origins of Loch Ree and Lough Neagh (the latter connected elsewhere with the dispersal of the northern people, Corcu Óche, 1223) and the tale of Lí Ban, who swam the seas as a salmon for three centuries, appears as a mermaid who was a christian believer, was baptised by St Comgall of Bangor, and, as Muirgein 'sea-born', became a wonder-working saint.
records.Location of the narrative: Lí Ban; St Comgall of Bangor
records.info:: 12th century (Ranke de Vries)

records.Title: Aided Echach meic Maireda (prose)
records.Beginning lines: Rí maith ro gab Mumain .i. Mairid mac Cairedo (prose)
records.Contents: A wonder tale in three parts (of different date, prose, and verse), folkloric and hagiographical, of the origins of Loch Ree and Lough Neagh (the latter connected elsewhere with the dispersal of the northern people, Corcu Óche, 1223) and the tale of Lí Ban, who swam the seas as a salmon for three centuries, appears as a mermaid who was a christian believer, was baptised by St Comgall of Bangor, and, as Muirgein 'sea-born', became a wonder-working saint.
records.Location of the narrative: Lí Ban; St Comgall of Bangor
records.info:: 12th century (Ranke de Vries)

records.Title: Aided Fergusa meic Róich
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia tá aided Fergusa maic Róich. Ní ansa. Bui Fergus for luinges i Connachtaib iarna sárugud
records.Contents: Fergus, in exile in Connacht, was slain by the spear-cast of Lugaid Dalléces, while washing in Finnloch in Mag nAí after he had swum around the lake entwined with queen Medb. Lugaid acted on the urging of her jealous husband Ailill.
records.Location of the narrative: Fergus mac Roích; Lugaid Dalléces; queen Medh, king Ailill.

records.Title: Aided Finn
records.Beginning lines: Ar toidhecht arrsaighechta do Finn ua Baíscne ro airighset a muintir fair
records.Contents: Brief and fragmentary narrative of the death of Finn, of which there are several accounts.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn; Aiclech son of Dub Drenn, and the three sons of Urgriu

records.Title: Aided Guill meic Carbada & Aided Gairb Glinne Rigi
records.Beginning lines: Gessa & ilberta bítis for Coin Culaind for clothmaccáem Cróebrúade
records.Contents: A tale of Cú Chulainn, probably ironic, told in the inflated style of the twelfth century … It tells of his combat with the gaint overseas warrior from Germany, Goll mac Carbada, whom he slays; his fight with Garb of Glenn Rige, whom he kills; and his fraught relations with king Conchobar and the Ulstermen.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn; Goll mac Carbada; Garb of Glenn Rige; king Conhobar and Ulstermen
records.info:: CODECS: late Middle Irish

records.Title: Aided Lóegaire Búadaig
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia tá aided Lóegairi Búadaig?
records.Contents: Áed mac Ainchinne, the poet, committed adultery with Mugain Aitennchaírchech, wife of king Conchobar. When discovered, he chose death by drowning. No lake would drown him but that on the green of Lóegaire Búadach's house. Lóegaire saved Áed (and his own honour), but died by misadventure.
records.Location of the narrative: Áed mac Ainchinne; Mugain Aitennchaírchech, wife of king Conchobar; Lóegaire Búadach

records.Title: Aided Maelodráin
records.Beginning lines: Lóech amra ro boí do Dáil Moscorp Laigen .i. Mǽlodrán mac Dímma Cróin
records.Contents: Máelodrán, enemy of Uí Máil of Leinster, married to daughter of Aithechda, king of Uí Máil. His wife betrays him, he outwits his enemies, and makes peace with Aithechda. While bathing, Aithechda did treachery on Máelodrán and killed him with his own lance, the Carr. Aithechada married Máeldrán's second wife. On the anniversary of the killing, Aithechda lay abed with his wife gazing on the Carr. His wife warns that Máelodrán will avenge himself. Suddenly, Máelodrán appears, thrusts his own lance into Aithechda, and kills him.
records.Location of the narrative: Máelodrán, Aithechda, king of Uí Máil and his daugher.
records.info:: Middle Irish, with Old Irish forms. David Greene suggests that the text may date back to the Old Irish period: “In their present form these stories [Aided Máelodráin and Orgguin trí mac Díarmata mic Cerbaill] show a confusion of earlier and later forms, and there are so many minor variations of wording that it would be hard to come to any conclusion as to the original text. But enough archaic forms are preserved […] to make it possible that the date of the original composition was within the Old Irish period.” David Greene "Fingal Rónáin and other stories" 1955, 44

records.Title: Aided Meic Con
records.Beginning lines: Baí Lugaid Mac Con trá iar sin trícha bliadna a rígi nÉrenn. Bennaid banbrugaid is í ro baí isin Temraig ar chind Meic Con
records.Contents: A brief account of the deposition and death of Mac Con, separate from that in Cath Maige Mucrama. He is represented as ruling at Tara for thirty years, but his rule was inauspicious and the land waste. Driven from Tara by his false judgement, he behaved treacherously towards Ailill Ólom, who had him slain, and who then ruled Munster for seven years after the death of Mac Con.
records.Location of the narrative: Mac Con; Ailill Ólom

records.Title: Aided Meidbe al. Aided Medba Crúachan
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia tá aided Meidbe ingine Echdach Feidlig a Temraig?
records.Contents: A brief tale of the crimes of queen Medb's family - planned patricide, triple full-sibling incest, and finally the murder of Medb herself by her sister's son as she bathed naked out of doors. This looks like a clerical exemplum of the evils of paganism by one who had read the deeds ofthe House of Atreus, but the reader is given no context.
records.Location of the narrative: Queen Medb

records.Title: Aided Muirchertaig meic Erca
records.Beginning lines: Dia mbuí Muirchertach mac Muiredaig meic Eógain, ríg Érenn, i tig Cletig ós ur Bóinne
records.Contents: On the surface a tale of a violent royal death, that of Muirchertach mac Erca, high-king (†534; see AU 534.1, itself a non-historical entry). Drawing on rich and resonant older motifs, this text is a subtle literary discourse by a clericsavant on the deeds of Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn, king of Ireland (r. 1156-66), a commentary on his personal life, and his relationships with the church, and perhaps on his final treachery and violent death.
records.Location of the narrative: Muirchertach mac Erca, high-king (†534); Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn, king of Ireland (r. 1156-66)
records.info:: Late Middle Irish (Nic Dhonnchadha).

records.Title: Aided Nath Í al. Aided Dathí & a adnacol al. Suidigud tellaig na Cruachna
records.Beginning lines: Ro gab Nath Í mac Fíachrach hÉrind & ro insaig co Slíab nElpa (prose); Atá fótsu rí fer Fáil Da Thí mac Fiachrach in áig (poem 1); Níam & Drúcht is Dathi trí ingena Rois achi (poem 2)
records.Contents: A prosimetrum tale that has its origin in the genealogies of Uí Fiachrach of Connacht. It tells briefly of the death of Nath Í, king of Ireland, and his burial at Cruachain in Connacht. The greater part of the text is an antiquarian account (prose and verse), of the notables buried in Cruachain and other pagan cemetries.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Fiachrach of Connacht; Nath Í, king of Ireland

records.Title: Aided Óenfhir Aíe
records.Beginning lines: Cia fochann ara ro marb Cú Chulainn a mac? (recension 1); Dia ndechaid Cú Chulainn do foglaim gaiscid i ndAlbain co Scáthaig (recension 2)
records.Contents: The tale tells how Cú Chulainn killed his own son, Connla (al. Conláech), whose mother was Aífe, the daughter of Scáthach. Scáthach had trained Cú Chulainn in arms. The young Connla challenged the Ulstermen and only Cú Chulainn could overcome him …
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn; Connla; Aífe, daughter of Scáthach; Scáthach

records.Title: Aígidecht Athirni
records.Beginning lines: Do-dechaid tra Aithirne fecht and for turus isin fhogomur do thaig a daltai
records.Contents: A short tale of the legendary poets Aithirne and Amairgen, a framework for four fine poems on the seasons and five pieces of verse on the best animals for meat, and how to cook it.
records.Location of the narrative: poets Aithirne and Amairgen
records.info:: 11th century (Meyer)

records.Title: Airec Menman Uraird meic Coisse
records.Contents: A complex text on the poet's privileges. Its meaning is often obscure and technical, its language difficult and allusive … Cenél nÉogain pillaged and destroyed the house of the poet Urard mac Coisse (†990). He seeks compensation from their king, Domnall (†980), king of Tara ... Orgain cathrach Maíl Milscothaig ... tells, in showy poetic language, of the destruction of Máel Milscothach's cathair and, in technical legalese, of the compensation due to Máel Milscothach ... The text, an eloquent apologia for the poet's profession, sets the honour-price of every ollam filed 'master poet' as equal to that of the king of Tara.
records.Location of the narrative: Urard mac Coisse (†990); Domnall (†980), king of Tara; Máel Milscothach; Cenél nÉogain; Flann, fer léiginn

records.Title: Áirem muintire Finn al. The enumeration of Finn's people
records.Beginning lines: Áirem muintiri Finn in so .i. dechnemar & secht fichit rífhéinnidh a lín
records.Contents: A munster of the fian, a description of the remarkable qualities of bravery, dexterity, and learning required of them for admission, and a roll of Finn's personal retainers. The text sets out the legal relationship between members of the fian and society in general ... These provisions reflect the legal position of members of royal forces in twelfth-century Ireland.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn
records.info:: 12th century (Meyers)

records.Title: Airne Fíngein
records.Beginning lines: Baí Fíngen mac Luchta aidchi Samna i nDruim Fíngin
records.Contents: One tale of a series about the prehistoric king, Conn Cétchathach. Rothníam, the fairy woman of Síd Cliach, revealed to Fíngen, every samain, the remarkable events that were to occur in Ireland and among the hosts of the síd. Now she relates the wonders of the night of the birth of Conn, his future rule, and its effect on the life and fortunes of Fíngen.
records.Location of the narrative: Conn Cétchathach; Rothníam, the fairy woman of Sí Cliach; Fíngen
records.info:: CODECS: early Middle Irish or late Old Irish

records.Title: Aislinge Meic Con Glinne
records.Beginning lines: Cathal mac Findguine .i. rí mór Muman co ngéire chon, co llongad chapaill (short recension); Cetharda as chuintesta da cach elathain, iss ed as chuintesta don eladain-se (long recension)
records.Contents: A rollicking satire, pointed but fairly genial, of clerics and learning, kings and churches, in eleventh-century Ireland. All learned genres and pretensions are parodied, and food and drink are exuberantly celebrated with great eloquence and goliardic gusto. This is an early take on the Land of Cokaygne in which a clericus vagans is protagonist and anti-hero.
records.Location of the narrative: Aniér MacConglinne, scholar from Armagh; Cathal mac Finnguine

records.Title: Aislinge Óenguso
records.Beginning lines: Boí Óengus in n-aidchi n-aili inna chotlud.
records.Contents: Óengus and his love for Cáer Ibormeith of the Otherworld beings.
records.Location of the narrative: Óengus al. In Mac Óc; Cáer Ibormeith of the Otherworld

records.Title: Aithed Emire
records.Beginning lines: Luid Cú Chulaind laithi n-áen ann do forom ar énlaithib la táeb Trágha Baile
records.Contents: A brief tale of infidelity, Emer, wife of Cú Chulainn, fell in love with Tuir Glésta … son of the king of Lochlainn, who had come on a plundering raid to Cú Chulainn's home territory. She ran off with him and his booty to Lochlainn (Viking Scotland). Cú Chulainn went in pursuit, fought and killed Tuir Glésta in single combat, and recovered the errant Emer. The tale ends qith three stanzas spoken by Cú Chulainn, one a salty comment on female faithlessness.
records.Location of the narrative: Emer, wife of Cú Chulainn; Tuir Glésta
records.info:: Thurneysen: “Die kurze Erzählung findet sich jetzt nur — ohne Titel — in K. Ir. Ac, D. 4. 2 (um 1300) [...] Viel älter als jenes wird sie nicht sein, ist jedenfalls nicht über das 12. Jahrhundert hinaufzurücken. So fehlt sie anch in beiden Sagenlisten”.

records.Title: Athirne & Midir
records.Beginning lines: Athirne Áilgessach mac Ferchertne, is é is doichlechu ro boí i nhÉrind
records.Contents: An anecdote that tells how Athirne the poet was supernaturally cured of his stinginess and inhospitality.
records.Location of the narrative: Athirne the poet

records.Title: Athirne & Amairgen son of Eccet Salach
records.Beginning lines: Baí goba amra i nUltaib .i. Eccet Salach goba a ainm
records.Contents: Amairgen was the grotesquely ugly, filthy, and dumb child of Eccet Salach, the master smith from near the river Bush in Ulster. Athirne the poet sent his servant Greth on an errand to Eccet Salach. Amairgen suddenly spoke in strange words to Greth who was so alarmed at this mysterious command of language that he and his master Athirne came to kill Amairgen. Meanwhile his father, too, had divined his genius from his speech, and protected his son. He would-be-killer, athirne, had to pay seven bondmaids in compensation, the honour-price of Eccet, and take Amairgen as a foster-son whom he trained in poetry and who succeeded him as chief poet of the Ulstermen.
records.Location of the narrative: Amarigen; Greth; Athirne; Eccet Salach

records.Title: Baile Binnbérlach mac Búain
records.Beginning lines: Trí uí Capa maic Cinga maic Rossa maic Rudraige .i. Monach, Buan & Fer Corb
records.Contents: A tragic love story between Baile and Aillinn, requited not in this life but in the next … It has its origin in the genealogies of Dál nAraide in Ulster but it expresses rather the reflections of poets and scholars on writing and their art. It represents them as writing visions, feasts, loves and wooings on wax tablets and bringing them to a royal feast, and their being preserved at the royal court. A vision of this tale existed in the ninth century.
records.Location of the narrative: Baile; Aillinn

records.Title: Baile Briccíne
records.Beginning lines: Baí Bricíni Tuama Dreccon aithliu corgois céstai móir aidche cásc forémid techt asa tig abbad dond eclois
records.Contents: Early Irish tale in which an angel visits St Bricín(e), abbot of Túaim Dreccon (Tomregan, Co. Cavan), and reveals to him the names of many future churchmen in Ireland.
records.Location of the narrative: St Bricíne
records.info:: Codecs: late Old Irish/Early Middle Irish

records.Title: Bórama
records.Beginning lines: Ardri ro gab for hÉrind .i. Tuathal Techtmar mac Fiachach Findolaid (MS i); Tanic thra Tuathal tar muir iartain co hErind (MS ii)
records.Contents: This lengthy narrative, in prose and verse, is a compilation of loosely strung historicist episodes rather than a finished tale. Its colourful and pointedly stories treat of troublesome and worldly saints and the warlike and stubborn kings who bother them and their churches. Long aho a heavy tribute was laid on the Leinstermen by the legendary Tuathal Techtmar, king of Ireland, for the culpable death of his daughters at their hands. The result was bitter hostility for centuries between Leinster and Uí Néill, until the tribute was remitted by king Fínnechta through the pia fraus of St Moling, patron of south Leinster. These are stories from the greater Leinster churches perhaps put together at Tech Moling (St Mullins, Co. Carlow), Cell Rannairech (Kilranelagh) and elsewhere.
records.Place text was written: Tech Moling (St Mullins, Co. Carlow); Cell Rannairech (Kilranelagh) and elsewhere
records.Location of the narrative: Tuathal Techtmar, king of Ireland; Uí Neiller, Lenister; king Fínnechta, St. Moling

records.Title: Bruiden Átha Í
records.Beginning lines: Fecht do Find úa Baíscni i Cind Cuirrig. Baí-seom cin mnaí fri ré cian.
records.Contents: The plot of a tale, not a tale. Finn taking Badammair as his wife. Cuirrech Lifi of the Leinstermen had slain her foster-brother, and Finn went to kill in turn. Instead Cuirrech killed Finn's wife. This led to a bloody feud between Finn and Cuirrech's relatives especially Fothad Canainne.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn; Badammair his wife; Cuirrech Lifi of the Leinstermen; Fothad Canainne
records.info:: There is a cross reference to Baile in Scáil. Text roughly 700 words.

records.Title: Bruiden Da Choca
records.Beginning lines: Bátar Ulaidh hi comairle íar ndíth Conchobair día fis cía día ttibérdais ríghe (recension 1); Dia mbádar Ulaidh go héineirt iar n-éag Conchabhair (recension 2)
records.Contents: There is evidence for a lost early tale, Togail Bruidne Da Choca. The present text is a later tale, drawing on earlier materials. It was created by a learned author at Clonmacnoise, a member of the scholarly literary lineage Meic Cuinn na mBocht whose large estates are memorialised in this narrative. After the death of Conchobar, the Ulaid offer the kingship to his son, Cormac Conn Longes, an exile in Connacht. His return to Ulaid is fraught, he breaks his gessa, and an encounter with the goddess of death and other signs errily portend his doom. He and his party overnight in Da Choca's Hostel. Here they are slaughtered by the Connachta. Recension 2 is a re-working of the tale in the late bombastic style.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: a member of the scholarly literary lineage Meic Cuinn na mBocht
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac Conn Longes; Ulaid; Ailill; Medb; Badb; Da Coca; Connachta
records.info:: Early 12th century (Toner)

records.Title: Bruiden Meic Da Reo al. Orgain Chairpre Chindchait
records.Roman dates: s. xi/xii, a reworking of an earlier text
records.Beginning lines: Baí fodord mór ic aithechthuathaib Érenn i n-aimsir trí ríg nÉrenn
records.Contents: This is an exemplary fable of the massacre of the royalty of Ireland by the aithechthúatha or vassal peoples, the infertility of land and sea that followed, and the subsequent restoration of the true lineages, for three queens had fled Ireland, carrying royal offspring in their wombs. This is a tale of legitmacy and tyranny.
records.info:: possibly 11th or 12th century (O'Connor)

records.Title: Buile Shuibhne
records.Roman dates: s. xii, reworked from earlier texts
records.Beginning lines: Dála Shuibhne mhic Colmáin Chuair, righ Dál Araidhe
records.Contents: A tale, in prose and verse, of Suibne, king of Dál nAraide, who had violently outraged St Rónán and was cursed by the saint. He went mad with terror at the battle of Mag Rath (AD 637) and wandered as a wild bird-man through the woods of Ireland, living with the creatures of nature. Tales and verse concerning Suibhne have their origin in the ninth century and before, and his story became a vehicle for highly imaginative and striking nature poetry. In the end, Suibhne was received back into society and saved by St Moling.
records.Location of the narrative: Suibne, king of Dál nAraide; St Rónán; St Moling
records.info:: Late Middle Irish or Early Modern. Some of the verse may be predate the composition of this text.

records.Title: Cáin Éimíne Báin
records.Beginning lines: Do-lotar flaithi Laigen isin duinebath co a rríg
records.Contents: Miraculous story which relates how the community of St Éimíne Bán at Ros Glaise (probably Monasterevin, Co. Offaly) received a charter of privileges from the king of Leinster. It is said to have been granted after Éimine and his 49 monks sacrificed their lives to save Bran úa Fáeláin (d. 693), king of Leinster, and 49 chiefs of the province from the plague. Hagiologial tale.
records.Location of the narrative: Bran úa Fáeláin (d. 693), king of Leinster; St Éimíne Bán and his community

records.Title: Caithréim Cellaig
records.Beginning lines: Rí ro gab for Connachta .i. Éogan Bél mac Cellaig meic Oilella Muilt (recension 1); Rí airrdirc ágmar uasal ro gab airdrígi cúigid Chonnacht .i. Eógan Bél (recension 2)
records.Contents: The hagiographical legend of the life and death of bishop Cellach, son of king Éogan Bél.
