The killing of this sixth-century cleric was instigated by a king of Connacht, and vengeance was exacted by his brother, Muiredach. The text bears the impress of Clonmacnoise, and may have been written there.
records.Location of the narrative: bishop Cellach, son of king Éogan Bél; his brother Muiredach
records.info:: Máire Herbert (1997) has argued for a milieu centred on Clonmacnoise as the place of composition and suggested a date between the 11th and early 12th century.

records.Title: Cath Airtig
records.Beginning lines: Do-rónad comthinól oc Ultaib iartain iar ndíth Cormaic i mBruidin Da Cocae (MS i); Ro fhodail thra Cumscraid Meand Macha mac Conchobair a fherand (MS ii)
records.Contents: A tale about the relations between Ulaid and Connachta after the slaughter at Bruiden Da Choca, by one of the same school as the author of Bruiden Da Choca. It was written, therefore, at Clonmacnoise in the early twelfth century. Crích Malond al. Fir Malann claimed by both parties, is in the parish of Dumraney, barony of Kilkenny West, Co. Westmeath, an estate owned by Meic Cuinn na mBocht of Clonmacnoise.
records.Location of the narrative: Ulaid; Connachta;  Críh Malond al. Fir Malann
records.Characters in the narrative: parish of Dumraney, barony of Kilkenny West, Co. Westmeath, an estate owned by Meic Cuinn na mBocht of Clonmacnoise.

records.Title: Cath Almaine al. Battle of Allen Recension 1
records.Beginning lines: Cath Almaine etir Laigniu ocus Uí Néill. I teirt Íd Decembris to cuired in cath-sa (recension 1)
records.Contents: The tale of an author learned in the annals and literature that tells of events leading to, and the consequences of, the battle of Allen (AD 722) between Fergal mac Maíle Dúin, king of Uí Néill, who was killed there, and Murchad mac Brain, king of Leinster (r. 715-27), the victor. It is a historical tale, not history. It is not 'heroic saga'; its opposite rather. The second recension (perhaps written in Lismore) is artifically and superifically linked with Cathal mac Finguine, king of Munster (r. 721-42).
records.Location of the narrative: Fergal mac Maíle Dúin, king of Uí Néill; Murchad mac Brain, king of Leinster (r. 715-27)

records.Title: Cath Almaine al. Battle of Allen Recension 2
records.Beginning lines: Baí cocad mór iter Chathal mac Findguine & Fergal mac Maíli Dúin fri ré fota (recension 2)
records.Contents: The tale of an author learned in the annals and literature that tells of events leading to, and the consequences of, the battle of Allen (AD 722) between Fergal mac Maíle Dúin, king of Uí Néill, who was killed there, and Murchad mac Brain, king of Leinster (r. 715-27), the victor. It is a historical tale, not history. It is not 'heroic saga'; its opposite rather. The second recension (perhaps written in Lismore) is artifically and superifically linked with Cathal mac Finguine, king of Munster (r. 721-42).
records.Location of the narrative: Fergal mac Maíle Dúin, king of Uí Néill; Murchad mac Brain, king of Leinster (r. 715-27);  artifically and superifically linked with Cathal mac Finguine, king of Munster (r. 721-42).

records.Title: Cath belaig Dúin Bolc
records.Beginning lines: Feacht n-oen dia ndechaid Cummascach mac Aeda meic Ainmireach ar cuairt ríg
records.Contents: A tale of an expedition by Áed mac Ainmirech, Uí Néill, king of Ireland (†598), against Brandub, king of Leinster (†605/8), to avenge the death of his son, Cummascach, killed for his ill-deeds ona  royal circuit (cuairt rí) of Leinster. Áed outraged St Áedán who was sent to negotiate terms, whereupon the saint cursed him and the misfortunes began ... led to his death in the battle of Dún Bolc. The narrative retails the origin legend of the foundation of the monastery of Dísert Diarmata (Castledermot, Co. Kildare), where the tale may have been written. This tale occurs in the Bórama (993) in a more elaborate form ...
records.Place text was written: monastery of Dísert Diarmata (Castledermot, Co. Kildare)
records.Location of the narrative: Áed mac Ainmirech, Uí Néill, king of Ireland (†598); Brandub, king of Leinster (†605/8); his son, Cummascach; St Áedán

records.Title: Cath Cairn Chonaill
records.Beginning lines: Diarmait mac Áeda, Sinech Cró ro-d-nalt. No bertis Connachtai a bú-si co tarat imchosaít móir
records.Contents: Diarmait (†665), son of Áed Sláne, king of Tara, defeated Guaire Aidne (†663), king of Connacht, and his Munster allies, at the battle of Carn Conaill (AD 649). Guaire submitted to Diarmait. Impressed by Guaire's charity and generosity, Diarmait becomes his admiring friend. This is the historical framework on which a complex political and ecclesiastical narrative is constructed, including the assertion, by the church of Clonmacnoise, of its rights in property against the claims of the king of Meath, who is obliged to its clergy for their prayers on his behalf. Guaire, in turn, is obliged to the church of Inis Celtra, to its patron, St Caimmíne, and to Cuimmíne Fota, saint-abbot of Clonfert.
records.Location of the narrative: Diarmait (†665), son of Áed Sláne, king of Tara; Guaire Aidne (†663), king of Connacht, and his Munster allies; St Caimmíne; Cuimmíne Fota, saint-abbot of Clonfert
records.Characters in the narrative: battle of Carn Conaill (AD 649); church of Clonmacnoise; church of Inis Celtra

records.Title: Cath Cinn Abrat al. Battle of Cenn Abrat
records.Beginning lines: Rígda ro laad in chomdál sa do dénam ag Mac Con i Cind Abrat & Ailill Ólom i Muig Lacha
records.Contents: A short tale of the battle of Cenn Abrat between Mac Con and his foster-father, Ailill Ólom, where Ailill planned to bring about Mac Con's death by treachery … This is a tale of the relationships of Éoganacht, Érainn, Corcu Loígde, Múscraige, Corcu Baiscind and other Munster dynasties - a present artistically set in remote times in which dynastic founders and eponyms represent the lineages who claim descent from them.
records.Location of the narrative: Mac Con; his foster-father, Ailill Ólom;  relationships of Éoganacht, Érainn, Corcu Loígde, Múscraige, Corcu Baiscind and other Munster dynasties
records.info:: late Middle Irish (Dillon)

records.Title: Cath Crinna
records.Beginning lines: Galenga tair & tíar, Ciannachta tess & túaid, Luigne tair & tíar (recension 1); Baí rí amra for Éirinn .i. Cormac mac Airt. Buí rí for Ultaib in inbaid sin .i. Fergus Duibdédach (recension 2)
records.Contents: Late Middle Irish account of the battle of Crinna, in which Cormac mac Airt is said to have defeated the Ulstermen with the aid of Tadg son of Cían. The saga offers an origin legend of the Cíannacht Breg, explaining how it came to settle near Tara but did not attain the kingship of Tara. The tale in all its variant is hostile to the Uí Néill.
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Airt; Tadg son of Cían; Cíannacht Breg; Uí Néill.
records.info:: The extant version of the story is late Middle Irish, but a forerunner may originally have been composed in the eighth century in the aftermath of this disaster (Charles-Edwards, Early Christian Ireland (2000): 551)

records.Title: Cath Cúla Dremne al. Tucait catha Cúla Dremne
records.Beginning lines: Doronad feis Temrach la Diarmait mac Fergusa Ceirrbeoil fecht n-and co maithib cóic cóiged nÉrenn (recension 1); Boi Curnan mac Oeda meic Echach inn aitiri lie Diermaid mac Cerbaill (recension 2)
records.Contents: A Middle-Irish tale of Columba al. Colum Cille and his role in the battle of Cúl Dremne. The first recension begins with the spare style of earlier medieval Irish saga, but the later part of the tale was heavily re-worked in the inflated late Middle Irish style, and material is inserted in the interest of Uí Maine: Columba's blessing of them, and their payments to him, in return, are recited.
records.Location of the narrative: Colum Cille; Uí Maine

records.Title: Cath Maige Mucrama
records.Beginning lines: Ailill Ólom mac Moga Núadat do ṡíl Ébir meic Míled Espáin, rí Muman didiu int Ailill
records.Contents: A complex, learned, and poorly constructed tale confected from layers, varying in style, date, and intent, of the stories concerning Mac Con, Éogan son of Ailill Ólum, and Art mac Cuinn the representatives of the three conflicting dynasties, Dáirine, Éoganacht and Uí Néill. Sons of Éogan and Art - lone progenitors of their lineages - were conceived on the night before the battle of which their doomed fathers were to die. The victorious Mac Con then toook the kingship of Ireland for seven years. The now childless Ailill Ólom brought about Mac Con's death by treachery, and reigned as king of Munster for the next seven years. The author's learned digression ruin the narrative; its elements are too loosely stitched together; and, towards the end, its intent is quite lost in learned blather.
records.Location of the narrative: Mac Con, Éogan son of Ailill Ólum; Art mac Cuinn; three conflicting dynasties, Dáirine, Éoganacht and Uí Néill
records.info:: 9th century O'Daly

records.Title: Cath Maige Ráth I
records.Contents: A tale of the battle of (Mag) Roth (AD 637) between Congal Clóen, king of Dál nAraide and overking of  Ulaid and Domnall Brecc († 642), king of Dál Riata on the one hand and Domnall († 642)  mac Áeda, overking of Uí Néill, on the other. Congal was defeated and slain. THis is not a historical narrative ... high-flown language in describing the battle ... The text is not  well preserved, many cruxes remain and most of the added verse (if added) is tedious.
records.Location of the narrative: Congal Clóen, king of Dál nAraide and overking of  Ulaid; Domnall Brecc († 642), king of Dál Riatal; Domnall († 642) mac Áeda, overking of Uí Néill
records.info:: Dillon (Éigse 7: 201) suggests that the text “may be as early as the tenth century”.

records.Title: Cath Maige Tuired I al. Cath Muige Tuired Cunga
records.Beginning lines: A Chlann Nemid na nert mór cid ima tá bar tionól?
records.Contents: This is a two-part narrative, in prose and verse … The first part tells … of the wanderings of the legendary Fir Bolg and of the coming of Túatha Dé, who were skilled in weapons and wizardry. The second treats of their parleys and battle. Tuatha Dé demand that Fir Bolg share Ireland with them. They refuse. The battle occurs. Finally, after much bloodshed, Fir Bolg accept the province of Connacht as their share. The leading personages of the god-folk - Nuadu, Dagda, Lug, Elatha, Dian Cécht, Goibniu, Ogma, Bres Delbáeth, Cian, Bodh & c. - are all present.
records.Location of the narrative: Fir Bolg; Túatha Dé

records.Title: Cath Maige Tuired II al. Cath Maige Turedh & Genemain Bres meic Elathan
records.Beginning lines: Bátar Tuathai Dé Danonn i n-indsib tuaiscertacha in domain aig foglaim fesa
records.Contents: The text is much concerned with those suitable to hold the office of king. The Fomorians represent the Vikings, Túatha Dé Danann the Irish. The immediate political message is that alliances and dynastic intermarriages with the Vikings have evil consequences, and are to be avoided ... author to draw on his remarkabble knowledge of pagan mythology and beliefs ...
records.Location of the narrative: Formorians; Túatha Dé Danann
records.info:: According to Gerard Murphy, the text is “the product of an eleventh or twelfth-century redactor working mainly upon ninth-century material” Gerard Murphy, ‘Notes on Cath Maige Tuired’, Éigse 7 (1953–1955): 195; Ó Corráin: There are some evidence interpolations, and it breaks off imperfectly. Here an inherited and many-layered tale is turned to fresh purposes.

records.Title: Cath Ruis na Ríg for Bóinn
records.Beginning lines: In am a mbaí Conchobar i nEmain mínétrocht Macha ar cur chatha na Tána lais (recension 1); Tráth fá raibhe Conchubhar mac Fachtna Fathaigh áird-rígh Uladh a mertine & a móir-cheas ré rae chían (recension 2)
records.Contents: A 12th century tale of Conchobar mac Nessa and his Ulstermen, an epiloque to Táin Bó Cuailgne, with anachronistic historical reflexes of the Viking peroid and of Viking settlements in Scotland and Ireland.  Conchobar lay in dejection because of his defeat. The druid Cathbad advised him to await the summer and gather his allies, foreign and domestic ... The Ulstermen refuse reparations ... a great battle ... is fought at Ros na Ríg, on the Boyne.
records.Location of the narrative: Conchobar mac Nessa and his Ulstermen; Cathbad
records.Characters in the narrative: Ros na Ríg, on the Boyne
records.info:: Uáitéar Mac Gearailt dates the LL version to “possibly mid-way through the second half of the twelfth century” Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 44 (1991): 128–153; prose, prosimetrum (primary) verse (secondary).; Ó Corráin: The tale is poorly constructed, interspersed with dull verse (some wholly irelevant), and written in the baroque inflated style of the peroid. The much later second recension may derive ultimately from an original contemporary with the first.

records.Title: Ces Noínden al. Noínden Ulad al. Ces Ulad al. Tochmarc Cruinn & Macha
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia mboí in ces for Ultaib. Ní ansae. Boí aithech somæ di Ultaib i mbennaib slíab et díthrub (recension 1); Noínden Ulad cid dia tá? Ni andsa. Cruinniuc mac Agnomain di Ultaib briuga cétach (recension 2); Cruinn mac Agnamain mic Fír-Ulad .i. Muredach Munderg (recension 3)
records.Contents: … appears to explain the debility to which all the Ulstermen succumbed when their strength was most needed. Cú Chulainn, not a true Ulsterman, was excepted. Scholars, as is their wont, have imaginatively but unconvincingly explained this as the couvade or, alternatively, as something connected to rituals of seasonal death and rebirth. It may rather be a normative text (though involving the goddess Macha) that teaches that private domestic life (including childbirth) and the public sphere ought to be kept strictly apart in a well-ordered society, and that failure to do so brings diaster.
records.Location of the narrative: Ulstermen; Cú Chulainn; Macha
records.info:: One of the remscéla of the Ulster Cycle. Not to be confused with Ces Ulad, which attributes the weakness of the Ulstermen to a different event.

records.Title: Ces Ulad
records.Beginning lines: Luid Cú Chulaind do rerim inbuis la Bóainn
records.Contents: A very brief anecdote that gives quite another origin for Ces Noínden (1022). Cú Chulainn encountered Fedelm Foltchaín, wife of Elcmaire, at the Boyne, and became her lover for a year and a day. She displayed herself naked to the Ulstermen and this caused their debility. It is unclear what all this is meant to convey.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn; Fedelm Foltchaín, wife of Elcmaire
records.info:: One of the remscéla in the Ulster Cycle. Middle Irish Vernam Hull, ‘Ces Ulad. The affliction of the Ulstermen’, Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 29 (1962–1964).

records.Title: Cia tréide cétna-labratar íarna genemain fo chétóir?
records.Roman dates: s. xi, reworkings of earlier texts
records.Beginning lines: Cia tréide cétna labratar iarna genemain fó chétoir ⁊ cid ro-labraiset
records.Contents: Three short tales of Aí mac Ollamon, Morand, and Noíndiu Noíbrethach. All spoke just after their birth; all related to poetry and law; all have Otherwordly associations …
records.Location of the narrative: Aí mac Ollamon; Morand; Noíndiu Noíbrethach

records.Title: Compert Con Culainn
records.Beginning lines: Boí Conchubar et maithi Uloth i n-Emuin. No thathigtis énlaith mag ar Emuin (recension 1); Luid Decteir siur Concobuir coecait ingen for aithed (recension 2).
records.Contents: A remarkable story, in two forms, from the earliest surviving level of the Ulster tales, derived from the now-lost manuscript, Cín Dromma Snechta. It is in the spare diction of the earliest sagas … It relates the mysterious and otherworldly triple birth of the hero Cú Chulainn.

records.Title: Compert Conchobair
records.Beginning lines: Ness ingen Echach Sálbuidi boí inna ríg-suide i maig ar Emain (recension 1); Boí rí for Ultaib .i. Eochu Sálbuide mac Lóich (recension 2)
records.Contents: In recension 1, Ness … ask Cathbad the druid what the present hour is good for. On his replying that it is good for begetting a king upon a queen, she invites him to her, becomes pregnant by him, and gives bith to Conchobar, the future king of Ulaid. Recension 2 is much later, longer, and more complex. Her husband, the warrior-druid Cathbad, is not father of her son Conchobar but her lover, king Fachtna Fáthach. And on Cathbad's request, she delays his birth by a day so that Conchobar will be king of Ulaid and be born on the same day as Christ.
records.Location of the narrative: Ness; Cathbad; Conchobar; Fachtna Fáthach

records.Title: Comrac Liadaine & Cuirithir
records.Contents: The poet Cuirithir (of Fir Maige Féine) loved the poetess Liadain of the church of Achad Coinchimm, in Corcu Duibne (now parish of Killaha, barony of Magunihy, Co. Kerry) … The lovers put themseleves under the spiritual guidance of St Cuimmíne Fota … Cuirithir went on his pilgrimage to Cell Letrech. Liadain followed him and expressed her love and her regrets. Cuirithir went overseas on pilgrimage. She saw him no more, but  languished where he had prayed until her death.
records.Location of the narrative: Cuirithir (of Fir Maige Féine); Liadain of the church of Achad Coinchimm; St Cuimmíne Fota
records.Characters in the narrative: Cell Letrech; Corcu Duibne (now parish of Killaha, barony of Magunihy, Co. Kerry)
records.info:: c. 875 (Murphy); prosimetrum, prose, verse (primary)

records.Title: Conthoth Lóegaire co cretim & a aided
records.Beginning lines: Baí comthinól fer nÉrend hi Temraig i n-aimsir Lóegaire meic Néill
records.Contents: An aetiological legend of the putative reform of Irish law and cultural institutions and their acceptance by the Christian clergy in the time of king Lóegaire, imagined as a fifth-century king of Ireland. To this is attached an account of Lóegaire's levying of tribute on Leinster, his wrongful invocation of the forces of nature as his guarantors, and his death on that account.
records.Location of the narrative: king Lóégaire
records.info:: No date provided but it is found in LU an 11th/12th century manuscript.

records.Title: Conall Corc & Corco Luígde
records.Beginning lines: Fedelm ingen Moethaire de Corc' Óche, ind aimmit, muimme Conaill Chuirc maic Luigthig
records.Contents: The core of this late seventh-century tract is a version of the foundation legend of the Éoganacht; the birth, deeds, exile to Britain, and return of Conall Corc, legendary founder of the dynasty that ruled Munster from Cashel. To this is grafted a partisan history of the Éoganacht in the seventh century and before; and very early Éoganacht genealogies, at odds with those a century or two later. It was written at the church of Clúain Úama (parish and diocese of Cloyne, Co. Cork), whose founding saint is represented as patron of the favoured and most powerful lineage, Éoganacht Glendamnach, by a scholarly clerical supporter who drew on earlier written records. It is not neccesary to place it, as do some, as late as the reign of Cathal mac Finguine, king of Munster (r. 713-42), but one cannot exclude superficial modification the better to fit his ambitions.
records.Place text was written: church of Clúain Úama (parish and diocese of Cloyne, Co. Cork)
records.Location of the narrative: Conall Corc; Éoganacht; Cathal mac Finguine, king of Munster (r. 713-42)

records.Title: Conall Corc's exile al. Longes Chonaill Chuirc
records.Beginning lines: … Áth Cliath co n-accai na llonga oc dul taris. Luid leo taris sair co n-accai slébe Alban
records.Contents: … this is a variant of the origin legend of the kingship of Cashel and of Corc, progenitor of the Éoganacht dynasty (1029), imagined to have lived in the early fifth century; his banishment to Britain, his fated good fortune; his relationship with, and subsequent marriage to, the daughter of Feradach Finn Fechtnach, king of Britain; his well-timed return; and how heaven destined Cashel for him and his successors reveal to him by angels as the seat of future and enduring kingship (1031). Legal problems about pre-martial child and its mother enter into the tale, indicating that its author was a lawyer, as well as a cleric-scholar.
records.Location of the narrative: kingship of Cashel and of Corc, progenitor of the Éoganacht dynasty; daughter of Feradach Finn Fechtnach, king of Britain

records.Title: Conall Corc and the Finding of Cashel al. Senchas fagbála Caisil andso sis & beandacht ríg
records.Beginning lines: Hi Catair Étainn Tairb & Teamair Eimín táeb ro baí Corc mac Luigdeach in tan ro follsigid Caisil do Duirdrind do muicid ríg Éile (text 1); Do-luid Duirdrinn muicid ríg Éile & Cuirirán muicid ríg Músgraige (text 2)
records.Contents: Two different narratives to the effect that the kingship of Cashel was preordained by God for Corc and his descendants. The first (Dillion, §§1-3 infra.) tells how ...  Duirdriu, swineheard of the king of Éile, and Cuirirán, swineherd of the king of Múscraige, put their swine to mast  ... in a vision, see an angel blessing Corc; they are shown the succession of kings of  Munster and their prosperity ... Duirdriu told the vision to the king of Éile. Corc bought Cashel from him. There follows an interpolated list of the kings down to Cathal mac Finguine (r. 713-42), later extended to Dub Lachtna (r. 888-95) ... In the second narrative (§§4-8) the swineherds see a cleric with two choirs, and an angel who decleares that whoever kindles a fire at Cashel will be king of Munster ... Corc ... hurries to Cashel, lights a fire ... Corc resolves possible conflict with the kings of Múscraige and Éile. Duirdriu's descendants have the right to pronounce the angel's blessing on each king of Cashel, and none so blessed will die of violennce if he be just and merciful.
records.Location of the narrative: Corc and his descendants; Duirdriu, swineheard of the king of Éile; Cuirirán, swineherd of the king of Múscraige; Duirdriu; Cathal mac Finguine (r. 713-42); Dub Lachtna (r. 888-95)
records.info:: According to Myles Dillon, the composition of the first part (§§ 1-3 in his edition) can be dated to the 8th century, while the second part (§§ 4-8) may have been composed in the 10th century. Myles Dillon, ‘The story of the finding of Cashel’, Ériu 16 (1952): 63–64

records.Title: Conall Corc Anecdotes: (i) Birth of Conall Corc al. Genemain Chonaill Chuirc; (ii) Conall Corc's fosterers and his succession to the kingship of Cashel
records.Beginning lines: Do geinamain Chuirc meic Luigdeach so, uair nir Chorc a chetainm acht Conall. Is airi ad-bertha Corc mac Lairi fris, ar Feideilm ingen Mothairi (text 1); Rob é Niall mac Eachach Muidmedoin robo rig for Éirind in tan do-luid Corc mac Luigdeach tairis (text 2)
records.Contents: (i) A summary, inserted at the end of the Éoganacht genealogies, of the story of Corc's birth and exile, and his later dealings with Gregraige, Corcu Daula and Mennrige, an aetiology of the early relations of these petty lordships with the king of Cashel. (ii) A brief account of Croc's fosterers, the reign of Crimthann Már mac Figaig, and Corc's finding of Cashel, and his succession to the kingship of Munster.
records.Location of the narrative: Éoganacht; Corc; Gregraige; Corcu Daula; Mennrige; Crimthann Már mac Figaig

records.Title: Cuslinn Brigte & Aided Meic Díchoíme al. Aided Meic Díchóeme
records.Beginning lines: Baí rí amra for hIb Failgi fecht n-aill .i. Eochaid a ainm
records.Contents: The first part is a folktale. Eochaid, king of Uí Ḟailge, had horse's ears. He hid this blemish by wearing a diadem and by killing each barber who shaved him. The king's nephew, Mac Díchóeme, was beloved of the queen, and the jealous king had him shave him, and marked him for death. But Mac Díchóeme was too swift for him and it was agreed that he should live and keep the king's secret. But the secret made him ill, three streams of blood issued from his body, three saplings grew from them, and they sang out the king's secret Mac Díchóeme made a double pipe from the saplings, and succeeded as king of Uí Failge. The second part tells how St Brigit took the pipe from Mac Díchóeme because he abducted a virgin follower of St Sen-Brigit and how, deprvied of his love and his pipe, he expired.
records.Location of the narrative: Eochaid, king of Uí Ḟailge; Mac Díchóeme; St Brigit
records.info:: The text of MS i is a legend of the church of Kildare. The variant in MS ii, part of the gloss and commentary on Amrae Coluimb Chille, has only the folklore.

records.Title: How the Dagda got his magic staff
records.Beginning lines: Aed Abaid Essa Ruaid misi .i. dagdia druidechta Tuath De Danann
records.Contents: A fragment attributed to Aed, abbot of Assaroe. The Dagda's son, Cermait, was slain. With his son on his back, Dagda searched the world for the means to revive him and found in the eastern world a staff that could kill and revive. He swore, 'by sun and moon, land and sea' to use it to kill his enemies and bring his friends back to life.
records.Location of the narrative: Aed, abbot of Assaroe; Dagda's son, Cermait

records.Title: De chophur in dá muccida
records.Contents: The remscél of Táin Bó Cuailgne that tells of two swineherds, Friuch and Rucht, respectively of the síd of Bodh in Munster and the síd of Ochall in Connacht … then preternatural water-worms, Cruinniuc and Tummuc. These are consumed by the cows of Medb and Dáire and reborn as the two bulls, Findbennacch Aí of Connacht and Donn Cuailgne of Ulster, the two great bulls of the Táin.
records.info:: MS i has the older form of the tale; MS ii is a reworking, some of its material being as late as the twelfth century.  Prose, verse

records.Title: De gabáil int Ṡída al. The taking of the Síd
records.Beginning lines: Boí rí amra for Túathaib Dé i nÉre, Dagán a ainm
records.Contents: Dagda … divided the síde among the leaders of Túatha Dé, Lug and Ogma, and kept five síde including Síd in Broga (Bruig na Bóinne, Newgrange on the Boyne) for himself. His lackland son, In Mac Óc, persuaded his father to give him Síd in Broga for a day and a night. When asked to leave he declared that 'the whole world was day and night', and he remained in Síd in Broga ever after.
records.Location of the narrative: Túatha Dé; Lug; Ogma; In Mac Óc
records.Characters in the narrative: Síd in Broga (Bruig na Bóinne, Newgrange on the Boyne)

records.Title: De maccaib Conairi Máir
records.Beginning lines: Trí bráthir Cairpre Músc & Cairpre Baschaín & Corpre Rigfota, trí meic Conaire meic Eterscéoil
records.Contents: A learned and difficult historicist tale of the sons of Conaire Már and Sárait - the eponymous Cairpre Músc, Cairpre Baschaín (Basicind) and Cairpre Rigḟota (Riata) - and how they avenged their father's death on Nemed mac Srobcind, king of Érainn. This tale is linked to Togail Bruidne Da Derga on one side and to Múscraige, Érainn and Éoganacht 'pre-history' on the other (cf. the related text De Síl Chonairi Máir 1038). This is a geneaological origin legend, not a history of the settlement of the Múscraige and their kinsmen in Munster. The names of the sons of Conaire are extracted from the dynastic names Múscraige, Corcu Baiscind and Dál (or Corcu) Riata.
records.Location of the narrative: the sons of Conaire Már and Sárait - the eponymous Cairpre Músc, Cairpre Baschaín (Basicind) and Cairpre Rigḟota (Riata); Nemed mac Srobcind, king of Érainn

records.Title: De Ṡíl Chonairi Máir
records.Beginning lines: De thuidecht Múscraige de Muig Breg. Gnáthal do-lluid .i. mac Conruith meic Rodai meic Ma-Fede
records.Contents: The first part of the text tells how Conaire Már became king of Tara through the magic worked by his part-Otherworld mother, Mess Buachalla … The second part … Gnáthal mac Conruith, seven generations later … lost the kingship of Tara and came into Munster in search of a territory. He met the sons of Ailill Ólom in Bregon and they promised him land if he fought with them against Mac Con moccu Loígde. Mac Con was defeated. Here the text breaks off in historical notes and a third and dissonant narrative begins. Three sons of Conaire Már now come for the first time into Munster: Óengus, ancestor of Múscraige, Érainn, and Corcu Duibne ...; Ailill Baschaín, ancestor of Corcu Baiscind; and Eochaid Rigḟota ancestor of Dál (Corcu) Riata. These - otherwise known as the epongymous Coirpre Músc, Coirpre Baschaín and Coirpre Rigḟota (1037) - took the lands of the Érainn of Munster and established kingdoms there.
records.Location of the narrative: Conaire Már; Mess Buachalla; Gnáthal mac Conruith; sons of Ailill Ólom; Mac Con moccu Loígde

records.Title: Do ḟaillsigud Tána bó Cúailnge
records.Contents: A meta-textual explanation of how the learned of the seventh century came to know Táin Bó Cúailgne, supposedly a tale of seven centuries before their day. It occurs in three short texts and in the longer text, later and brilliantly satiric Tromdám Gúaire. All state that Táin Bó Cúailgne was a written narrative and recount the agreeable scholastic legend that the manuscript had been exchanged for the Culmen, and thus lost to Irish scholars. This is the tale of its recovery the heroic Fergus is summoned from the grave to narrate it.
records.info:: “The two versions extant in LL and D iv.2 (FTBC I and II) appear to be Old Irish or, at least, late-Old Irish; whereas the younger version (FTBC III) may have been created during the late-Old Irish to early-Middle Irish period”; “The language of the earliest extant version in LL appears to be Old Irish but it is difficult to give it a definitive date because of the brevity of the text; there is not a sufficient number of significant linguistic features upon which to base a solid argument” (Cleary 2018: 60, 83). Similary, Kevin Murray says that “Apart from a light veneer of Middle Irish, the language of the narrative [of the Book of Leinster version] is Old Irish [...] It seems probable that the composition of the Finding of the Táin should be dated to the late Old Irish period (that is, to the ninth century)” and goes on to list relevant linguistic features (2001: 19).

records.Title: Echtra Chondla al. Echtrae Chonnlai
records.Beginning lines: Connlae Ruad mac do Chunn Chétchathach a mboíe laa n-and for láim a athar i n-úachtar Uisnig
records.Contents: An Early Old-Irish narrative of Connlae's journey to the Otherworld … This is one of the earliest, if not the earliest, Irish prose tale. It is a subtle commentary on the relationship between Irish pagan beliefs and christianity, on mortality and immortality.
records.Location of the narrative: Connla

records.Title: Echtrae Chormaic meic Airt
records.Beginning lines: Laa n-æn do bai Cormac ua Cuind madan moch i cétamun a ænur for Múr Tea i Temraig co n-acca in t-æn-óclach forosta findliath a dochum
records.Contents: An Otherworld personage … visits king Cormac at Tara, bearing a silver branch with three golden apples. He takes away Cormac's daughter, son, and wife in succession. Cormac pursues them and finds himself alone in a land of wonder.  He has been brought to the Land of Promise ... where he is given an Otherworld golden cup that can distinguish truth from lie. On awakening, he finds himself on the green of Tara, with his family, the silver branch, and golden cup,
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac, king of Tara
records.info:: Two Middle Irish recensions and a modern one are distinguished. The second and third recensions are independent texts, whereas the first recension of this tale is found in a composite text known as Scél na Fír Flatha, Echtra Cormaic i Tír Tairngiri, ⁊ Ceart Claidib Cormaic (sometimes shortened to Scél na Fír Flatha). Here it forms the second tale, standing between Scél na Fír Flatha and Ceart claidib Cormaic, and corresponds to §§ 25-54 of Stokes' edition from this recension.

records.Title: Echtrae Fergusa meic Leti
records.Beginning lines: Bátar trí prímchinéla i nhÉre .i. Féni & Ultaig & Gailni .i. Laigin
records.Contents: The early tale of king Fergus mac Leti and his fight with the sea monster occurs solely in a legal context. This saga, written in the law schools, is an outstanding teaching text on the law of distraint. It also offers an origin for social customs associated with personal submission and observes the rule that the king must possess bodily integrity cf. Aided Fergusa meic Leite (970).
records.Location of the narrative: Fergus mac Leti

records.Title: Echtra Finn I al. Finn and the phantoms
records.Contents: The text consists of three episodes: (i) A nightmare encounter of Finn and his warriors with a fearsome giant and his monstrous household. When they awakened, all had vanished. Finn divined that these were the phantoms of Ibarglend. The material is close to the poem, inc. Óenach indiu luid in rí Óenach Life cona lí' (1046) which derives from it. (ii) A desultory series of combats and incidents, closely connected with the dinnshenchas of Áth Luain (Snám Dá Én). (iii) Finn's prophecy of the coming of St Ciarán of Clonmacnoise.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn
records.info:: 10th or even 9th century Kuno Meyer, Fianaigecht (1910): xxiii (no. xix).

records.Title: Echtra Finn II a. Find & the phantoms
records.Beginning lines: Óenach indiu luid in rí Óenach Life cona lí
records.Contents: A verse recension of some of the elements of Echtra Finn. It is notably rich in the place names of SW ireland that it must have its origin there.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn
records.info:: The version in the Book of Leinster is Middle Irish. Gerard Murphy also dates the version in the Duanaire Finn to the Middle Irish period. John Carey, however, has shown that in its received form, the latter poem supports an Early Modern Irish date and lacks linguistic clues that an earlier poem from the Middle Irish period had been reworked. Without the existence of the LL copy, the poem could not “persuasively be dated earlier than the thirteenth century, and even a later date would be difficult to rule out”.

records.Title: Echtra Láegaire meic Crimthainn go Mag Mell
records.Beginning lines: Bátar Connachta fecht and i ndáil oc Énloch for Mag Aí
records.Contents: Láegaire mac Crimthainn of the Connachta and fifty of his warriors answer the call of Fiachna of the Otherworld for help to recover his wife from Goll, king of Mag Mell. He is victorious. That night Láegaire slept with Der Gráinne, daughter of Fiachna, and fifty fairy women lay with his warriors. They wish to return to Ireland ... The Connachta will make Láegaire king, with all the kingdom's riches, he declares 'one night of the fairy nigghts I will not exchange for your kingdom'. He goes back to the Otherworld, and never returns.
records.Location of the narrative: Láegaire mac Crimthainn; Fiachna of the Otherworld;  Goll, king of Mag Mell; Der Gráinne, daughter of Fiachna

records.Title: Echtra Láegaire meic Crimthainn go Mag Mell
records.Beginning lines: Bátar Connachta fecht and i ndáil oc Énloch for Mag Aí
records.Contents: Láegaire mac Crimthainn of the Connachta and fifty of his warriors answer the call of Fiachna of the Otherworld for help to recover his wife from Goll, king of Mag Mell. He is victorious. That night Láegaire slept with Der Gráinne, daughter of Fiachna, and fifty fairy women lay with his warriors. They wish to return to Ireland ... The Connachta will make Láegaire king, with all the kingdom's riches, he declares 'one night of the fairy nigghts I will not exchange for your kingdom'. He goes back to the Otherworld, and never returns.
records.Location of the narrative: Láegaire mac Crimthainn; Fiachna of the Otherworld;  Goll, king of Mag Mell; Der Gráinne, daughter of Fiachna

records.Title: Echtra mac nEchach Muigmedóin al. Adventure of the sons of Eochu Mugmedón
records.Beginning lines: Baí Rrí amra airegda for Éirinn .i. Eochaid Muigmedón. Bádar cúig meic aige .i. Brian, Ailill, Fiachra, Fergus, Niall.
records.Contents: A dynastic tale, placed in pre-historic time, that establishes the hierarchical relationhip betwee the Uí Néill on the one hand, and those represented as their relations - Uí Briúin, Uí Ḟiachrach, Uí Ailella - the rulers of Connacht. The  superior destiny of Niall, and thus of his descendants, Uí Néill, is articulated in four chronologically linear incidents, and expressed with great skill in terms of inherited myths of kingship.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Néill;  Uí Briúin, Uí Ḟiachrach, Uí Ailella - the rulers of Connacht.

records.Title: Echtra Nerai al, Táin (bó) bé Aingen
records.Beginning lines: Bui Ailill ocus Medb aidchi samna i rRaith Cruachan cona techluch
records.Contents: Fashioned (or possibly re-fashioned) as a foretale (remscél) of Táin bó Cúailnge, this is a mysterious tale of human relations with the Otherworld (here the síd of Cruachan) in which human time dissolves and becomes non-sequential. There is no agreement either about the integrity of the narrative and its interpreation.

records.Title: Erchoitmed ingine Gulidi al. The excuse of Guilide's daughter
records.Beginning lines: Rí ro gab Mumain .i. Feidlimid mac Crimthainn. Luid side fecht and for mórchuairt Muman
records.Contents: Feidlimid mac Crimthainn (†847), king of Munster and his retinue, on circuit in West Munster, are caught in heavy snow and seek hospitality. The nearest house is that of Guilide of Áth Lóche, a bitter satirist. He is reluctant to entertain them. He sends out his daughter and she makes eloquent excuses ... She led Feidlimid into the house, he stayed for three days, and never in his reign did he get better food. A later salty Modern-Irish version entitled Ceasacht inghine Guilr, occurs in modern Munster MSS ...
records.Location of the narrative: Feidlimid mac Crimthainn (†847), king of Munster; Guilide of Áth Lóche

records.Title: Esnada Tige Buchet al. Feis Dúin Buchet al. Songs of Buchet's House
records.Beginning lines: Boí coire féile la Laigniu, Buchat a ainm. Tech n-óeged fer ṅh-Érenn a thech in Buchat (recension 1); Bóe coire féile la Laigniu .i. Buchet a ainm, maccu mBlæ a slonnud. Tech n-óeged fer nÉrenn a thech (recension 2); Cathaír cenn cóiced Banba ó tá in rígrad rochalma (recension 3).
records.Contents: Buchat had had a house of hospitality but was ruined by the demands of the brothers of his foster-daughter, Eithne, the greedy sons of Cathaír Már, king of Leinster. He complained to the aged Cathaír who could do nothing. Buchat fled to Kells with his foster-daughter and lived in a cabin. King Cormac mac Airt found Eithne, discovered her devotion to her foster-father, and sought to marry her. She accepted him only on condition he restored her foster-father's fortunes. And Buchat's house was again filled with music, laughter, and guests.
records.Location of the narrative: Eithne; Cathaír Már, king of Leinster, and his sons; Buchat; king Cormac mac Airt
records.info:: May be 10th century or earlier in origin (Greene, Stokes) David Greene, Fingal Rónáin and other stories (1955): 27. Whitley Stokes, ‘The songs of Buchet’s house’, Revue Celtique 25 (1904): 19;

records.Title: Fástini Airt meic Cuind & a chretem
records.Beginning lines: Lá ro boí Art mac Cuind ic selga i mBregaib (prose); Caín do Denna Den doma addonrúacht (verse)
records.Contents: Art mac Cuind, on his hunt at Duma Derglúachra, was vouchsafed a heavenly vision. He foresaw, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, his defeat in battle against Mac Con at Mag Mucrama and his own death. He believed, and willed to be buried where he had had the vision, the site of the future monastery of Trevet ... This prosimetrum text takes as read he tale of the battle of Mag Mucrama (1015). Thus the pagan ancestor of Uí Néill is made a precocious and devout christian, and buried at the monastery of Trevet (the dynastic church of the Uí Néill kingdom of Southern Brega) whose clergy thus claim the favour and protection of their Uí Néill overkings.
records.Location of the narrative: Art mac Cuind; Mac Con

records.Title: Feis Tige Chonáin
records.Beginning lines: Sealg throm-thorthach shaor-aoibhinn árd-aigeantach mhór-mheanmnach do comóradh le Fionn mac Cubhaill mic Tréinmhóir uí Bhaoiscne & le fianaibh gúsmhura gairg-bhéodha gníomh-éachtacha Gáoideal
records.Contents: … Conán questions Finn, who replies by telling tales. The style is painfully verbose, inflated with compound alliterating adjectives, piled one upon another. In fact, the tales are submerged in a tide of useless verbiage.
records.Location of the narrative: Conán; Finn

records.Title: Fingal Rónáin al. Aided Mael Fothartaig meic Rónáin
records.Beginning lines: Rí amra ro boí for Laignib .i. Rónán mac Aeda & Ethni ingen Chummascaig maic Eogain do Déisib 'na fharrad
records.Contents: … Rónán, king of Leinster, has unwisely married a young wife. He has a handsome and beloved son, Mael Fothartaig, from a previous union … Rónán's young wife solicits Mael Fothartaig with tragic results for all. The Irish tale is naturalistic: Mael Fothartaig seeks in vain to avoid his own dishonour, and the shame of others.
records.Location of the narrative: Rónán, king of Leinster; Mael Fothartaig
records.info::
Late Old Irish.(2) On the verse Greene and O'Connor remark that it “appears to belong to the Old Irish period, [but] there are some rhymes (fo-roígéne: fogéba: cúaine: úairi) that point to a later date”. “The absence of rhetorics and the length of the poems point to a comparatively late work; on the other hand, the language, consistent throughout, points to the end of the OIr. period, and the story [...] is given in the LL saga-list. All these considerations would suggest a date early in the tenth century”. David Greene, Fingal Rónáin and other stories (1955): 2.; 
Early 10th century (Greene)(3) or late 9th century (Greene and O'Connor).(4) composed probably towards the end of the ninth century”. David Greene • Frank O'Connor, A golden treasury of Irish poetry, A.D. 600 to 1200 (1967): 93.

records.Title: Finn & Gráinne
records.Beginning lines: Luid Find ua Baiscne do thochmarc Graindi ingine Cormaic uí Chuind
records.Contents: On the surface, this is a short tale about the difficult marriage of Gráinne, daughter of king Cormac mac Airt, and Finn. In fact, it is a legal exemplum on divorce law that concerns Gráinne's unhappy marriage to Finn, and the circumstance of its dissolution.
records.Location of the narrative: Gráinne, daughter of king Cormac mac Airt; Finn.

records.Title: Finn and the Man in the Tree
records.Beginning lines: Fo chosmailius do-rigne Finn úa Baíscne. In tan baí in fian oc Badamair for brú Siúire
records.Contents: Two short prose stories about Finn, cited in the commentary to the Senchas Már as a gloss on the term imbas forosnai. The first, about Finn's encounter with the supernatural thief Cúldub, tells how Finn acquired the gift of imbas, while the second story, about Finn and the gilla Derg Corra, tells how Finn put this gift to use.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn; Cúldub; Derg Corra moccu Daigre
records.info:: Meyer points to linguistic features which may indicate that the text belongs “to the late eighth or early ninth century”. Kuno Meyer, Fianaigecht (1910): xviii–xxix.

records.Title: Fled Bricrenn
records.Beginning lines: Boí fled mór la Bricrind Nemthenga do Conchobar mac Nessa & do Ultaib huile
records.Contents: Bricriu Nemthenga, the prime trouble maker, prepares a lavish feast in a splendid hall for the warriors of Ulaid, who take every precaution to avoid the conflict and slaughter he seeks to bring about. Without success, though they put him out. He sets the women of Ulaid to quarrell ... and he starts contention for the champion's portion between Cú Chulainn, and the other warriors ... In the end, Cú Roí ... challenges the contending warriors to a beheading game, from which Cú Chulainn alone coms out triumph.
records.Location of the narrative: Bricriu Nemthenga; Cú Chulainn; Cú Roí; Ulaid

records.Title: Fled Bricrenn & Loinges mac nDuíl Dermait
records.Beginning lines: Baí rí amra for Ultaib .i. Conchobar mac Nesa ainm in ríg. Do-rónad recht lais iar ngabáil rigi
records.Contents: The feast of Bricriu, his offence that it is not marked by any heroic deeds, and the mission of the Ulstermen to meet this remarkable demand. This leads to varied, often bloody, adventures of Cú Chulainn at home and abroad, and his final return to Emain Macha with his treasures. This poorly structured tale has intertextual echoes of Fled Bricrenn ... and of Táin Bó Cuailnge.
records.Location of the narrative: Bricriu; Cú Chulainn; Ulstermen
records.info:: Late Old Irish. Kaarina Hollo has concluded that “the general conservatism of the verbal system, the relatively high incidence of the neuter article and the handling of suffixed pronouns in LMDD are not inconsistent with a late Old Irish date of composition”; there are some later (e.g. Middle Irish) innovations to be found in the transmitted text, but on balance, LMDD “is best regarded as a text first written in the late Old Irish period that was subject to a certain amount of revision in the course of its manuscript transmission”.Kaarina Hollo, Fled Bricrenn ocus Loinges mac nDuíl Dermait and its place in the Irish literary and oral narrative traditions (2005): 38–49.

records.Title: Fled Dúin na nGéd
records.Contents: … literary accounts of the battle of (Mag) Roth (AD 637) between Congal Clóen, king of Dál nAraide and overking of Ulaid and Domnall Brecc (†642), king of Dál Riata on the one side and Domnall (†642) mac Áeda, overking of Uí Néill, on the other. Congal was defeated and slain. Domnall mac Áeda is represented as living at Dún na nGéd ... on the Boyne where he held a great feast for the men of Ireland. His servants outraged St Erc of Slane by seizing for the feast the saint's goose eggs, his penitential nourishment. The saint cursed the feast and hence the evil deadly conflict between Congal and Domnall ... Though Congal has twelve apostles of Ireland bless his feast, they failed to avert the curse. Congal feeling humiliated and wronged, left in a towering rage.  The saints, who failed to persuade him to return in peace, cursed him. He went to Britain, gathered a great foreign army, fought a doom-laden battle against Domnall mac Áeda at Mag Roth, and was defeated and slain.
records.Location of the narrative: Congal Clóen, king of Dál nAraide and overking of Ulaid; Domnall Brecc (†642), king of Dál Riata; Domnall (†642) mac Áeda, overking of Uí Néill; Congal; St Erc of Slane
records.Characters in the narrative: Mag Roth; Dún na nGéd; Boyne

records.Title: Fochonn loingse Fergusa meic Róig
records.Contents: The warriors, Dubthach Dáel Ulad and Fergus mac Roích, absent themselves from the splendid feasting of the Ulstermen in Emain Macha … Two fearsome ugly warriors come … The doorkeeper tells them that no man without an art may enter. They answer that they have many arts ... They are admitted. Here the text breaks off.
records.Location of the narrative: Dubthach Dáel Ulad; Fergus mac Roích

records.Title: Forbais Droma Damgaire
records.Beginning lines: Da saorclaind socheneoil batar ind Eirinn; as iat luatter o sunn amach .i. Fiacha Muilleathan mac Eoguin dalta Moga Ruith & Cormac mac Airt mheic Cuinn. Ocus in oenlo ro marbait a dha n-athair i cath Mucraimhe
records.Contents: A tale of great battle between Cormac mac Airt, legendary King of Ireland and Fiachu Muillethan, equally legendary king of Munster, in which Fiachu calls on the magical powers of the blind druid Mug Ruith, ancestor of Fir Maige Féne, to protect Munster against Cormac's aggression. Mug Ruith's reward is the terrority his descendants occupy Munster. This is developed from an unpublished Old Irish historicist narrative in the genealogies of Fir Maige Féne ... Another recension is referred to in the early Éoganacht documents ... In its twelfth-century form it is a response to the contemporary aggression of Uí Chaím (of Éoganacht Glendamnach),
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Airt, legendary King of Ireland; Fiachu Muillethan, legendary king of Munster; druid Mug Ruith, ancestor of Fir Maige Féne; Uí Chaím (of Éoganacht Glendamnach)

records.Title: Forfess Fer Falgae
records.Beginning lines: Incipit Forfess Fer Falgae .i. Fer Manonn isiside foillsigthi do Ultaib
records.Contents: An extremely succinct and difficult tale in Early Old Irish, from the lost Cín Droma Snechta, recounting Cú Chulainn's expedition to, and attack on, the Isle of Man and its king (or in the opinion of some the Otherworld). Much of this short text is in the form of three retorics.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn

records.Title: Fotha Catha Cnucha al. Cath Cnucha
records.Beginning lines: Dia mboí Cathaír Mór mac Fedelmthi Fir Urglais meic Cormaic Geltai Gaíth
records.Contents: …the origins of Finn, why he held Almu, and how deadly enmity arose between his family and Clann Morna.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn; Clann Morna
records.info:: 11th century Meyer

records.Title: Cnucha cnoc os cind Life
records.Beginning lines: Brughaidh cédach ro bui i crich Midhi, Brocán brughaidh a ainm (prose); Cuncha cnoc os cind Life ro boi uair ba hairithe (verse)
records.Contents: A prosi-metrum composition loosely linked to Cnucha (townland and parish of Castleknock, Co. Dublin). The prose appears to be an aetiological explanation of the name Dún Samhnaighe (townland and parish of Dunsany, barony of Skreen, Co. Meath), from Samhnach al. Samhnat.
records.Location of the narrative: Cnucha (townland and parish of Castleknock, Co. Dublin); Dún Samhnaighe (townland and parish of Dunsany, barony of Skreen, Co. Meath)

records.Title: Genemain Áeda Sláine
records.Beginning lines: Temair na ríg is sí ba dodgnas díles do cech ríg no gebed hÉrind (prose); Mugain ingen Choncraid chain (verse)
records.Contents: A royal tale of rivalry among the queens of Diarmait mac Cerbaill … The childless Mugain, deeply jealous of the king's other queens with famous sons, is blessed by St Finnén to make her fertile. She gives birth to a … Áed Sláne, the dynastic heir (ancestor and eponym of Síl nÁeda Sláne of Southern Uí Néill), whose virtues are lauded. The precise nuances of this remarkable tale for the dynasts of Southern Uí Néill remain to be grasped. The attached poem, inc. 'Mugain ingen...' attributed to Flann Mainistrech (†1056), rehearses the tale.
records.Location of the narrative: queens of Diarmait mac Cerbaill; Mugain; St Finnén; Áed Sláne, the dynastic heir (ancestor and eponym of Síl nÁeda Sláne of Southern Uí Néill)

records.Title: Genemain Chormaic al. Birth of Cormac
records.Beginning lines: Luid Art mac Cuind Cétchathaich do thabairt catha Mucrama i n-aigid Meic Con. Is ed luid co morsluagaib fer nErenn dar Sinainn siar
records.Contents: This is an early version of the birth legend of Cormac mac Airt and thus of Uí Néill origins. It links him closely to Luigne, Corcu'r Trí and Greccraige, early dynasties of the North Connacht area that declined in the early eighth century and before. These are represented as the fosterers and protectors of the infant Cormac, and thus the lineages and kingdoms of their descendants deserve the favour and protection of Uí Néill. This tale has its origin in a very early peroid before Uí Néill cut loose from their humbler North Connacht origins and re-shaped their history more grandly. Scéla Éogain & Cormaic (1094) is a reworking of this material. See also Lugna Fer Trí & Cormac mac Airt (1079)
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Airt; Uí Néill; Luigne, Corcu'r Trí and Greccraige, early dynasties of the North Connacht
records.info:: “on the whole Middle Irish”, although certains forms, especially in the rhetorics, “may have been inspired by an Old Irish source” Vernam Hull, ‘Geneamuin Chormaic’, Ériu 16 (1952): 80–81; Hull suggests that the text as a whole may be dated to c. 1250 and represent "a later reworking of much earlier material" Vernam Hull, ‘Geneamuin Chormaic’, Ériu 16 (1952): 81.

records.Title: Immacallam Choluim Chille & ind Óclaig
records.Beginning lines: Immacaldam Choluim Chille & ind oclaig oc Carraic Eolairg; as-berat alaili bad é Mongán mac Fiachnai
records.Contents: Colum Cille's conversation with a mysterious shape-shifting Otherworld youth at Carraic Eolairg, near Lough Foyle (he is Mongán, son of Manannán mac Lir).
records.Location of the narrative: Colum Cille; Mongán, son of Manannán mac Lir
records.info:: Despite archaising tendencies in orthography, “cartt for card = carn, Maggán, genir are genuine archaic spellings; and lastly, there are two forms which are not found outside our oldest glosses. These are mucintar (l. 26) and in tain (l. 25). The former represents a mixture of the oldest form of the word, montar (Wb. 7 c 5), and the later muinter. The use of the accusative in intain 'when' is another undoubted sign of great age, pointing to an Old-Irish original as the source from which our copy is derived. This original cannot have been later than the ninth century and may even be assigned to the eighth” Alfred Nutt • Kuno Meyer, ‘The colloquy of Colum Cille and the youth at Carn Eolairg’, Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 2 (1899): 314.

records.Title: Immacallam in dá thúarad al. Acallam in dá suad al. The colloquy of the two sages
records.Beginning lines: Adna mac Uithir de thuathaib Ól nÉcmacht ollam hÉrenn i n-éicsi & fhilidecht. Ata-comnaic mac laiside .i. Néde
records.Contents: Adna mac Uithir was ollam of Ireland. His son Néde had gone to Britain to study poetical wisdom with its masters. Néde learned, by divination, that his father had died and that his robe of office … had been given to Ferchertne the poet as his successor. He returned and, in the absence of Ferchertne, he donned the robe and sat in the poet's chair. When Ferchertne came back he engaged the youthful upstart Néde in a lengthy exchange on poetry and soical order in obscure and allusive language ... At its end, Néde gave up the robe to Ferchertne and recognises him as his senior and second father ...
records.Location of the narrative: Adna mac Uithir, ollam of Ireland; Néde; Ferchertne

records.Title: Immathchor (n)Ailella & Airt
records.Beginning lines: Léiccis Ailill Aulom a bein
records.Contents: On the surface, a text concerning the legendary kings Ailill Aulum (Ólom) and Art mac Cuind, but in reality a subtle treatment, in dramatic poetic dialogue, of the legal problems of affiliation and joint fosterage …
records.Location of the narrative: legendary kings Ailill Aulum (Ólom) and Art mac Cuind
records.info:: c. 700 (Corthals)

records.Title: Immram Brain al. Voyage of Bran
records.Beginning lines: Cóeca rand ro-gab in ben a tírib ingnad for lár in taige do Bran mac Febáil
records.Contents: Bran's voyage to a mysterious and enchanting Otherworld. He encounters the sea-god Manannán for whom the sea is a flowery plain. He and his companions reach the Land of Women, a place of pre-lapsarian beauty, without sin or death. Christian and pagan themes are mingled with great artistry.
records.Location of the narrative: Bran; Manannán

records.Title: Immram curaig Maíle Dúin - prose
records.Beginning lines: De Éoganacht Ninussa do Máel Dúin iar mbunadus. Ailill Ochair Ága a athair (prose)
records.Contents: A prosimetrum wonder-tale of Máel Dúin, love-child of Ailill Ochair Ága and an abbess, who puts to sea, with 17 companions and three supernumerary foster-brothers, to avenge himself on his father's killers. They reached islands … They now voyaged … '… they reached many peoples in the isles' ... They encounter austere Irish hermits, whose frugal nourishment comes direct from heaven. The last of these predicts that Máel Dúin will return, and find his father's killers, but urge him to seek no vengence.
records.Location of the narrative: Máel Dúin; Ailill Ochair Ága

records.Title: Immram curaig Maíle Dúin - verse
records.Beginning lines: Ardrí uasal inna n-uile tustid domuin (poetic text)
records.Contents: A prosimetrum wonder-tale of Máel Dúin, love-child of Ailill Ochair Ága and an abbess, who puts to sea, with 17 companions and three supernumerary foster-brothers, to avenge himself on his father's killers. They reached islands … They now voyaged … '… they reached many peoples in the isles' ... They encounter austere Irish hermits, whose frugal nourishment comes direct from heaven. The last of these predicts that Máel Dúin will return, and find his father's killers, but urge him to seek no vengence.
records.Location of the narrative: Máel Dúin; Ailill Ochair Ága

records.Title: Imram curaig Ua Corra
records.Beginning lines: Flaithbrugaid cétach comramach ro chinestar di chóiced Chonnacht .i. Conall Derg ua Corra Find
records.Contents: There are early medieval references Uí Chorra. This loosely structured ecclesiastical wonder tale belongs to the second half of the twelfth century. Among the author's concerns are violence towards the church, penitential pilgrimage, sabbatarianism, and marriage regulations. Mention of 'the Point of Spain', co Rind Esbainne (§75), may be an oblique reference to the pillgrimage of St James to Santiago de Compostela.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Chorra

records.Title: Imram Snédgusa & Meic Ríagla al. Echtra Chlérech Coluim Chille al. Merugud cléirech Coluim Chille - prose
records.Beginning lines: Baí dochraite mór for Feraib Roiss iar ndíth Domnaill meic Aeda meic Anmirech & ba hé fochand a ndochraide (prose recension A); An tan tánic derid tígi & aimsiri do Domnall mac Aeda meic Ainmirech d'airdríg Érenn do-rigni timna (prose recension B)
records.Contents: Fir Roiss slew their ruler, the oppressive Fiachu, brother of king Donnchad. The king imprisoned them and thought to burn them alive, but then he sought the judgement of Colum Cille (Columba). The Iona clerics, Snédgus and Mac Ríagla, returned with that judgement viz. ... On their way back to Iona, Snédgus and Mac Ríagla decided to make voyage on the ocean ... They return bringing two precious relics, the cowl and the cuilebad (flabellum).
records.Location of the narrative: Fir Roiss; Fiachu, brother of king Donnchad; Colum Cille; Snédgus; Mac Ríagla
records.info:: The oldest version of this tale, of the tenth century, is the poetic one in 76 st. in the metre dechnad cummaisc, attributed to a fer dána in the prose. The prose itself derives from the poem, as Thurneysen (1904) elegantly proves.

records.Title: Imram Snédgusa & Meic Ríagla al. Echtra Chlérech Coluim Chille al. Merugud cléirech Coluim Chille - verse
records.Beginning lines: Snédgus & Mac Riaghail do munntir Colum Cille (verse)
records.Contents: Fir Roiss slew their ruler, the oppressive Fiachu, brother of king Donnchad. The king imprisoned them and thought to burn them alive, but then he sought the judgement of Colum Cille (Columba). The Iona clerics, Snédgus and Mac Ríagla, returned with that judgement viz. ... On their way back to Iona, Snédgus and Mac Ríagla decided to make voyage on the ocean ... They return bringing two precious relics, the cowl and the cuilebad (flabellum).
records.Location of the narrative: Fir Roiss; Fiachu, brother of king Donnchad; Colum Cille; Snédgus; Mac Ríagla

records.Title: Imthecht Cáenchomraic al. Scél Saltrach na Muice
records.Beginning lines: Espuc amra boi hi Cluain Meic Nóis, Coenchomrac Indsi Endoim a ainm
records.Contents: Ecclesiastical legend of Cáenchomrac (†903), a holy bishop of Clonmacnoise and Inis Éndoim (Inchenagh or Inshenagh) in the north of Lough Ree, near its east shore; his wonderful powers; and his dealings with the mysterious underwater monastery of Lough Ree and its remarkable community. This legend is connected with historicist materials about Meic Cuinn na mBocht, a lineage of hereditary clerics and scholars at Clonmacnoise. According to interpolated annals, Cáenchomrac, bishop and abbot of Lugmad (later pilgrim at Clonmacnoise), was the fosterer/teacher Dúnadach (†955) and Óenucán (†947/949) mac Écertaig. In the tale the fosterlings become Éogan and Écertach, two sons of Áeducán. In effect the tale expresses the claim of Meic Cuinn na mBocht to the churches and income of bishop Cáenchomrac.
records.Location of the narrative: Cáenchomrac (†903); Meic Cuinn na mBocht; Cáenchomrac; Dúnadach (†955); Óenucán (†947/949) mac Écertaig; Éogan and Écertach, two sons of Áeducán
records.Characters in the narrative: Clonmacnoise and Inis Éndoim (Inchenagh or Inshenagh) in the north of Lough Ree

records.Title: Imthechta Tuirill Picreo & a mac al. Oidheadh Chlainne Tuireann
records.Beginning lines: Imthechta Tuirill Picreo & a mac .i. Brian, Iuchair, Iucharba, is ed at-fedar hi sunn & do Delbæth mac Ogma (version 1, prose); Étsid in senchas slúagach fo-chan écsi ilbúadach (version 1, verse); Rígh sochrach saoirchinéalach ro ghabh flaithios agus forlámhas ar Thuathaibh datháille Dé Danann (version 2)
records.Contents: Brian, Iuchair and Iucharba, divine figures of the Túátha Dé, killed Ethliu at Brug na Bóinne and his son Lug demanded precious talisman as his éraic (the list varies with the versions); the horses of the king of Sicily, the spear of Assal, the pig skin of Dúise, the swine of Essach, the pup of the royal smith of Irúaid, and, besides, the uncovering of the undersea island of Caire Cennfine and its apples. They perform all these labours.
records.Location of the narrative: Brian, Iuchair and Iucharba, divine figures of the Túátha Dé; Ethliu; Lug;
records.info:: There are two versions. The eleventh-century fragmentary text is verse (the earlier form), and its somewhat later but still medieval prose derivative. The early-Modern Irish one, Oidheadh Chlainne Tuireann, is complete and has its origin, perhaps, in the fourteenth to the sixteenth centuries.

records.Title: Longes mac nUislenn (Uisnig)
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia mboí loṅges mac nUsnig? Ní ansa. Bátar Ulaid oc ól i taig Ḟeidlimthe maic Daill scélaigi Conchobuir
records.Contents: Conventionally regarded as a fore-tale (remscél) of Táin bó Cúailnge … in the story of the ominous and fore-doomed Deirdriu, the human struggle against fate, and the evil outcome of unjust kingship …
records.Location of the narrative: Deirdriu

records.Title: Lugna Fer Trí & Cormac mac Airt: fragmenta
records.Roman dates: s. xii; reworking of very early material s. vi/vii?
records.Beginning lines: Ceitgęin Cruachna mac Conaill Cruachna tar ęis Forgusa (i); Ro gab Cormac ua Cuind rígi Érenn doridisi ar tuitim na trí Fergus leis i cath Crinna (ii); Fecht n-aon do-luid Aedh Oirnidhi mac Neill Frosaidh (iii)
records.Contents: (i) This brief historicist tale of early relations between king Cormac mac Airt, Lugna Fer Trí and his son Nia Noí Gráinne, preserved in a tract on the prehistoric kings of Connacht, is a faint echo of tales of Lugna Fer Trí and the origin legends of the once-powerful Luigne, Gailenga, Grecraige and other North Connacht dynasties. (ii) A late fragment, Cormac's dream, is a short, richly symbolic, tale of Cormac's expulsion from the kingship of Tara. cf Genemain Chormaic (1068). (iii) The tale of the drinking-horns of Cormac mac Airt ... (Early Modern Irish text)...
records.Location of the narrative: king Cormac mac Airt;  Lugna Fer Trí and his son Nia Noí Gráinne

records.Title: Macgnímartha Finn al. Boyhood deeds of Finn
records.Beginning lines: Dorala comtinol aigh & imfich debtha imon fianaigecht & im ardmaeraigecht Eirenn
records.Contents: This account of the youthful exploits of Finn is a scholar's compilation, made in the twelfth century, derived from written materials about Finn as old as the ninth, or indeed older. This is reflected in references to ancient lineages (for example, Corcu Óche) and in 'Finn's poem in May' (inc. 'Cétamain, cain cucht rée rpshaír rann': s. ix), which occurs in the text.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn
records.info:: As a narrative it is too loosely structured, but it may not be intended as a narrative; 12th century (Meyer)

records.Title: Macha Mongrúad al. Dindshenchas of Emain Macha
records.Beginning lines: Cid diatá Eomuin Machæ? Ní anse. Bui righi nErenn hi comflaithius
records.Contents: A brief text on the princess Macha who, by force and guile, shares the kingship of Ulster in her turn with rival male heirs. She overpowers her opponents, the five sons of Díthorbae, militarily and sexually, and forces them to dig the ramparts of Emain Macha, as she marks them out with her brooch.
records.Location of the narrative: Macha; the five sons of Díthorbae

records.Title: Mesca Ulad al. Baothrém Ulad co Temair Luachra
records.Beginning lines: Ó do-riachtatar Meic Míled Espáine hÉrind tánic a ṅgáes timchell Túaithi Dé Danann
records.Contents: Extant in two recensions, both defective. The second dates to the twelfth century. In the first part, king Conchobar invited the aristocracy to a great feast at Emain Macha, where he is allowed to be king of the divided province for a year. Under his rule, by fragile agreement, Ulster prospers. The second part, poorly spliced to the first, describes a wild drunken Ulster chariot ride across Ireland, led by Cú Chulainn, to Temair Luachra in SW Munster, where Cú Roí mac Dáire is lord, and the high jinks of the Ulstermen on arrival.
records.Location of the narrative: Conchobar; Cú Chulainn; Cú Roí mac Dáire
records.Characters in the narrative: Temair Luachra, SW Munster; Emain Macha, Ulster
records.info:: The language is inflated, the events extravagant, the style parodic…

records.Title: Mongán Tales (1. Compert Mongán; 2. Scél asa mberat co mbad hé Find mac Cumaill & aní díá fil Aided Fothaid Airgdig; 3. Scél Mongán, 4. Tucait Baile Mongán; 5. 'Why Mongán was deprived of noble issue '
records.Beginning lines: Boí Fiachnae Lurgan, athair Mongáin, ba hoínrí a chóicid (Compert Mongán); Boí Mongán hi Ráith Móir Maigi Line ina rígiu (Scél asa mberar…); Dia mboí dano Forgoll fili la Mongán fecht n-and (Scél Mongán); Eissistir ben Mongáin .i. Findtigernd do Mongán ara n-indissed dí diuiti a imthechtae (Tucait Baile Mongán); Eochaid Rígéiges ardfili na hÉrend ro baí Fiachna oca chuired ('Why Mongán was deprived of noble issue')
records.Contents: These are tales of Mongán (†625) mac Fiachnai, of the royal dynasty of Dál Fiatach in Ulster that have their origin in the Ulad genealogies. According to §1 Mongán is really son of Manannán mac Lír … and is Find mac Cumaill redivivus. Three tales have to do with the royal poet (§§2, 3, 5): Dallán Forgall al. Eochaid Rígéces is by times greedy, extortionate of his king, wrong-headed, mean (by implication) to his student poet, and ignorant ... The final (§6) draws on the stories of Mongán as a source for a merry and astringent clerical tale of royal loves and marriages, which ends with the amorous king of Leinster waking up, sober, with the old hag of the mill in his bed.
records.Location of the narrative: Mongán (†625) mac Fiachnai, of the royal dynasty of Dál Fiatach;  son of Manannán mac Lír; Find mac Cumaill; Dallán Forgall al. Eochaid Rígéces
records.info:: The re-telling is the sardonic work of a learned and witty man of letters who knew the early stories of Mongán well and used them skillfully as sources and, very likely, as intertextual resonants, for his new creation.

records.Title: Mongán Tales -  6. Compert Mongáin & serc Duibhe Lacha)
records.Beginning lines: Feacht n-æn dá ndeachaid Fiachna Find mac Bædáin mheic Murcertaigh mheic Muiredhaigh (Compert Mongáin & serc Duibe Lacha)
records.Contents: These are tales of Mongán (+625) mac Fiachnai, of the royal dynasty of Dál Fiatach in Ulster that have their origin in the Ulad genealogies. According to §1 Mongán is really son of Manannán mac Lír … and is Find mac Cumaill redivivus. Three tales have to do with the royal poet (§§2, 3, 5): Dallán Forgall al. Eochaid Rígéces is by times greedy, extortionate of his king, wrong-headed, mean (by implication) to his student poet, and ignorant ... The final (§6) draws on the stories of Mongán as a source for a merry and astringent clerical tale of royal loves and marriages, which ends with the amorous king of Leinster waking up, sober, with the old hag of the mill in his bed.
records.Location of the narrative: Mongán (†625) mac Fiachnai, of the royal dynasty of Dál Mongán (†625) mac Fiachnai, of the royal dynasty of Dál Fiatach;  son of Manannán mac Lír; Find mac Cumaill; Dallán Forgall al. Eochaid Rígéces
