records.Title: Orgain Néill Noígíallaig al. Aided Néill Noígíallaig
records.Beginning lines: Fecht n-aill do-luid Echu mac Énna ó thig Néill fodes dia thír
records.Contents: A king-tale … created about the ancestor and eponym of Uí Néill. It has two separate themes: bitter dynastic conflict, in Brega, between Uí Néill and Uí Chennselaig (Laigin), here represented by their eponymous ancestors; and memories of Irish overseas raiding in Late Antiquity, unhistorically attached to Niall. Both serve to glorify Uí Néilll.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Néill; Uí Chennselaig (Laigin)
records.CODECS:: https://codecs.vanhamel.nl/Orcuin_N%C3%A9ill_No%C3%ADg%C3%Adallaig; https://codecs.vanhamel.nl/Aided_N%C3%A9ill_No%C3%ADg%C3%Adallaig; Cf. the longer version in Orcuin Néill Noígíallaig, and a verse version in the dindsenchas poem Déiccid ferta níthaig Néill.
records.info:: Fragments of a much older version of the first theme, favourable to Laigin, are embedded in the earliest genealogies of Uí Chennselaig …

records.Title: Orgain Denna Ríg
records.Beginning lines: Boí Cobthach Cóel Breg mac Úgaine Móír i rríge Breg
records.Contents: A scholar's tale of the killing at Dinn Ríg, the Leinster stronghold near Leighlin on the river Barrow, of the jealous and murderous Cobthach Cóel Breg, king of Brega, and his retinue of thirty kings, fired in an iron house by Labraid Loingsech Móen, mythical ancestor of the Leinstermen. It reflects the centuries-long hostility between Leinster and Brega ... It is clear that it is constructed from much earlier material in the Leinster genealogies and origin legends.
records.Location of the narrative: Cobthach Cóel Breg, king of Brega; Labraid Loingsech Móen, mythical ancestor of the Leinstermen
records.Characters in the narrative: Dinn Ríg, the Leinster stronghold near Leighlin on the river Barrow; Brega

records.Title: Orgain trí mac Diarmata meic Cerbaill
records.Beginning lines: Lotar meic Diarmata meic Fergusa Ceirrbéoil fecht i tír Laigen for creich
records.Contents: Three sons of king Diarmait mac Cerbaill, king of Tara, raided Leinster. They encountered and attacked the warrior Máelodrán, son of Dímma Crón, who pursued them … he killed them. Later, Diarmait is reconciled with Máelodrán who becomes his battle champion. The tale, which purports to deal with an event of the mid seventh century is not historical.
records.Location of the narrative: Three sons of king Diarmait mac Cerbaill, king of Tara; Máelodrán, son of Dímma Crón
records.info:: Old and Middle Irish "In their present form these stories [Aided Máelodráin and Orgguin trí mac Díarmata mic Cerbaill] show a confusion of earlier and later forms, and there are so many minor variations of wording that it would be hard to come to any conclusion as to the original text. But enough archaic forms are preserved […] to make it possible that the date of the original composition was within the Old Irish period.” David Greene, Fingal Rónáin and other stories (1955).

records.Title: Finn & Oisín
records.Beginning lines: Is derb lem-sae cia domaimse in fer laith (poem); Boí Find úa Baíscne fo Érinn oc cuinchid a maic .i. Oisín (prose)
records.Contents: An obscure prosimetrum on conflict between Finn and his son, Oisín.
records.Location of the narrative: Finn; Oisín
records.info:: The poem “must have been composed during the Old Irish period, perhaps even as early as the eighth century”, although the text is imperfectly preserved in later manuscripts (Hull, following Meyer) Vernam Hull, ‘The quarrel between Finn and Oisin’, Modern Language Notes 57 (1942): 434.

records.Title: Reicne Fothaid Canainne - prose
records.Beginning lines: Buí rígféinnid for Condachtaib fecht n-aill .i. Fothad Canainde (prose)
records.Contents: The great warrior Fothad Canainne wins … wife of Ailill mac Éogain, and makes off with her. Ailill pursues and kills Fothad …
records.Location of the narrative: Fothad Canainne; wife of Ailill mac Éogain; Ailill mac Éogain

records.Title: Reicne Fothaid Canainne - verse
records.Beginning lines: A ben nacham-aicille! ní friot atá mo menmo (verse)
records.Contents: The great warrior Fothad Canainne wins … wife of Ailill mac Éogain, and makes off with her. Ailill pursues and kills Fothad …
records.Location of the narrative: Fothad Canainne; wife of Ailill mac Éogain; Ailill mac Éogain

records.Title: Scél na Fírflatha, Echtra Chormaic i Tír Tairngire & Ceart Claidib Chormaic
records.Beginning lines: Rí uasal oirdnide rogabastar flaithius & forlámus for Érinn fecht n-aill .i. Cormac ua Cuind eisidhe (recension 1); Fechtus do bi Cormac hua Cuinn a Liatruim (recension 2)
records.Contents: This is a composite text made of parts separate in origin and date. The reign of king Cormac mac Airt was a golden age of prosperity and good law. Twelve ordeals … the authors avers … The text is a series of imaginative reflections, some in narrative form, by a very learned lawyer and scholar, on law (including its written form), society, literacy, and culture.
records.Location of the narrative: king Comarc mac Airt

records.Title: Scél Túain maic Cairill al. Immacallam Túain fri Finnio
records.Contents: When St Finnio brought the gospel to Ulster, he encountered an aged venerable cleric, Túan mac Cairill, settled on his father's lands. When Finnio asked the ancient about the history of Ireland, he narrated its pre-history since its first occupation … Túan himself was the sole survivor ... reborn as the son of king Cairell. When an old man he was baptised by St Patrick ... creating the Irish origin legend, of an obvious problem viz. how remote Irish pre-history could have been known and preserved.
records.Location of the narrative: St Finnio; Túan mac Cairill; St Patrick

records.Title: Scéla Cano maic Gartnáin
records.Beginning lines: Baí imchosnom im rígi nAlban iter Oedán mac Gabráin & Gartnán mac Æeda maic Gabráin
records.Contents: A historical romance of Cano's flight to Ireland, his sojourn with kings Diarmait and Blathmac; his visit to king Guaire, and his love for Créd, daughter of Guaire and wife of Marcán, king of Uí Maine; his long stay with Illann, king of Corcu Loígde; his triumphant return to Scotland; his attempted final tryst with Créd, and their deaths. The characters are historical, not the tale.
records.Location of the narrative: Cano; kings Diarmait; king Blathmac; king Guaire; Créd, daughter of Guaire and wife of Marcán, king of Uí Maine; Illann, king of Corcu Loígde

records.Title: Scéla Conchobuir meic Nessa
records.Beginning lines: Ropo ḟer amra airegda inti Conchobar mac Nessa. Imráter sunda for Ulltaib
records.Contents: The story tells how Conchobar, son of the female warrior Ness (daughter of Eochu Sálbuide) and Cathbad, born at exactly the same time as Christ, became king of Ulster …
records.Location of the narrative: Conchobar, son of the female warrior Ness (daughter of Eochu Sálbuide); Cathbad
records.info:: The first three paragraphs also found in Compert Conchobuir; early Middle Irish Whitley Stokes, ‘Tidings of Conchobar mac Nessa’, Ériu 4 (1910): 18; This is to be read as an intertextual commentary on the classic sagas, and lest the reader miss the point, Táin bó Cúailnge is named and there are clear cross-reference to Scéla mucce meic Dathó and Fled Bricree - and to the troublemaker Bricriu ...

records.Title: Scéla Éogainn & Cormaic al. Scéla Geine Cormaic
records.Beginning lines: Luid Éugan Mór do chath Mucruime. Fíu hi tig Tréth moccu Chreccai
records.Contents: A version of the birth tale of Cormac mac Airt, linguistically the earliest, historically the latest. Here the plot of Genemain Chormaic (1068) is reworked. The role of Lugna and Connacht is much reduced, and Cormac's principal protector is Fiachrae Cassán ... is ancestor of Ind Airthir, the branch of Airgialla that controlled Armagh, and this recension may represent the claim of Armagh and its ruling lineages to favour of the Uí Néill kings. The opening of the tale that tells of the birth of Fiachu Muillethan does not properly belong here.
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Airt; Fiachrae Cassán
records.info:: Ó Cathasaigh argues that the two manuscript versions derive from a common ancestor written in classical Old Irish. While he allows for the possibility that the latter may be a reworking of the text made in the Middle Irish period, “we can be reasonably sure that the content of the story is much as it was in the O. I. ancestor of L and H”. Tomás Ó Cathasaigh, The heroic biography of Cormac mac Airt (1977): 115–117.

records.Title: Scéla Mo Shauluim & Maic Con
records.Beginning lines: Ailill Mo Ṡaulum mac Moga Núadat ba rí for leith hÉirenn & ba druí
records.Contents: Ailill Ólom … evidently an early figure in Munster pre-history, occurs in the genealogies and narrative texts, an ancestor of the Eóganacht rulers of Munster. This is a compilation of several narratives, some very early (s. vii, or before), some later, on the kingship of Munster and the rights to sovereignty of the competing dynasties, Dáirine (al. Corcu Loígde) and Éoganacht ... alleged lineage founders, Mac Con and Ailill Ólom respectively ... The text is larded with interpolated genealogy, an important early legal passage on paternity, and indifferent verse by an editor with more learning than taste.
records.Location of the narrative: Ailill Ólom; Mac Con; Dáirine (al. Corcu Loígde); Éoganacht
records.info:: 9th century (O'Daly)

records.Title: Scéla mucce meic Dathó
records.Beginning lines: Boí rí amrae for Laignib, Mac Dathó a ainm. Boí cú occo
records.Contents: The story tells of a dispute between the Conachta, led by Ailill and Medb, and the Ulaid, led by Conchobar mac Nessa, over the acquisition of the hound of Leinster, Ailbe. The dispute is ultimately resolved through the plan of the king of Leinster, Mac Da Thó, to hold a feast at his hostel ...
records.Location of the narrative: Conchobar; Ailill; Medb; Dátho

records.Title: Sénad Saigre
records.Beginning lines: Sluaighedh la Donnchadh mac Flainn mhic Mailsechlainn do dhénumh múir & cluidh i timchill Saighri Ciaráin
records.Contents: A historicist narrative on the dubious, indeed infernal, origin of crossáin … and their art that may mark their rise in status and perhaps their convergence (at least in part) with professional poets. This narrative, from within and about the literary milieu itself, reflects the changing nature of the poetic order and its craft in the twelfth century, when its relationship with society in general, and with the church in particular, greatly changed.

records.Title: Senchas na relec
records.Beginning lines: Mórrí mórbrethach ro gab os hErind .i. Cormac mac Airt (prose); Án sin a maig Meic ind Óc fairsing do rót rethaib cét (verse)
records.Contents: A tale about the death of king Cormac mac Airt (one of the pagan kings represented as believers in the christian God) and his prescriptions about his burial, viz. that he be buried not in the pagan cemetery of Brug na Bóinne al. Newgrange, but at Ros na Ríg, near the great church of Slane. This is followed by a discourse on the pagan burial places of Ireland to which is appended a poem on Brug na Bóinne (1152, 22st.) attributed to Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975).
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Airt
records.Characters in the narrative: Brug na Bóinne; Ros na Ríg

records.Title: Serglige Con Culainn & Óenét Emire
records.Beginning lines: Óenach dognithe la Ultu cecha bliadna .i. trí lá ria samfuin & tri laa iarma & lathe na samna feisne. Iss ed eret no bítis Ulaid insin i mMaig Murthemni (text); Nírbat taerrechtach debtha déne dóergairce (Briatharthecosc)
records.Contents: A tale in prose and verse of the love-sickness of Cú Chulainn induced by Fand, wife of Manannán mac Lir, Cú Chulainn's journey to her court in the Otherworld, his love for Fand, and the jealousy of his wife Emer … The text, somewhat unskillfully, combines two originally separate narratives, one perhaps of the tenth century, the other of the eleventh, and these, in turn, go back to an earlier tale, perhaps of the eighth century.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn; Fand, wife of Manannán mac Lir; Emer

records.Title: Síaburcharpat Con Culainn
records.Beginning lines: Dolluid Patraic do Themraig do erail creitme for ríg nErend .i. for Loegaire mac Néill (recension 1); Luith Patraic do Temraig & rl. Luith Laogairi doa agaltam Patraic (recension 2)
records.Contents: This text, clearly a product of the schools of Armagh and in the tradition of the Patrick legend, is a reflection, in narrative form, on the relationship between the church and the heroic pagan past and its literature…
records.Place text was written: product of the school of Armagh
records.Location of the narrative: St Patrick; Cú Chulainn

records.Title: Suidigud Tellaig Temra
records.Beginning lines: Bátar Uí Néill fecht and i Maig Breg
records.Contents: A learned mythical and cosmological text on the origins of Ireland, its people, its qualities, its laws, and its divisions, as narrated by Fintan, an antediluvian survivor, who thus knows all prehistory and who cites as his authority a mysterious Trefuilgnid Treochair ....
records.Location of the narrative: Fintan

records.Title: Táin bó Cúailnge
records.Beginning lines: Tarcomlad slóig mór la Connachtu .i. la hAilill & la Meidb & hetha húaidib cossna trí chóiced aili (recension 1); Fecht n-óen do Ailill & do Meidb íar ndérgud a rígleptha dóib i Crúachanráith Chonnacht (recension 2); … n-aidhed congresa iad nó do rothaibh in carbaid iarnaidi (recension 3); As andsin do hiomraidheadh ag fearoibh Eirionn cia budh coir do chathughadh re Coin ccathbhuaghach cCulainn (recension 4)
records.Contents: Táin bó Cúailnge tells of the great Connacht expedition to seize the Brown Bull of Cúailnge.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn

records.Title: Táin bó Dartada al. Darta
records.Beginning lines: Boí Eochu Bec mac Corpri rí Cliach i nDún Cuilne
records.Contents: … remscél of Táin bó Cúailnge … Ailill and Medb, rulers of Connacht, seek the help of king Eochu Becc of Clíu in provisioning their army which is to attack Ulster. Eochu agrees to help … Otherworld figures … Eochu falls. The same uncanny Otherworld figures urge Ailill, whose son loves Dartaid, daughter of Eochu Becc, to drive off Dartaid's cattle, and they accoutre his troops with the equipment of Eochu's fallen retinue. They then warn the Munster hero, Corb Cliach mac Tassaig, of the impending raid. Except for Ailill's son and eight warriors, all the Connacht raiders are slain, and Dartaid, too, is killed.
records.Location of the narrative: Ailill; Medb; king Eochu Becc;  Dartaid, daughter of Eochu Becc; Corb Cliach mac Tassaig
records.info:: “Die ältere Fassung [YBL/Egerton] zeigt die Sprache und Erzählungsart der älteren irischen Sagen etwa des 9. Jahrhunderts” (Thurneysen 1921).

records.Title: Táin bó Flidais
records.Beginning lines: Boí Flidais ben Ailella Find i crich Ciarraige. Caris Fergus mac Rooig ar a airscélaib (recension 1); A haithle Chloinne hUislenn do mharbhadh ar slánaighecht Fherghusa mhic Róigh táinic bhuidhéin co hEamhain Mhacha (recension 2)
records.Contents: A Connacht tale, created in part from earlier materials, about the relationship between Fergus mac Róig and Ailill & Medb, on the one hand, and Fildais (who loves Fergus) and her husband Ailill Finn, on the other. It issues in violent conflict, slaughter and pillage, and the bloody defeat of Ailill Finn. Flidais becomes the consort of Fergus.
records.Location of the narrative: Fergus mac Róig; Ailill; Medb; Fildais; Ailill Finn

records.Title: Táin bó Fraích
records.Beginning lines: Fróech mac Idaith do Chonnachtaib, mac side do Bé Find a sídaib
records.Contents: The tale is a compilation of two dissonant originally independent parts, loosely joined. The first is a stylish tale of the handsome Fróech's wooing of Findabair, daughter of Ailill and queen Medb … The short second part … tells of Fróech's recovery, with the help of Conall Cernach, of his stolen herds from beyond the Alps. And Fróech goes on to Táin bó Cúailnge. That part, to judge by its end (§30), was written at the monastery of Bangor and reflects the link with Lombardy and Bobbio. The conventional title only belongs to the second part.
records.Location of the narrative: Fróech; Findabair; Conall Cernach

records.Title: Táin bó Regamain
records.Beginning lines: Laechbrugaid amra ro bi la Connachta i n-aimsir Ailella & Medba (MS i)
records.Contents: The cattle-rich Connacht warrior Regamon had seven daughters, loved by seven sons of king Ailill and Medb, but these rulers needed cattle to feed troops. They sent their relunctant sons to get them. All is restored amicably. Regamon's herds are returned, his daughters marry the sons of Ailill, and are given a dowry of 140 cows, which animals are food for the hosts on Táin bó Cúailnge.
records.Location of the narrative: Regamon, his seven daughters;  seven sons of king Ailill and Medb

records.Title: Táin bó Regamna
records.Beginning lines: Dia mbai Cú Chulaind ina cotlad i nDún Imrind co cuala in gém
records.Contents: Cú Chulainn, awakened by a fearful roar from the north, goes with his charioteer to find its source. He encounters a chariot … which sits a red woman … As Cú Chulainn is about to spring into the chariot, she and the chariot vanish, and she re-appears as a black crow. She is Badh, the goddess of death, and she warns Cú Chulainn that, in many shapes she will bring about his doom.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn; Badh

records.Title: Talland Étair al. Forbais Étair
records.Beginning lines: Bói fer amnas étrócar i nÉre .i. Aithirne Áilgesach a ainm, mac-side Ferchertni di Ultaib.
records.Contents: This is a parodic tale of the poet Athirne's circuit of Ireland, his outrageous demands, and the dire consequences of his actions, namely, the mutual slaughter of the Ulaid and the Laigin. It is directed at the excesses of poets and the disastrous results of so-called heroism and honour.
records.Location of the narrative: Athirne; Ulaid; Laigin
records.info:: The references to Eochaid Ballderg … and Derb Fhorgaill ingen ríg Lochlainne … indicate a date in the end of the ninth century at the earliest, more porbably the tenth.

records.Title: Tesmolto Cormaic & Aided Fhinn al. Aided Fhinn
records.Beginning lines: Airdrigh uasal oirmitnech ro gab uas Erinn .i. Cormac mac Airt meic Cuinn Chétchathaig
records.Contents: A high-flown panegyric of king Cormac mac Airt and the wonderful abundance of all good things in his reign. Meanwhile, Finn. The commander of his troops, was the finest of soliders and military leaders. However, he was slain in battle by the Lúaigne, near the Boyne. The author of this text was familiar with the classical translations of the twelfth century and may have been a lawyer.
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Airt; Finn; Lúaigne
records.info:: 12th century (Meyer).(1)

records.Title: Tochmarc Ailbe
records.Beginning lines: Baí fic idir Cormac ua Cuind & Find ua Baíscne. Ba hé fochonn na debtha .i. Gráinne (text); Fris comart duid a chaím a Citruaid (retoiric)
records.Contents: Situated at the court of Cormac, king of Ireland, at the time of the Feast of Tara … this prosimetrum tale of marital relations, past and future, between the daughters of king Cormac and the older warrior Finn … ; (A significant part of the text is taken up by their conversations, which involve a series of riddles and verbal games that establish their mental and intellectual complementarity.)
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Airt; Finn; Ailbe

records.Title: Tochmarc Becfhola
records.Beginning lines: Baí Diarmait mac Aeda Sláne i rrígi Temrach, Crimthann mac Áeda i ndaltus dó
records.Contents: A mysterious, part-Otherworldly and part-ironic tale of explicit and assertive female desire, and the reaction to the protagonist, Becfhola, of three very different men: Diarmait mac Áeda Sláine, king of Tara; his foster-son and hostage, Crimthann, a Leinster prince; and the enigmatic Flann ua Fedaig, a lord embroiled in a lineage feud. The dénouement is missing, and the ending (§12) appears to be a later substitution. The tale may have been written at the church of Devenish.
records.Location of the narrative: Becfhola; Diarmait mac Áeda Sláine, king of Tara; his foster-son and hostage, Crimthann, a Leinster prince; Flann ua Fedaig

records.Title: Tochmarc Emire
records.Beginning lines: Baí rí amrae airegdae i nEmain Macha fecht n-aill .i. Conchobar mac Fachtnai Fáthaig. Baí már de amru ina flaith la Ulltu
records.Contents: … Cú Chulainn's courtship of Emer and of his training in arms by Scáthach.
records.Location of the narrative: Cú Chulainn; Emer; Scáthach

records.Title: Tochmarc Étaíne
records.Beginning lines: (i) Baí rí amra for Eirinn do Thuathaib De a chenel, Eochaid Ollathair a ainm; (ii) Gabais Eochaidh Airium rigi nErenn. Airgiallsat coic coicidh Erenn do; (iii) Feachtas n-aili asraracht Eochaid Aireann ri Teamrach (MS iii)
records.Contents: … tales of Étaín …wooed and won in the Otherworld by its king Midir. She was turned into … fly by her rival Fúamnach, who blew her into this world. She was swallowed in a drink by a queen in Ulster, and reborn as human. In the end, she was won back to the Otherworld by Midir.
records.Location of the narrative: Étaín; king Midir; Fúamnach

records.Title: Tochmarc Ferbe al. Fís Conchobar
records.Beginning lines: Aslinge Conchobar chóir meic Cathbad cróda findmóir (verse); … airgit oengil friu lénti bangela co n-esnadaib corcraib (prosimetrum)
records.Contents: … remscél to Táin bó Cúailnge. According to Thurneysen the development of the texts is as followed: the poem, remscél to the Táin as it states…, is the earliest (s. x); the mid twelfth century prosimetrum in the Book of Leinster … is based directly on the poem; and the prose recension (MS ii) is a later reworking of the same.

records.Title: Tochmarc Lúaine & Aided Athirne
records.Beginning lines: Baí Conchobar mac Nessa i Cuma & i toirsi & i ndomenmain dermáir
records.Contents: Conchobar's ugly messenger searches Ireland for a suitable wife for him and finds the extravagantly beautiful Lúaine. Meanwhile Athirne Áilgesach the poet and his two sons visit Lúaine, desire her, and threaten to satirise her if she does not yield to them. She refuses, they satirise her, and she dies of shame. They flee in fear of Conchobar and the Ulstermen. These take their vengeance. They raze and burn Athirne's house, and kill him, his family and his followers, including his two daughters.
records.Location of the narrative: Conchobar; Lúaine; Athirne Áilgesach the poet and his two sons; Conchobar and the Ulstermen
records.info:: second half of the 12th century (Breatnach)

records.Title: Tochmarc Momera al. The courtship of Momera
records.Beginning lines: Fecht n-óen d'Eugan Taidlech for faithche baile a athar fęsin Mogha Néit hic Raith Airthir Ḟęmin
records.Contents: Éogan Már, ancestor and eponum of the Éoganacht, is informed by the sons of the druid of Éber, king of Spain, that his descendants are to rule Ireland and the king's daughter is to marry him and bear him illustrious offspring. Éogan sails next day for Spain, marries the princess, and returns. Soon after she bears his first son, Ailill Ólum.
records.Location of the narrative: Éogan Már; sons and daughter of the druid of Éber, king of Spain; their son Ailill Ólum.

records.Title: Tochmarc Treblainne
records.Beginning lines: Fróech mac Fidhaigh ḟoltrúaigh ó Sídh Ḟidhaigh
records.Contents: A later reworking of Táin bó Fróech that tells of Fróech's wooing of Treblann of Túatha Dé Danann, in spite of her human foster-father, the king of Tara, and in breach of his own gessa, and the violent struggles that ensue.
records.Location of the narrative: Fróech; Treblann of Túatha Dé Danann
records.info:: 1150-1200 (Jennings)

records.Title: Togail Bruidne Da Derga - recension 1
records.Beginning lines: Buí rí amra airegda for Érinn, Eochaid Feidhleach a ainm. Do-luid fechtus n-ann dar Aenach mBreg Léith
records.Contents: …tale of king Conaire Már and his violent death … deep reflections on kingship: its preternatural character, its getting, its loss, and the prudence and integrity required in its exercise.
records.Location of the narrative: Conaire Már

records.Title: Togail Bruidne Da Derga - recension 2
records.Beginning lines: Buí rí amra airegda for Érinn, Eochaid Feidhleach a ainm. Do-luid fechtus n-ann dar Aenach mBreg Léith
records.Contents: …tale of king Conaire Már and his violent death … deep reflections on kingship: its preternatural character, its getting, its loss, and the prudence and integrity required in its exercise.
records.Location of the narrative: Conaire Már

records.Title: Togail Bruidne Da Derga - recension 3
records.Beginning lines: Buí rí amra airegda for Érinn, Eochaid Feidhleach a ainm. Do-luid fechtus n-ann dar Aenach mBreg Léith
records.Contents: …tale of king Conaire Már and his violent death … deep reflections on kingship: its preternatural character, its getting, its loss, and the prudence and integrity required in its exercise.
records.Location of the narrative: Conaire Már

records.Title: Tromdám Guaire
records.Beginning lines: Bai ri uasal oirdnighe for Airghiallaibh feacht n-aill
records.Contents: Evidently from Clonmacnoise, this tale of poets and clerics … by a learned and astringent author … The extortionate poets have lost their greatest tale and many essential skills, but not their arrogance and presumption. The clerical scholars are represented as leading them to the recovery of their literature and proper life.
records.info::
“The language is late Mid. Irish in its transition stage into Mod. Irish” (Joynt); 
“Tromdám Guaire is substantially a late creation. The linguistic evidence would indicate that the text as it stands belongs to a date in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century, but this evidence, in so far as it has been examined, is unsatisfactory and even contradictory. On the other hand, the text seems to have been known to Giolla Brighde Mac Con Midhe [c.1210-c.1272] [...] which would indicate that it was in existence by the mid-thirteenth century” (Ó Coileáin).(3)(4) “[B]ased on the evidence of a number of Norman-French and English loanwords in the texts as well as certain morphological and syntactic aspects of the author’s language”, Feargal Ó Béarra has suggested that the present text was “composed no earlier than ca. 1300, probably west of the river Shannon”, even if some of the materials used may date from an earlier time. Feargal Ó Béarra, ‘Tromdhámh Guaire: a context for laughter and audience in Early Modern Ireland’ in Laughter in the Middle Ages and early modern times... (2010): 415 and 415 n. 9..

records.Title: Tuathal Techtmar & Fiachra Cassán
records.Beginning lines: Luid Feidilmid Rechtaid o Themair do sháerchuaird for Laigniu
records.Contents: This is a short Uí Néill legitimist tale created in Armagh. As the aithechthúatha 'vassal folk' ruled under Éllim mac Conrach as king of Tara, Fiachra Cassán, commander of 150 mercenaries under that king, protected Tuathal Techtmar, sole survivor of the legitimate line, and advised him to go overseas, find troops, and restore his dynasty. This he did, and with 700 men he overthrew Éllim at the battle of Achall.
records.Location of the narrative: Éllim mac Conrach, king of Tara; Fiachra Cassán; Tuathal Techtmar

records.Title: Tucait fagbála in fessa do Finn & marbad Cúlduib
records.Beginning lines: Fecht aili do Find a Cind Chuirrig: is inti ba gnáthach som
records.Contents: A brief tale of the taking of Finn's food - a roasted pig - by the Otherworld Cúldub, of Finn's pursuit of him to the door of the síd, and his catching his thumb as the door closed, leaving the mortally wounded Cúldub within …
records.Location of the narrative: Cúldub; Finn
records.info:: Meyer points to linguistic features which may indicate that the text belongs “to the late eighth or early ninth century

records.Title: Tucait indarba na nDéssi al. Tairired na nDessi al. Tochomlod na nDési ó Themraig - recension 1
records.Beginning lines: Ceithri maic batar la hArttchorb mac Mes Chuirb .i. Brecc & Óengus & Eochuid & Forad (recension 1)
records.Contents: This is the migration legend of the Déisi, from Tara to Leinster and then to east Munster where they got land for settlement through their offspring, Eithne Uathach, wife of Óengus mac Nad Fraích, king of Cashel.  This tale is not historical. It links the Déisi to an early point in the legends of Uí Néill (as the Fothairt are linked in other texts).
records.Place text was written: Déisi; Eithne Uathach, wife of Óengus mac Nad Fraích, king of Cashel
records.Location of the narrative: Tara, Leinster, east Munster
records.info:: Recension A is Old Irish and has been dated to the middle of the 8th century Kuno Meyer, ‘Gauls in Ireland’, Ériu 4 (1908–1910); The later Recension B predates the compilation of LU (AD 1106). "How much earlier than this date [...] remains open to question since it also preserves a number of Old Irish forms. At any event, the almost complete absence of independent objective pronouns in the Lebor na Huidre copy suggests a date of composition at least some fifty or more years before previous to A.D. 1106" Vernam Hull, ‘The later version of the expulsion of the Déssi’, Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 27 (1958–1959): 15 note 5,

records.Title: Tucait indarba na nDéssi al. Tairired na nDessi al. Tochomlod na nDési ó Themraig - recension 2
records.Beginning lines: Cid dia tá cóechad Cormaic hi Temraig? (recension 2)
records.Contents: This is the migration legend of the Déisi, from Tara to Leinster and then to east Munster where they got land for settlement through their offspring, Eithne Uathach, wife of Óengus mac Nad Fraích, king of Cashel.  This tale is not historical. It links the Déisi to an early point in the legends of Uí Néill (as the Fothairt are linked in other texts).
records.Place text was written: Déisi; Eithne Uathach, wife of Óengus mac Nad Fraích, king of Cashel
records.Location of the narrative: Tara, Leinster, east Munster

"How much earlier than this date [...] remains open to question since it also preserves a number of Old Irish forms. records.Title: Úath Beinne Étair al. Aithed Gráinne re Diarmait
records.Beginning lines: Fechtus diaraiuhe Diermait mac Duinn I Duipni ind-Uaim Penn hEdair (text); Fuit, fuid, fuar inocht Mag lethon Luirc (verse)
records.Contents: Diarmait is pursued by Finn for having carried off Gráinne, daughter of king Cormac mac Airt. He takes refuge in a cave in the Hill of Howth but is betrayed by a crone, who has herself been deceived by Finn. She denies Diarmait and Gráinne by trickery so that Finn can catch them.
records.Location of the narrative: Hill of Howth

records.Title: Verba Scáthaige
records.Beginning lines: Incipiunt uerba Scáthaige fri Coin Culainn oc scarad dóib isnaib randaib thair (praefatio); A mbeë eirr óengaile arut-ossa ollgábud (verse)
records.Contents: The brief … verse prophecy, in rosc, Scáthach …, the amazon who trained Cú Chulainn in arms beyond the Alps. It foretells his fate, especially in Táin bó Cúailnge.

records.Title: Medieval lists of tales
Cethrur macclérech
records.Beginning lines: Cethrur macclerech do ḟeraib hÉrend do-chótar ina n-ailithre
records.Contents: A subtle and sardonic anecdote on pilgrimage and on worldy and unworthy clerical morality.

records.Title: Epscop do Gáedelaib
records.Beginning lines: Epscop do Gaedelaib do-choid do Róim
records.Contents: A subtle and ironic tale of a sinful pilgrim bishop, an adulterous queen, and an ingenuous king deluded by both and, perhaps, by the mercy of God.
records.info:: According to Boyle (below), the Book of Leinster version “should perhaps be placed ... into the Middle Irish period: we might date it (very tentatively) to the tenth or eleventh century, though no later than that”, whereas the Leabhar Breac version represents a later reworking of the text exhibiting a degree of modernisation, with features of Early Modern Irish.

records.Title: The prilgrim clerics and their cat
records.Beginning lines: Triar macclerech do ḟeraib hErend do-chotar inna n-ailithre
records.Contents: Three pilgrim clerics put to sea with a cat, allow their boat to drift, and settle on a island in the ocean. The cat fished for them, but his catch was too rich for their ascetic life. They divided their prayers of the liturgy between them. He who chose Hymum dicat as his prayer lived longest and won heaven. St Brendan (of Clonfert) found him ... blessed him, and gave him the last rites.

records.Title: Niall Frossach & the act of truth
records.Beginning lines: Bui rí fírén forglide fíal fossad flaithemda i n-ardrígi for hErind .i. Niall Frossach mac Fergaile
records.Contents: Saga about Níall Frossach mac Fergaile (d. 778), king of Tara from the Cenél nÉogain.
records.Place text was written: Níall Frossach mac Fergaile (d. 778), king of Tara

records.Title: Mac Dá Cherda & Cuimmíne Fota
records.Beginning lines: Cumaín Foda mac Fiachna suí ecna & ardespoc Muman (tale 1); Mac Teléne do feraib Muman cend imarbága hÉrend (tale 2); In Mac Dá Cherda imráiter sund mac side Maíle Ochtraig meic Dínertaich (tale 3).
records.Contents: Three brief comic tales of Mac Dá Cherda (king of Déissi) and St Cuimmíne Fota … The first, a verse dialogue of Cuimmíne Fota and Mac Dá Cherda, is a pointed but fair genial social commentary on clericalism, puritanism, charity, anger, sexual mores, and salvation. The second is a broad social comedy of king, clerics and the learned, set at the court of Guaire, king of Connacht. The third, a defective text, tells how Mac Dá Cherda, son of Mael Ochtraig, king of the Déissi, was made royal jester as punishment for adultery ...
records.Place text was written: Cuimmíne Fota; Mac Dá Cherda; Guaire, king of Connacht
records.info:: On the basis of the designation ‘archbishop of Munster’ for Cummíne, Clancy suggests that the prose prologue may be of the 12th century or later.; Thomas Owen Clancy has tentatively dated the text to the 10th century.

records.Title: The salvation of Máel Suthain Ó Cerbaill
records.Beginning lines: Triar mac fogluma tangatar ó Choindire do denum a léigind d'innsaigid anmcharat Briain meic Cendéitid
records.Contents: Sardonic moral teaching for shady clerics ... Máel Suthain's three alumni go on pilgrimage to Jerusalem and die there. In accord with their solemn promise, they visit their master to tell him how long he is for this life and his fate in the next … He mends his ways scrupulously. They return on the day of his death and he goes with them to his appointed place in heaven. The text ends ironically: 'The writings of that good man are still in the church of Inisfallen'.

records.Title: The abbot of Drimnagh
records.Beginning lines: Aroile óclách ro baei i n-abdaine Druimenaigh
records.Contents: Brief medieval Irish story about a young, unnamed abbot of Druimenaig (Druim Eanaig, now Drimnagh, Co. Dublin), who at Easter finds himself transformed into a woman, sleeps with the erenagh of Croimglenn (Crumlin, Co. Dublin), gives birth to seven children, and changes back to being a man again.
records.Place text was written: abbot of Druimenaig (Druim Eanaig, now Drimnagh, Co. Dublin); erenagh of Croimglenn (Crumlin, Co. Dublin)

records.Title: Ambacuc and St Ciarán
records.Beginning lines: Ferthair Oenach Talten la Diarmait mac Cerbaill
records.Contents: A Clonmacnoise wonder tale … of Ambacuc who, invoking St Ciarán as witness at the fair of Tailtiu, perjured himself about his adultery … Ciarán brought him to Clonmacnoise where he lived headless for seven years after the saint's death. A woman was brought to him and he fathered a son on her from whom desend the lineage called Sogain. And he is buried near the cross of St Comgall at Clonmacnoise. The tale pillories the six Sogain, based lineages of Uí Maine.
records.Location of the narrative: fair of Tailtiu; Clonmacnoise

records.Title: Tales of Mo Ling
records.Beginning lines: 1)  Fechtas do M'Ling is Toídin co-acca Mael Doborchon; 2)  Drochcomaithech ro baí i n-ocus dosom .i. Grác & a ben; 3)  Mo Ling Luachra dalta do M'Aedóc Ḟerna; 4) Fechtas dósom oc ernaigthi ina eclais; 5) Caillech dorat a mac dósum do M'Ling. Findat a h-ainm; 6) Fechtas aile do M'Ling is toidin co n-accai nonbur dona dibergachaib cuci
records.Contents: Six ... Hagiographical anecdotes … about St Moling of Tech Moling (St Mullins, Co. Carlow), and his doings.
records.Location of the narrative: St Moling of Tech Moling (St Mullins, Co. Carlow)

records.Title: Baile Findachta ríg Connacht
records.Beginning lines: Codlad ro chotail Fíndachta mac Tomaltaich iar mór-sáethar
records.Contents: Fínnechta (†848) fled the kingship of Connacht … he settled in Uí Chennselaig in south Leinster … prophesied the next twenty kings of Connacht …
records.Location of the narrative: Fínnechta (†848)

records.Title: Baile Chuind Chétchathaig
records.Beginning lines: Ibthus Art íer cethorchait aidche comnart caur con-beba Muccruimi
records.Contents: Uí Néill & Airgialla - The earliest list of Uí Néill overkings … dating to the reign of Fínnechta Fledach (AD 675-95) of Síl nÁeda Sláine, as seen through the eyes of his lineage.
records.Location of the narrative: Fínnechta Fledach (AD 675-95) of Síl nÁeda Sláine; Uí Néill & Airgialla

records.Title: Baile in Scáil al. Phantom's Frenzy
records.Beginning lines: Laa ro buí Cond i Temraich íar ndíth dona rígaib at-racht matin moch
records.Contents: Uí Néill & Airgialla - ... medieval Irish text which purports to be a prophecy recite by an Otherworld phantom in the presence of Conn Cétchathach, king of Tara, detailing all the future kings of Tara that would descend from him. The phantom is identified as the god Lug.
records.Location of the narrative: Conn Cétchathach, king of Tara; Lug; Uí Néill; Airgialla

records.Title: Ar-síasair coimdiu Tailten al. Airgialla charter poem
records.Beginning lines: Ar-síasair coimdiu Tailten suidi coimdemmar
records.Contents: Uí Néill & Airgialla - A legal and historicist poem (49 st.) on the relationship between Uí Néill overkings and the kingdom of Airgialla.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Néill; Airgialla

records.Title: Senchas Airgiall al. Tale of the Collas
records.Beginning lines: Na hAirgialla trá at é ata nessom do hÚib Néill aithliu Connacht
records.Contents: Uí Néill & Airgialla - … narrative prefixed to the Airgialla genealogies, that purports to explain the present relationship between their Uí Néill overlords and Airgialla…
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Néill; Airgialla

records.Title: Milesian invasion of Ireland
records.Beginning lines: Luid longos do chenel Iafed meic Noí a tírib Gréc co mbadar i nEigept la Forand
records.Contents: Very early brief scholastic notes on the prehistoric invasion of Ireland by the sons of Míl.
records.Location of the narrative: sons of Míl

records.Title: Máel Muru of Othain (†887), Can a mbunadas na nGáedel?
records.Beginning lines: Can a mbunadas na nGáedel gair cloth nglédend
records.Contents: A historicist poem (87 st.) in which Máel Muru, 'royal poet of Ireland' (i.e. poet to Flann Sinna … over-king of Uí Néill), sets himself to explain the origin of the Irish.
records.Location of the narrative: Máel Muru of Othain (†887)

records.Title: Leabhar Gabhála
records.Contents: Leabhar gabhála represents the last stages of a long scholastic tradition that can be traced as far back as the seventh century, one devoted to the creation of a learned Irish origo gentis. This is elaborated as an extensive and wholly historical body of genealogy, the early stages of which are, of course, wholly fictional. Learned poets of the eleventh and twelfth centuries recast much of this in dreary, if polished, verse. From this an elaborate prose text was worked up.

records.Title: Eochaid ua Flainn al. Eochaid ua Flannacáin (c. AD 934-1004) - Éitset áes ecna aíbind
records.Beginning lines: Éitset áes ecna aíbind fo laíd linn lecda léiginn
records.Contents: … Eochaid ua Flannacáin, 'master of poetry and history', belonged to the aristocratic lineage that ruled Armagh and was ancestor of a line of its abbots. A brother, Dub Dá Leithe (†998), was abbot; another Muiredach (†984), was head of its schools, and Eochaid may have succeeded him. In his obit he is entitled superior of Les Oíged at Armagh and of the church of Cluain Fiachna. This long historicist poem, signed by Eochaid in the final stanza, offers a variant of the quite fictional prehistory of Ireland in Leabhar Gabhála.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Eochaid ua Flainn al. Eochaid ua Flannacáin (c. AD 934-1004)
records.Location of the narrative: Eochaid ua Flannacáin; Dub Dá Leithe (†998), was abbot; Muiredach (†984)

records.Title: Leabar comaimsiręchda al. Comaimser ríg Asar re rígaib hÉrenn indso
records.Beginning lines: Adam primus pater fuit et Eua cętbhean in beatha & cétmháthair na n-uile (version 1); Isind bliadain deireanaig ria ndílind táinic Cęsair I nÉrind & nírbo beo d'ę(fada)s díleand díb-sein acht Fintan (version 2)
records.Contents: A chronological and synchronistic tract, like those in Leabhar gabhála. There are two versions, the first from Creation, the second from the Flood. Irish imaginary prehistory is synchronised with the kings of the Assyrians, the Medes and the Roman emperiors ... It ends with the birth of St Patrick and the accession of Lóegaire mac Néill ...

records.Title: Dindshenchas, Metrical & Prose
records.Contents: A large body of literary-scholastic compositions, verse and prose, on conspicuous places: Neolithic sites such as Tara, Newgrange, Rathcroghan, Knockaulin … The Dindshenchas is late ninth to twelfth century in date, belongs to a scholarly fashion of that peroid, was written in the ecclesiastical schools, and attributed, plausibly, to known monastic scholars (for example, Máel Muru Othna (†887), Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), Mac Liac (†1016), Cúán ua Lócháin (†1024), Eochaid Eolach Uá Céirín (fl. 1050), Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Giolla na Naomh Ó Duinn (1102-60), and others.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Máel Muru Othna (†887), Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), Mac Liac (†1016), Cúán ua Lócháin (†1024), Eochaid Eolach Uá Céirín (fl. 1050), Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Giolla na Naomh Ó Duinn (1102-60)

records.Title: Suidiugud Tige Midchuarta
records.Beginning lines: Suidiugud Taige Midchuardda mithig dún a rád
records.Contents: A poem (22 st. in the Book of Leinster, but longer in other MSS) on the kinds of guests received at the Tech Midchúarta, the so-called Banqueting Hall at Tara, and the cuts of meat suitable for each. In effect this is a text on status …

records.Title: Roddet a hInis find Fáil
records.Beginning lines: Roddet a hInis find Fáil i nÉrind cen immarbáig
records.Contents: An early twelfth-century poem (24 st. in MSS i-ii) on the good qualities and merits of the kingdoms of Ireland and their dynasties, put in the mouth of Flann Fína al. king Aldfrith of Northumbra (r. c. 685-705). Armagh is the only church mentioned by name and it is lauded for ... 'supremacy of learning, primacy, fair honour to the Son of God, noble prosperous sages' - enough to suggest the hand of its clergy.
records.Location of the narrative: Flann Fína al. king Aldfrith of Northumbra (r. c. 685-705)

records.Title: Leabhar na gCeart al. Book of Rights
records.Beginning lines: Incipit do Libur na Cert. Indister do chísaib & tuarustlaib Éirenn amal ro ordnaig Benén mac Sescnén salmchétlaid Pádraic
records.Contents: A prosimetrum compilation, by different authors, purporting to set out the tributes of the kings to their overkings, and the gifts (tuarastal) of the overkings to their sub-kings …

records.Title: Senchas Gall Átha Cliath al. Atá sund in senchas seng
records.Beginning lines: Ata sund in seanchas seng is maith le Gallaib Éirenn
records.Contents: A historicist poem (51 st.) setting out Armagh's claim to primacy over Dublin and to church dues from it. The conversion of Dublin is presented as the work of St Patrick in the course of his imagined visit to the city …
records.Location of the narrative: St Patrick

records.Title: Tributes of the kings of Cashel, Cruachain and Uí Briúin
records.Beginning lines: Ceart ríg Caisil ó chríchaib andso sís: dligid d'Osraigib uili (text 1); Ceart Cruachan for cách .i. gach ní dlighes & gach ní delegar de (text 2); Do shochar ríg Ó mBriúin an tan nach leó righe Connact (text 3)
records.Contents: These lists of tributes are structured just as those in Leabhar na gCeart (1146), but are not identical with them. Remarkably, according to text 2, the king of Connacht is entitled to tribute from Uí Chonchobair of Corcu Modruad. The same text is keen to push the claim of Uí Briúin Breifne to the kingship of Connacht.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Chonchobair of Corcu Modruad; Uí Briúin Breifne to the kingship of Connacht

records.Title: Máel Muru Othna (†887), Fland for Erind hi tigh togaid
records.Beginning lines: Flann for Erind hi tigh thogaid Tuathail Techtmair
records.Contents: A historicist poem (83 st.) for Flann Sinna mac Máel Sechnaill, high-king of Ireland (r. 879-887). It is attributed to Máel Muru in both MSS … Tuathal Techtmar, Flann's legendary heroic ancestor, has left an illustrious inheritance that has come to Flann, passed through a noble line, to his grandfather, to his father ...
records.Location of the narrative: Flann Sinna mac Máel Sechnaill, high-king of Ireland (r. 879-887); Tuathal Techtmar; Máel Muru Othna (†887)
records.info:: 879 x 887, i.e. between the beginning of Flann’s reign as king of Tara and the date of Máel Muru’s death, provided that the ascription to Máel Muru holds true (Carey). John Carey, ‘Máel Muru Othna (d. 887)’ in Oxford dictionary of national biography... (2004).

records.Title: Flannacán mac Cellaig, king of Brega (†896), Innid scél scaílter n-airich
records.Beginning lines: Innid scél scaílter n-airich irdirc úas Banba blodhaich
records.Contents: A poem (28 st.) on the death days of mythical and historical warriors by the royal poet, Flannacán mac Cellaig, king of Brega (killed by the Vikings in 896). His son Mael Mithig (†919), king of Brega, was also a poet. Quite apart from the poet's skill in versification, this poem is important as an independent witness to the existence of Old Irish version of many sagas.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Flannacán mac Cellaig, king of Brega (†896)
records.Location of the narrative: Flannacán mac Cellaig, king of Brega (†896)

records.Title: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), Achall
records.Beginning lines: Achall ar aicce Temair ros-carsat óicc a hEmain.
records.Contents: A poem (22 st.) ... It is claimed, within the text …, to be a work of Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), a poet of aristocratic lineage and probably cleric, who enjoyed the patronage of Congalach Cnogba (†956), high-king of Ireland, and Amlaíb Cuarán (†981), king of Dublin. It is apparently written for Amlaíb Cuarán. The poet purports to explain, by reference to saga, the name Achall (Acall), the Hill of Skreen, near Tara, and then he devoutly distances himself from the pagans of the saga.
records.Location of the narrative: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975);  Congalach Cnogba (†956), high-king of Ireland; Amlaíb Cuarán (†981), king of Dublin
records.Characters in the narrative: Achall (Acall), the Hill of Skreen, near Tara

records.Title: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), Brug na Bóinne I
records.Beginning lines: Án-sin a maig Mic ind Óc fairsing do rót rethaib cét
records.Contents: In this poem (22 st.) to Congalach Cnogba (†956), high-king of Ireland, the imagined pre-history of the Neolithic site of Brug na Bóinne (Newgrange, Co. Meath) is directly attached, as a glorious past, to the Uí Néill - Niall, Eochu Mugmedón and their famous mythical ancestors ...
records.Location of the narrative: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975); Congalach Cnogba (†956), high-king of Ireland; Uí Néill
records.Characters in the narrative: Neolithic site of Brug na Bóinne (Newgrange, Co. Meath)
records.info:: 10th century (Meyers)

records.Title: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), Bend Étair
records.Beginning lines: Étar étan ri dílind in clár cétach túath Cúalaind
records.Contents: A very artifical dindshenchas poem (21 st.) that provides fictional eponyms for Étar (Howth) and Mag nElta (the plain to its west, in which Clontarf lies). This poem may be intended as a compliment to the king of Dublin in whose small kingdom both were places of note.
records.Location of the narrative: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975)
records.Characters in the narrative: Étar (Howth) and Mag nElta (the plain to its west, in which Clontarf lies).

records.Title: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), A chloch thall for elaid úair
records.Beginning lines: A chloch thall for elaid úair Bute búain maic Brónaig báin
records.Contents: This poem (11 st.) retails a variant of a christian legend about the pagan weapon that brough about the death of king Conchobar mac Nessa at the time of the Crucifixion … That pagan king was saved by his faith, in fact baptised in his own blood. The weapon, it is said, was perserved at the church of Monasterboice, a relic revealed by God to its founder, St Buite, who used it as his pillow. This piece reflects, and reflects on, the tangled problem of the reception of literature about pagan kings and the pagan past in a christian society.
records.Location of the narrative: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975); Conchobar mac Nessa; St Buite

records.Title: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975), Fíanna bátar i nEmain al. Aidedha foirni do huaislib Érenn inso al. Deaths of Irish heroes
records.Beginning lines: Fíanna bátar i nEmain i rRáith Chrúachan i Temair
records.Contents: In Stokes's enumeration, st. 1-36 are the work of Cináed; st. 37-47 are by Find (+1160), bishop of Kildare … Cináed's composition, of little worth as literature, has the merit of indicating what tales were known in late tenth-century Ireland. The value of Finn's even duller labours is purely historical.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975); Find (+1160), bishop of Kildare
records.Location of the narrative: Cináed ua hArtacáin (†975); Find (+1160), bishop of Kildare

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Advice to king Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill (†1022) … al. Druim Crïaich
records.Beginning lines: Druim Crïaich céte cúan ciasa díthrub ní dímbúan
records.Contents: Attributed only in the Book of Leinster … to Cúán ua Lócháin, prím éices Érenn 'chief poet of Ireland' (†1024), of aristocratic lineage and probably a cleric. Though taken into the Dindshenchas …, this appears to be a poem of advice (53 st.) to Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill, king of Tara (†1022) ...; CODECS: Poem and prose text on the dinnshenchas of Druim Criaich (Drumcree, Co. Westmeath), which is here said to have been known as Druim Cró and Druim n-úar nAirthir. In the Book of Leinster, the poem is attributed to Cuán ua Lothcháin (d. 1024). The poem falls into two sections. The story of the first is that of the quarrel between Eochu Feidlech, high-king of Ireland, and his three sons known as the three Findemna. On the night before the battle of Druim Criaich, in which the brothers are killed, their sister Clothru sleeps with each one of them in order to produce royal offspring. She later gives birth to Lugaid Riab nDerg, high-king of Ireland.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024); Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill (†1022); Eochu Feidlech, high-king of Ireland, and his three sons known as the three Findemna; Clothru; Lugaid Riab n Derg, high-king of Ireland

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Síd Nechtain sund forsin tṡléib al. Boand I
records.Beginning lines: Síd Nechtain sund forsin tṡléib lecht meic Labrada lán-geir
records.Contents: CODECS: Dinnshenchas poem of the River Boyne (Boand).
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024)

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Temair toga na tulach al. Temair III.
records.Beginning lines: Temair toga na tulach foatá Ériu indradach
records.Contents: This poem (47 st.) is an important medieval source for the topography and place names of Tara. Its list of the monuments and their names was created by one intimately familiar with them in the early eleventh century … Cormac mac Airt, represented as making a royal circuit of Ireland three times, is the model of the Uí Néill high-king and patron of poets and scholars ... In the final stanzas, the poet concedes that the pagan site of Tara belongs to the past but its ancient glory, he conveys, attaches to his patron, the contemporary king, Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22); CODECS: Dinnshenchas of Temair
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024);  Cormac mac Airt, high-king; king, Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22)

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Temair, Tailtiu, tír n-óenaig al. Temair V
records.Beginning lines: Temair, Tailtiu, tir n-óenaig, Raigne, Rachru, ráith n-úabair
records.Contents: The poet asserts (in 20 st.) the right of Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22) and his dynasty to hold the kingship of Ireland forever and he further asserts that the kings of Tara, of his line alone, have the right to rule over the kings of Ireland ... The long list of place names ... is meant to convey the extent of his dominion and, consequently, the illustrious nature of his rule.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024); Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22)

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), A chóemu críche Cuind chain al. Tailtiu
records.Beginning lines: A chóemu críche Cuind chain éitsid bic ar bennachtain
records.Contents: A poem on the Fair of Tailtiu (59 st.). It is imagined as a central institution of the high-kingship of Ireland … distinguished and storied ancestors of Uí Néill … It is blessed by Patrick, Brigit and other saints. In this context, the poet turns to a eulogy of ... Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill, his patron and king of Tara ... , whom he lauds grandiloquently ... as óen-mílid na hEórapa ... The poem dates to 1007 when Mael Sechnaill held the Fair of Tailtiu after it had long been in abeyance ...
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024); Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22)

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Atá sund Carn Uí Chathbath al. Carn Furbaide
records.Beginning lines: Atá sund Carn Uí Chathbath fors' rimred arm imathlam
records.Contents: An artificial origin legend of Carn Furbaide, apparently a cairn on Sliab Cairbre in Angaile, in Co. Longford.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024)
records.Characters in the narrative: Carn Furbaide, apparently a cairn on Sliab Cairbre in Angaile, in Co. Longford.

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Sáer-ainm Sinna saigid dún al. Sinann I
records.Beginning lines: Sáer-ainm Sinna saigid dún dáig rolaimid a lomthúr
records.Contents: A verse tale (16 st.) that the river Shannon owes its name to a beautiful Otherworld maiden, Sinann. Bearing her name, it flows from the Otherworld, from the well of Segais, where Crimall's magic hazel nuts from wisdom drop into it, in the Land of Promise. The Shannon is a metonym for king Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill's great kingdom of Meath.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024); Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22); Crimall

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Sinann, cá hadhar diatá al. Sinann II
records.Beginning lines: Sinann, cá hadbar diatá inneósad cen immargá
records.Contents: A scholastic poem (15 st.) on the origin of the Shannon, said in MS vii, to have been re-fashioned by Cúán ua Lócháin. It rises in the Otherworld, in the well of Connla … Crimall's magic hazel nuts of wisdom drop into it … The Shannon is a metonym for king Mael Senchnaill mac Domnaill's great kingdom of Meath.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024); Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22); Crimall; Connla

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024), Temair Breg baile na fían al. Verse Recension of Echtra mac Echdach Mugmedóin
records.Beginning lines: Temair Breg baile na fían ros-dedail Dia re domíad
records.Contents: A lengthy historicist poem (73 st.) attributed to Cúán ua Lócháin, prím-éces Érenn 'chief poet of Ireland', on the legendary encounter of Niall and his half-brothers and rivals with the goddess of sovereignty … It is a legitimist poem, stating the claim of the dynasty of his patron, Mael Sechnaill (r. 980-1002, 1014-22) mac Domnaill, to the kingship of Ireland.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024); Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22); Néill

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (+1024), A fhir áin iadas an tech al. Taboos of the Kings of Ireland
records.Beginning lines: Secht n-urgarta rígh Temrach innso (prose); A fhir áin iadas an tech is mé hÚa Lócháin laídech (poem)
records.Contents: Cúán's poem (37 st.) … The poem is written for the king of Tara and, if he obeys it prescriptions, he will (so the poet avers) have success … and at the end the poet, distances himself from prescrptions … in favour of christian charity …
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024); Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22)

records.Title: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024) (?), Trí croind Éirenn oiregdha
records.Beginning lines: Trí croind Éirenn oiregdha Ibar Asnat rob áebdha
records.Contents: The famous trees are Ibar Asnat 'Yew of St Asnat' in Crích Cairbre, Ibar I nDruim Thúamma 'Yew in Drumhome', and Dos na Rígh 'Tree of the Kings' at Síth Áeda, but the poem soon turns to other matters - a passage on some merit on nature … It appears to be the work of several hands and the mention of 'Cúán ó Cháendruim' ... is no proof of Cúán ua Lócháin's authorship.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lócháin al. Lothcháin (†1024) (?);  Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22)

records.Title: A Maíl Shechlainn meic Domnaill al. Boand II
records.Beginning lines: A Mail Ṡechlainn meic Domnaill do chlainn ingine Comgaill
records.Contents: A poem (15 st.) very likely by Cúán ua Lóchláin (†1024). Boand, the divine river Boyne, praised by the poet, is the Jordan of Ireland and, by metonymy, the kingdom of Máel Sechnaill (r. 980-1002, 1014-22), king of Meath and Tara, the object of the poet's celebration. The obscure st. 14-15 seem to refer to a failed attempt by Máel Mórda, king of Leinster, warring in Meath in 1012, to divert the Boyne to expose Máel Sechnaill's ship at Inber na mBarc. The river (the poet avers) escaped by God's mercy and relieved the king.
records.Location of the narrative: Cúán ua Lóchláin (†1024)

records.Title: Flann Ó Rónáin (fl. 1022), Dúnta in tech i táit na ríg al. Lament for Mael Sechnaill
records.Beginning lines: Dúnta in tech i táit na ríg maith du meth in drúchta déin
records.Contents: … lament (12 st.), by a poet otherwise unknown, for Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill, king of Meath and Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22), dated precisely to the day of the king's death, Sunday, 2 September 1022. It is clear from the text that the late king was the poet's patron.
records.Location of the narrative: Flann Ó Rónáin (fl. 1022); Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill, king of Tara (r. 980-1002, 1014-22)

records.Title: Aed ua Carthaig, Mide magen na marc mer
records.Beginning lines: Mide magen na marc mer slige fors' mbíd Art Oenḟer
records.Contents: A ... poem (13 st.) ... The poet argues that his patron, 'the mead-loving king of Mide' at Uisnech, has superior rights over the whole of Ireland because the aptly invented Mide, son of Brath kindled a mystic druidic fire that shed its 'fierceness' over the four quarters of Ireland and he cut out the tongues of all the druids and buried them at Uisnech. Thus, Ireland is ruled from Uisnech. Meath poets bearing the name Ua Carthaig, none eminent, occur in AFM 1067, 1097, 1131.
records.Location of the narrative: Mide, son of Brath

records.Title: On Brug na Bóinne and the birth of Óengus
records.Beginning lines: Sect o. f. n. nim-thabair i socht nó i sním
records.Contents: This poem (78 st.) is attributed to Cináed ua hArtacáin (+975), but in Thurneysen's view the language is over a century later. It appears to be a praise poem for Óengus (+1017), rígdamna Temrach, son of Donnchadh al. Carrach Calma (+969) descendant of Máel Sechnaill (+862)  mac Máel Ruanaid, king of Tara. It is based on Tochmarc Étaíne and tells of the birth of Óengus in Mac Óc, son of In Dagda.

records.Title: Dindgnai Temrach al. Do dindgnaib na Temrach
records.Beginning lines: Nemnach .i. firthipra fil ocon tsíd i n-airthiurdesciurt na Temrach
records.Contents: A survey in prose of the remarkable remains at Tara. It links the site and its monuments firmly to the legendary ancestors of Uí Néill and to the Uí Néill kings themselves, thus giving them an immemorial claim on the kingship of Ireland … The slaughter of the maidens by the Leinstermen and the false judgement pronounced at Tara by Lugaid mac Con of Dáirine are pointedly commemorated as the evil deeds of rival dynasties of Leinster and Munster.
records.Location of the narrative: Lugaid mac Con of Dáirine ; Uí Néill; Leinster; Munster

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056), World kingship al. Do fhlaithiusaib in domun móir indso sis al. Réidig dam a Dé do nim
records.Beginning lines: Réidig dam, a Dé do nim co héimidh a n-indisin
records.Contents: Flann Mainistrech (†25 November 1056) belong to an aristocratic lineage of Cianacht, a petty kingdom subject to Uí Néill overlordship. He was … fer léigind at Monasterboice … and according to the annals, poet and 'master of the historical lore of Ireland'. This is poem on world chronology ... It draws on various texts available in the Irish schools, among them Bede's Chronica maiora, but it is indebted to Irish chronological sources ultimately patristic in origin ... It was composed in 1056 by Flann ... as a teaching text for the schools.
records.Location of the narrative: Cianacht; Uí Néill

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Poems on the dynasties of Ailech, Mide & Brega
records.Beginning lines: (1) Cíá triallaid nech aisnis senchais; (2) Cind cethri ṅdíni iar Frigrind; (3) Ascnam ni seol sadal; (4) A ní do-rónsat do chalmu clann Eogain; (5) A ṅgluind a n-échta a n-oirgni; (6) Mide maigen clainne Cuind; (7) Síl Áeda Sláne na sleg
records.Contents: A suite of seven historicist poems on Uí Néill, attributed to Flann Mainistrech (†1056), fer léigind of Monasterboice. Poems 1-2, 4-5, all in the same metre (snédbairdne), are really a single poem on the dynasty of Ailech (Northern Uí Néill). Poem 4 recites the victories of the king of Ailech ... Poem 5 retails the personal exploits of the kings of Ailecht and, at its end Flann declares his authorship ... This composite work dates between 1030-1056. Poem 3 does not belong in the series: it is in a different metre and it ends imperfect and may not be the work of Flann. Poems 6 is a versified king list of Clann Cholmáin, prehistoric and historic, ending with the death of Conchobar ua Mael Scehnaill (+1073). Its ascription to Flann is erased in MS i. Poem 7 is a versified historical king list of Síl nAeda Sláine, ending with Muirchertach mac Congalaig (+995). Neither poem is ascribed to Flann in MS iv. and neither appears to be his work.
records.Location of the narrative: Ailech (Northern Uí Néill); Clann Cholmáin, prehistoric and historic, ending with the death of Conchobar ua Mael Scehnaill (†1073).
records.info:: MacNeill suggests that the ascription to Flann Mainistrech that heads the preceding poem in the Book of Leinster (see [[Dinnshenchas of Ailech II |Ailech II]]) is intended to refer to five successive poems, including the present one.

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Éstid a éolchu cen ón
records.Beginning lines: Éstid a éolchu cen ón mad áil duíb cor' inniseor
records.Contents: A poem (38 st. …), on the deaths … of the divine race of the Túatha Dé Danann. Here they are treated as mortal, as beings of a distant past whose existence is literary. For example, Brian, Iucharba and Iuchair … die by the hand of Lug mac Ethlend …
records.Location of the narrative: Túatha Dé Danann; Brian; Iucharba; Iuchair; Lug mac Ethlend
records.info:: ...embedded in a number of recensions of the Lebor gabála Érenn…

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Augaine Már mac ríg Érenn & Tuathal Techtmar ba rí Temrach
records.Beginning lines: Augaine Már mac ríg Érenn airdairc ruiri (poem 1); Tuathal Techtmar ba rí Temrach tolgda maigen (poem 2)
records.Contents: A short (7 st.) … and a long poem (53 st.), both in the same metre … that tell the story of the Bórama … the tribute, imposed by the legendary Tuathal Techtmar, king of Tara, on the Leinstermen and levied bloodily by kings of Tara. This is the re-assertion of Uí Néill rights over Leinster at a time when Diarmait mac Mael na mBó (r. 1042-72), king of Leinster, was the most powerful king in Ireland, and a threat to the Uí Néill kings of Meath.
records.Location of the narrative: Bórama; Tuathal Techtmar, king of Tara; Uí Néill; Diarmait mac Mael na mBó (r. 1042-72)

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Ríg Themra dia tesband tnú
records.Beginning lines: Ríg Themra dia tesband tnú adfessam a n-aidedu
records.Contents: A poem (35 st.) ascribed to Flann in the headings of both MSS, on the violent deaths of the kings of Irish pre-history, from Eochu Feidlech to Niall Noígiallach, Eochu mac Énna, and Nath Í mac Fiachrach. These latter kings reigned, in the traditional understanding, at the end of the pagan peroid. It is, of course, extracted mostly from literary texts.
records.Location of the narrative: Eochu Feidlech; Niall Noígiallach; Eochu mac Énna; Nath Í mac Fiachrach

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Ríg Themra tóebaige iar tain
records.Beginning lines: Ríg Themra tóebaige iar tain óa ḟlaith Lóegaire lendglain
records.Contents: A long poem (52 st.) on the deaths of the christian kings of Ireland, based mostly on the annals. It is attributed to Flann in the heading in MS I, and signed by him (st. 52). Among the kings, Brian Bóraime (†1014) is admitted to be ardrí Gall & Gaedal 'high-king of the Foreigners and the Irish', but the poet reserves his highest praise and his prayers for the Uí Néill kings, especially Mael Sechnaill (r. 980-1002, 1014-22), 'sole king of Ireland'. in whose lifetime the poem was written ...
records.Location of the narrative: Brian Bóraime (†1014); Uí Néill kings; Mael Sechnaill (r. 980-1002, 1014-22)

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056), Toísig na loingse dar ler
records.Beginning lines: Toísig na lloiṅgse dar ler dia táncatar meic Míled
records.Contents: A pseudo-historical poem (18st.) on the deaths, usually by violence, of those who invaded Ireland with the sons of Míl, that is, the imaginary ancestors of the Irish.
records.Location of the narrative: son of Míl

records.Title: Flann Mainistrech (†1056) (?), In eól dúib in senchas sen?
records.Beginning lines: In eól duíb in senchas sen ainm cech ríg ro gab Cassel
records.Contents: A versified list of the kings of Cashel (15 st., MS i; 22 st. MSS ii-iii) from Óengus mac Nad Fraích to Donnchad (†1064) mac Briain Bóraime (†1014) who reigned in Flann's lifetime. It is attributed to Flann, but may not be  his. His prayer that Donnchad 'may be a friend to all Ireland' )st. 15) is perhaps an allusion to the events of 1053, when Donnchad was in the Midlands as the ally of Conchonbar Ó Mael Shechlainn, king of Meath, campaigning against Diarmait mac Mael na mBó, king of Leinster (r. 1042-72). In MSS ii-iii, stanzas are intercalated in the interest of the Éoganacht, and the list is extended to the reign of Cormac Mac Carthaig, king of Munster (r. 1123-38).
records.Location of the narrative: kings of Cashel; Óengus mac Nad Fraích; Donnchad (†1064) mac Briain Bóraime (†1014); Conchonbar Ó Mael Shechlainn, king of Meath; Diarmait mac Mael na mBó, king of Leinster (r. 1042-72); Éoganacht; Cormac Mac Carthaig, king of Munster (r. 1123-38)

records.Title: Cétrí ro gab hÉrind uill
records.Beginning lines: Cétrí ro gab hÉrind uill do Sil Eogain a hĘchdruim
records.Contents: A poem (14 st.) listing the kings of Ailech who were, it is claimed, kings of Ireland, from the legendary Muirchertach (†c. 536) mac Ercae al. mac Muiredaig meic Éogain to the powerful Domnall ua Néill (r. 956-80), 'who died in the middle of Armagh'.
records.Location of the narrative: kings of Ailech; Muirchertach (†c. 536) mac Ercae al. mac Muiredaig meic Éogain; Domnall ua Néill (r. 956-80)

records.Title: Gilla Cóemáin (fl. 1072), Ériu ard inis na rríg
records.Beginning lines: Ériu ard inis na rrig magen moltbach na mórgním
records.Contents: Gilla Cóemán is evidently an ecclesiatical poet and teacher … It is a catalogue (151 st., with some additions) of the legendary pre-christian kings of Ireland … The poem is signed Gilla Cóemáin mac Gilla Samthainne (st. 151).

records.Title: Gilla Cóemáin (fl. 1072), At-tá sund forba fessa
records.Beginning lines: At-tá sund forba fessa fer nhÉrend cen ancessa
records.Contents: First the poet gives a careful list of the kings of Ireland … from Lóegaire to the death of Brian Bóraime (†1014) …
records.Location of the narrative: Lóegaire; Brian Bóraime (†1014)

records.Title: Gilla Cóemáin (fl. 1072), Annálad anall uile
records.Beginning lines: Annálad anall uile ó thus betha barrbuide
records.Contents: This long chronological poem (58 st.) records the peroids of time between notable events. Into this frame is fitted the synchronisation of Irish and world events, drawn directly or indirectly from Eusebius, Orosius, Isidore, and Bede … The intervals grow progressively shorter in the historic peroid and it is clear that the poem is increasingly, and then exclusively, based on accurate historical annals. The poem is dated internally to 1072 (st. 57).

records.Title: Gilla Cóemáin (fl. 1072), Gáedel Glas ó tát Gáedil
records.Beginning lines: Gáedel Glas ó tát Gáedil macside Niúil nertmaínig
records.Contents: … poem (43st.) on the remote and fabulous eponym of the Irish, his descendants, and their imagined adventures, is an intrinsic part of Leabhar gabhála, of which it is a tedious verse summary. In MS i the poem is explicitly said to the work of Gilla Cóemáin.

records.Title: Gilla Cóemáin (fl. 1072), Tigernmas mac Follaig aird
records.Beginning lines: Tigernmas mac Follaig aird ba flaith for Banba bithgairg
records.Contents: An intrinsic part of Leabhar gabhála, this poem (14 st.) represents Tigernmas as a culture hero who first smelted gold in Ireland and first produced coloured garments …
records.Location of the narrative: Tigernmas

records.Title: Gilla Cóemáin (?), A eólcha Alban uile al. Dúan Albanach
records.Beginning lines: A éolcha Alban uile a shluagh féuta foltbhuidhe
records.Contents: A catalogue of the kings of Scotland (27 st.) from the mythical Albanus to Mael Coluim Cennmór al. Malcolm III Canmore (†1093), who was alive at the time of composition (lines 101-4). It is attributed to Gilla Cóemáin (this is doubted) …
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Gilla Cóemáin mac Gilla Samthainne ? doubted
records.Location of the narrative: Albanus; Mael Coluim Cennmór al. Malcolm III Canmore (†1093)

records.Title: Giolla na Naomh Ó Duinn (1102-1160), Cúiced Lagen 'na lecht ríg
records.Beginning lines: Cúiced Lagen 'na lecht ríg inar chlecht cach dagfher dían
records.Contents: Giolla na Naomh Ó Duinn (†17 December 1160) was head of school (fer léigind) at the island church of Inis Clothrann (Inishcloghran on Lough Ree, near St John's). He is described in the annals (Atig, AFM 1160) as 'Ireland's chief authority on history and poetry and the outstanding master of the Irish'. His are historical poems ... The present poem (69 st., with some variation in the MSS) is signed by Ó Duinn in the final stanza. It lists the kings of Leinster and the length of their reigns from Bresal Bélach to Diarmait Mac Murchada (†1171), who is described as regnant.
records.Location of the narrative: kings of Leinster; Bresal Bélach; Diarmait Mac Murchada (†1171)

records.Title: Giolla na Naomh Ó Duinn (1102-1160), Cruacha Connacht ráith co rath
records.Beginning lines: Cruacha Condacht ráith co rath teallach Tinde meic Conrach
records.Contents: A versified king-list (74 st.), composed in the reign of Tairdelach Ó Conchobair (†1156), king of Connacht and of Ireland, by Giolla na Naomh Ó Duinn, fer léigind of the church of Inis Clothrann on Lough Ree. Fifty kings ruled Connacht from the reign of Amalgaid mac Fiachrach, alleged contemporary of St Patrick, to Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair (r. 1106-56).
records.Location of the narrative: Amalgaid mac Fiachrach; Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair (r. 1106-56)

records.Title: Giolla na Naomh Ó Duinn (1102-1160), Éri iarthar talman torthig
records.Beginning lines: Éri iarthar talman tortigh tír Fhodla ina fuinend grían
records.Contents: A long poem (121 st.), in four parts, being a summary of the Dindshenchas. It is organised by region, beginning with Tara and ending with Druim Cliab in NW Connacht … The poet's signature is in st. 121 … In st. 116 the date of composition is given as 1166 but the chronological criteria appear to be for 1160. The Tairdelbach, referred to in st. 111 as dying in May, is Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair (†20 May 1156), king of Ireland ... The poem, therefore, was written shortly after Tairdelbach's death and before or in 1160.
records.Location of the narrative: Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair (†20 May 1156)

records.Title: Gilla in Choimded Ó Cormaic of Tulach Léis, Aimirgein Glúngel tuir tend al. Authors and Laws of Ireland
records.Beginning lines: Aimirgein Glúngel tuir tend cétugdar amra Éirend
records.Contents: A scholastic poem (63 st.) on the legendary and historical authors and jurists of Ireland … The legend of the creation of the Senchas Már is rehearsed, and important legal texts are mentioned.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Gilla in Choimded Ó Cormaic (fl. 11th c.)

records.Title: Gilla in Choimded Ó Cormaic of Tulach Léis, A rí ríchid réidig dam
records.Beginning lines: A rí ríchid réidig dam tria gné n-eimid n-eladan
records.Contents: A scholastic poem (111st.) … Gilla in Chomdid úa Chormaic (fl. 11th c.) referring to events and personages from biblical, classical and native history …
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Gilla in Choimded Ó Cormaic (fl. 11th c.)

records.Title: Giolla Mo Dutu Ó Casaide (fl. 1147), Éri óg, inis na náem
records.Beginning lines: Éri óg inis na náem co n-imad ríagail ro-cháem
records.Contents: Firmly dated on internal evidence (st. 77) to AD 1143, this poem (84 st.) is a verse list of kings of Ireland and the length of their reigns from Lóegaire to near the writer's present … Lóegaire in the fifth century to Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill. After Mael Sechnaill, he lists the dynasties from which the kings of Ireland sprung. He holds with the common teaching that no later king ruled all Ireland., though he admits ... that his contemporary, Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair, is overcoming all opposition.
records.Location of the narrative: Lóegaire; Mael Sechnaill (†1022) mac Domnaill; Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair

records.Title: Giolla Mo Dutu Ó Casaide (fl. 1147), Cuibdeas comanmann na ríg
records.Beginning lines: Cuibdeas comanmann na ríg gabsad Érind cęn imshním
records.Contents: … poem (51st.) on the homonymous kings, imaginary and historic, who are understood to have ruled Ireland. The latest historic king mentioned is Domnall (†1121) mac Ardgair meic Lochlainn, king of Ailech and claimant to the kingship of Ireland. It is signed by the poet (st. 51) ... Clearly, a teaching text of the schools ...
records.Location of the narrative: Domnall (†1121) mac Ardgair meic Lochlainn, king of Ailech
records.info:: Kevin Murray observes that the previous stanza ends in a dúnad (as does the final stanza) suggesting therefore that the final stanza may have been added at a later stage.

records.Title: The prophecy of Berchán
records.Beginning lines: Aris biuc, a meic bic báin sí fri acallaim Bercháin
records.Contents: …poem of 206 st. mainly on the kings of Ireland and Scotland from the mid-ninth to the mid-eleventh century. Cast as a prophecy … appears to be the work of three or more hands. After a short introduction on St Berchán, and a dire pseudo-prophecy of the effects of Viking domination in Ireland ... It lists important Irish kings and their deeds by kennings with cryptic references; st. 52-6 are extremely hostile to Domnall ua Néill (†980) and Ruaidrí Ó Canannáin (†950) of Northern Uí Néill; st. 58-66, 72 are very sympathetic to Congalach Cnogba (†956) and Máel Sechnaill (†1022), both of Southern Uí Néill; st. 67-71 are unflattering about Brian Bóraime (†1014) ... the archane religious and hagiographical part (st. 99-115) is mostly concerned with the disputed resting places of SS Patrick, Brigit and Colum Cille and a prophecy of a great sage. ... The final part (st. 116-206) is a listing ... of the kings of Scotland and their deeds, to the late eleventh century, by one who had local knowledge.
records.Location of the narrative: Domnall ua Néill (†980); Ruaidrí Ó Canannáin (†950) of Northern Uí Néill; Congalach Cnogba (†956); Máel Sechnaill (†1022), both of Southern Uí Néill; Brian Bóraime (†1014); SS Patrick, Brigit and Colum Cille; St Berchán

records.Title: Clann Ollaman uaisle Emna
records.Beginning lines: Clann Ollaman uaisle Emna Ulltaig Sléibe lethain Liac
records.Contents: A poem of 80st … on the christain kings of Ulaid from Muiredach Muinderg, said to have ruled in the end of the fifth century, to Eochaid Mac Duinn Shléibhe (r. 1158-66), who was king when the poem was written (st. 73). St. 74-80 are a panegyric of Eochaid. The poet is accurate, his historical sources sound, and his verse is technically skilful.
records.Location of the narrative: Muiredach Muinderg; Eochaid Mac Duinn Shléibhe (r. 1158-66)
records.info:: thought by F. J. Fyrne to have been written in the reign of Eochaidh Mac Duinnshléibhe (1158-1166).

records.Title: Teallach féile Uí Echach
records.Beginning lines: Tellach féile Uí Echach drécht as lethan do síoladh
records.Contents: A learned encomium of Áed Mag Áengusa, king of Uí Echach Coba, but not king of Ulaid … he is a generous patron of poets, a theme well worked with intertextual references. This is the work of a poet-jurist as terms of art and recherché vocabulary reveal - aire échta ... tóla n-etho ... teinm laída ... The borrowed terms, oidhir, better eigre ... and cairt ... are no earlier than the twelfth century. The end is missing.
records.Location of the narrative: Áed Mag Áengusa, king of Uí Echach Coba

records.Title: A éigsi Banba na mbenn
records.Beginning lines: A éigsi Banba na mbęnd a eolcha amra Éirenn
