records.Contents: An achronological poem (61 st.), mostly … list of names of those imagined to have been kings of Ireland - mythological, pseudo-historical and historical … He ends with 'royal Ruaidrí - king without perfidy  - son of wrathful Tairdelbach' … i.e. Ruaidrí Ó Conchobair, who became king of Ireland in 1166 and died in 1198; and he closes with trite prayer that his leaden poetic labours may earn him salvation. This poem appears to be the work of Giolla Íosa Mór Mac Fir Bhisigh, and not his earlier namesake, 'a master of history, storytelling, poetry and computus', who died in 1301 ...
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Giolla Íosa Mór Mac Fir Bhisigh († 1301) ?
records.Location of the narrative: Ruaidrí Ó Conchobair, who became king of Ireland in 1166 and died in 1198

records.Title: Giolla Íosa Mac Fir Bhisigh, Réidig dam a Dé do nim
records.Beginning lines: Réidig dam a Dé do nim cindead coir ar chomaimsir
records.Contents: A chronological poem (94 st.), being a synchronism of Roman emperors and Irish kings from Octavian Augustus († AD 14), who is made contemporary with the legendary Conaire Már, to Theodosius II († AD 450), who is synchronised with Niall Noígiallach and Nath Í, whom Irish chronology places in the fifth century.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Giolla Íosa Mór Mac Fir Bhisigh († 1301)
records.Location of the narrative: Conaire Már; Niall Noígiallach; Nath Í

records.Title: Orthanach úa Coíllama (†840), Slan seiss a Brigit co mbuaid - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Slán seiss a Brigit co mbuaid for grúaid Lifi lir co tráig
records.Contents: A poem (26st.) attributed to Orthanach … The poet celebrates, with apparent nostalgia, the great and generous kings of pre-history, but they have vanished. In their place is the everlasting rule of holy Brigit, namely, that of the church of Kildare of which Orthanach himself was a bishop.
records.Location of the narrative: St Brigit
records.info:: “There can I think be no doubt that our poem was composed during the Old-Irish period” Kuno Meyer, Hail Brigit: an Old Irish poem on the Hill of Alenn (1912): 11.

records.Title: Orthanach úa Coíllama (†840), Masu de chlaind Echach aird - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Masu de chlaind Echach aird ataí a baird búaid cech óin
records.Contents: … martial celebration (in 34 st.) of the triumphs of the heroes of Leinster pre-history and legend. But now the heroes are gone, their fortresses empty and SS Patrick and Brigit preside over the land (st. 31). Orthanach's ambiguous stance between past and present is evident.
records.Location of the narrative: SS Patrick and Brigit

records.Title: Orthanach úa Coíllama (†840), A chóicid choín Chairpri crúaid - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: A chóicid chóin Chairpri crúaid coitset for slúaig slechta dúir
records.Contents: A bloodthirsty celebration of the violent legendary pre-history and early history of Leinster, particulary its warfare with Uí Néill, but also its victories over Munster. There is a single religious reference: St Brigit's effective intervention in the battle of Lúachair.
records.Location of the narrative: St Brigit; Uí Néill
records.info:: O'Daly: “There is nothing in the language of the poem (excepting that part which I believe not to have been written by Orthanach) that would make impossible in the first half of the ninth century or that cannot be made to conform with such a date without doing violence to the metre. The distinction between preterite and perfect is well maintained. Exceptions are: ro n-ort, ro loisc 4, do-rat 17, torchair 27. Occasionally a variant in one of the other MSS. introduces a perfect where N has a preterite: nírbo 10(B) (nipa N), nirbtar 30(L) (nibtar N). There are no instances of the neuter being replaced by masc. or fem. Even the short form of the npl. survives [...] The infixed pronoun is infrequent but there are no instances of the independent pronoun [...]. dīas the older dissyllabic form occurs in 2 (N) while in Rawl., B and B1 it is is monosyllabic, an extra syllable being introduced into the verbal form.”

records.Title: Dallán mac Móre (fl. 900), Cerball Cuirrig cáem-Life - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Cerball Currig cáemLife clód catha for Cond
records.Contents: A praise poem (24st.) on the triumphs of Cerball mac Muirecéin, king of Leinster (r. 885-909). Its date must lie between the defeat of Viking Dublin in 902 (st. 20) and the death of Cormac mac Cuilennáin in 908 (st. 14) … The poet ends devoutly with a request that St Patrick's prayers protect him.
records.Location of the narrative: Cerball mac Muirecéin, king of Leinster (r. 885-909); Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908); St Patrick
records.info:: “There can be no doubt that the poem was composed towards the end of the ninth century.” (Meyer

records.Title: Dallán mac Móre (fl. 900), Mochen, a chlaidib Cherbaill al. Song of sword of Cerball - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Mochen a chlaidib Cherbaill bát meinic i móreṅglaim
records.Contents: A poem (21 st.) addressed to the sword of Cerball mac Muirecéin, king of Leinster (r. 885-909), ascribed to his royal poet Dallán mac Móre and written after the king's death.
records.Location of the narrative: Cerball mac Muirecéin, king of Leinster (r. 885-909)

records.Title: Dallán mac Móre (fl. 900), Cell Chorbháin - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Cell Chorbbáin clár cen chreidim cus' tathaig dám is dirim
records.Contents: A poem (25st.) on the churchyard of Cell Chorbbáin at Nass (Co. Kildare) a seat of the Leinster kings, and on the famous people buried there. Either written by Dallán mac Móre or incorporating a text of his.
records.info:: James P. Carney, 'The dating of early Irish verse texts 500-1100'  Éigse 19 (1982–1983): 179 dates the poem, along with others, to the time-frame c.900-920.

records.Title: Dallán mac Móre (fl. 900), Cormac Femin, Fogartach - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Cormac Femhin, Fogartach, Colmán, Cellach crúaidh n-ughra
records.Contents: A versified list (12st.) of those who fell at the battle of Belach Mugna (AD 908), where Cormac, bishop-king of Munster, was defeated and slain by Cerball mac Muiricéin, king of Leinster (r. 885-909).
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac, bishop-king of Munster; Cerball mac Muiricéin, king of Leinster (r. 885-909).

records.Title: Dallán mac Móre (fl. 900), Mór liach Life longalach - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Mór liach Life longalach, gan Cerbhall cubaidh céileach
records.Contents: A lament for Cerball mac Muiricéin (†909), king of Leinster (r. 885-909), attributed to his court poet, Dallán mac Móre. However, it is associated with Gormlaith and thus with the Gormlaith suite of poems (1198), and this suggests that it may be later.
records.Location of the narrative: Cerball mac Muiricéin (†909), king of Leinster (r. 885-909); Gormlaith

records.Title: Dallán mac Móre (fl. 900), Truag a dála domnán dil - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Truag a dála domnán dill taitnit bága Fiadat fair
records.Contents: A touching lament (5 st.) for Cormac mac Cuilennáin king-bishop of Cashel and scholar, defeated and killed at the battle of Belach Mugna (AD 908). The poet's patron, Cerball mac Muircéin (†909), king of Leinster (r. 885-909) was the victor.
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Cuilennáin king-bishop of Cashe; Cerball mac Muircéin (†909), king of Leinster (r. 885-909)

records.Title: Broccán Cráibdech, Lecht Cormaic meic Cuilennáin - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Lecht Cormaic meic Cuilennáin i mmedón Lagen lerda
records.Contents: A poem of 56 st., later than AD 974 (see st. 9), the work of one Broccán Cráibdech … of the church of Cluain Mor M'Áedóc al. Clonmore Co. Carlow … a poet otherwise unknown. He begins with a long list of the graves of those who fell by the Leinstermen … He  then turns to other things, including ... He boasts of the 'bishops and superiors and the many poets' of the Leinstermen ... and declares 'I have not heard in any province, between eath and holy heaven, of a nun like St Brigit, of a cleric like St Kevin' ... He makes a more remarkable claim: 'It is a breach of the Creator's precept and it is against the covenanted word of Christ that any Irish king should attack the Leinstermen'.
records.Location of the narrative: Broccán Cráibdech; St Patrick; St Kevin

records.Title: Gein Branduib meic Echach & Áedáin meic Gabráin - Poems on Leinster - poem
records.Beginning lines: Ro bátar láeich do Laigneib oc ól meda mór raibnich (poem)
records.Contents: A narrative of the kinship of Brandub mac Echach, king of Uí Chennselaig and Leinster (†605/8), and Áedán mac Gabráin, king of Dál Riata in Scotland, who, according to this text, were born full brothers, and thus ought be allies. The poem reflects the power of Diarmait mac Máel na mBó (†1072), king of Leinster.
records.Location of the narrative: Brandub mac Echach, king of Uí Chennselaig and Leinster (†605/8); Áedán mac Gabráin, king of Dál Riata in Scotland; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó (†1072), king of Leinster.
records.info:: No linguistic analysis is known at this stage. Benjamin Hudson dates the text on historical grounds to the early 11th century, during the reign of Máel Coluim II (d. 1034).(1) This date is endorsed is by Máire Ní Mhaonaigh in her discussion of one version of Orcuin Néill Noígíallaig,(2) while Máire Herbert prefers a somewhat later date, during the reign of Díarmait mac Máel na mBó. Morgan Thomas Davies has remarked: “Both arguments, and both dates, seem plausible, though it is worth noting neither Hudson nor Herbert (nor for that matter Ní Mhaonaigh) provides any evidence for their dating of the text beyond the explanatory power conferred by the convenient correspondence with the reigns of Máel Coluim or Díarmait mac Máel na mBó.”

records.Title: Gein Branduib meic Echach & Áedáin meic Gabráin - Poems on Leinster - prose
records.Beginning lines: Eochu & Fáelán dá mac Muiredaig meic Óengusa meic Feidlimid (prose)
records.Contents: A narrative of the kinship of Brandub mac Echach, king of Uí Chennselaig and Leinster (†605/8), and Áedán mac Gabráin, king of Dál Riata in Scotland, who, according to this text, were born full brothers, and thus ought be allies. The poem reflects the power of Diarmait mac Máel na mBó (†1072), king of Leinster.
records.Location of the narrative: Brandub mac Echach, king of Uí Chennselaig and Leinster (†605/8); Áedán mac Gabráin, king of Dál Riata in Scotland; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó (†1072), king of Leinster.
records.info:: No linguistic analysis is known at this stage. Benjamin Hudson dates the text on historical grounds to the early 11th century, during the reign of Máel Coluim II (d. 1034).(1) This date is endorsed is by Máire Ní Mhaonaigh in her discussion of one version of Orcuin Néill Noígíallaig,(2) while Máire Herbert prefers a somewhat later date, during the reign of Díarmait mac Máel na mBó. Morgan Thomas Davies has remarked: “Both arguments, and both dates, seem plausible, though it is worth noting neither Hudson nor Herbert (nor for that matter Ní Mhaonaigh) provides any evidence for their dating of the text beyond the explanatory power conferred by the convenient correspondence with the reigns of Máel Coluim or Díarmait mac Máel na mBó.”

records.Title: Échta Lagen for Leth Cuind - Poems on Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Échta Lagen for Leth Cuind forsna clannaib i lLiathdruim
records.Contents: … anonymous poem (30 st.), meant to list the great deeds the Leinstermen perpetrated on the northern half of Ireland, is a dreary list of killings drawn from literature and pre-history … three or more victims are from Munster … stanzas … slaughter of the women at Tara by Dúnlang, king of Leinster ... stanzas, which retail the killing of great kings - Niall Glúndub (†919), Congalach mac Máele Mithig (†956) and Brian Bóraime (†1014) - are the later additions of an equally bad poet.
records.Location of the narrative: Dúnlang, king of Leinster; Niall Glúndub (†919); Congalach mac Máele Mithig (†956); Brian Bóraime (†1014)

records.Title: Cóic ríg tríchat triallsat róe al. Christian kings of Leinster - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Cóic ríg tríchat triallsat róc ó chraitim cen immargóe
records.Contents: A composite poem of 55 st. The first part ends at st. 37 when Fáelán (†942) was still ruling … His predecessor died in 917. Therefore the first part belongs to the year 917 x 942. The penultimate stanza of the second part (st. 54) represents Donnchad mac Dúnlaing (r. 1024-33; †1036) as regnant. The second was therefore composed 1024 x 1033.
records.Location of the narrative: Fáelán (†942); Donnchad mac Dúnlaing (r. 1024-33; †1036)
records.info:: Middle Irish poem (55qq) which enumerates early medieval kings of Leinster since the arrival of Christianity. According to M. A. O'Brien, who published an edition of the text, the poem is a composite work consisting of two parts: the first, longer series of stanzas (1-38) listing 35 kings from Crimthann mac Énnai Chennselaig to Fáelán mac Muiredaig (d. 934), together with two additional quatrains of slightly later date (39-40), and a final series (41-55) ending with Donnchadh mac Dúnlaing (d. 1036). The final kings in both parts are represented as being still alive.

records.Title: Éistid a Laigniu na lecht al. Fair of Carman - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Éistid a Laigniu na lecht a shlúaig ós Raigniu rathchert
records.Contents: It was a prerogative of the king of Leinster to hold the Fair of Carmann, the subject of this poem … The first part (st. 1-20 …) is the dindshenchas of the site and its name … probably early eleventh century in composition. The next part (st. 21-48) conveys the claim of Osraige to hold the Fair. At least part of this must belong to 1033 when Donnchadh mac Gilla Phátraic, king of Osraige and claimant to the kingship of Leinster, celebrated the Fair - so much is clear from the flattering references to Osraige (st. 41). There is some rewriting here: Diarmait mac Mael na mBó (st. 24d), of Uí Chennselaig, was king of Leinster from 1042 to 1072; and the reference to Uí Failge kings of Leinster (st. 40) anticipates the next section ... st. 50 ... belongs to 1079 or a little later when Conchobar Ua Conchobair, king of Uí Failge, made himself king and (later) joint-king of Leinster (1079-1115). To give dramatic expression ot his claim to such a high positoin ... he held the Fair in 1079.
records.Location of the narrative: Donnchadh mac Gilla Phátraic, king of Osraige; Diarmait mac Mael na mBó of Uí Chennselaig; Conchobar Ua Conchobair, king of Uí Failge
records.info:: It is not unitary … it divides into at least three sections … the divisions are not clear, and additional stanzas may have been added at various points.

records.Title: Timna Cathaír Móir al. The will of Cathaír Mór - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Is so tra timna Chathaír dia clainn .i. for a deich macaibh (praef. recension 1); Mo ordan, mor airechas mo chaoime mo chlothaighi (recension 1); At é andso Timna Chathaír Máir for a macaib aireagdaib & for a cholind chomarbais (praef. recension  2); Mo f(dot)laithis, mo ordan, mo s(dot)síri, mo s(dot)untaidi (recension 2)
records.Contents: A dynastic ranking of Leinster royal lineages, the 'will' of Cathaír Mór is modelled on Jacob's blessing of his sons … This is a skilled historicist text, created in the reign of Conchobar Ó Conchobair Failge, king and joint-king of Leinster (1079-1115), to support his claim to such an exalted position, one not held by his dynasty for centuries ... Though cast in an antique mould, the text is self-evidently late Middle Irish. The final section ... has been well reworked in the interest of the Uí Chennselaig kings of Leinster.
records.info:: Old Irish: “Some of the late verbal forms in the Testament can readily be restored as Old Irish. Others would require drastic emendation, but these may be explained as due to improvisation by scribes writing from memory a poem they could no longer fully understand, or substituting late forms for forms long since obsolete. The Testament may have been composed as early as the eighth century, and it may derive from an oral tradition even more ancient” (Dillon). 8th century(?). See Dillon above.

records.Title: Tuarastla Rossa Failge -  Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Ad-cear íarsin Cathaír i cath Tailltean & do-beart a seódu do Ros Ḟailge
records.Contents: A sequel to Timna Cathaír Móír … It represents Cathaír Mór as leaving his treasure to Ross (Russ) Failge, and instructing him to grant tuarastal (earlier rath), … to his sub-kings, to his brothers and to the Leinstermen in general. It then lists the tuarastal he gives the eponyms of the Leinster dynasties - Bresal Enechglas, Fiachu Baiccid, Tuathal mac Maine Máil, Dáire Barrach, Crimthannán and Nia Corb - the sign of their submission. The text belongs to the reign of Conchobar Ó Conchobair Failge, king and joint-king of Leinster (1079-1115), and is yet again historicist expression of his claim to supremacy over all Leinster dynasties.
records.Location of the narrative: Cathaír Mór; Ross (Russ) Failge; Conchobar Ó Conchobair Failge, king and joint-king of Leinster (1079-1115)

records.Title: Clanna Failge Ruis in ríg - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Clanna Failge Ruis in ríg clanna Dáre cén drochdil
records.Contents: A political poem (12 st.) in historicist terms. The Leinster dynasties, Uí Failge, Uí Bairrche and Uí Enechglais, are matrikin, descended from triplets borne by Medb, daughter of Bresal, and ought be allies, and each will rule Brega and North Leinster ... The poem probably belongs to the reign of Conchobar Ó Conchobair Failge, king and joint-king of Leinster (1079-1115), and reflects his ambitions and, possibly, his allies.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Failge, Uí Bairrche and Uí Enechglais; Medb, daughter of Bresal; Conchobar Ó Conchobair Failge, king and joint-king of Leinster (1079-1115)

records.Title: Clanna Bresail Bricc builid al. On the Leinster dynasties - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Clanna Bresail Bricc builid brith a rrúis is roduilig
records.Contents: A geneaological poem (13 st.) on the dynasties of Leinster, reflecting the changing political relationship between them - Uí Dúnlainge, Uí Chennselaig and now Osraige - in the eleventh century. The political message is subtly expressed through the poet's ranking of their remote ancestors.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Dúnlainge, Uí Chennselaig and now Osraige

records.Title: Andsu immarbáig la Laignib - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Andsu immarbáig la Laignib láthair ferda
records.Contents: A boastful poem (10st.), put in the mouth of the ancient poet, Dubthach moccu Lugair, on the prehistoric victories of the Leinstermen. It shares material and some expressions with 'Crimthann clothrí cóicid hÉrenn' (1219) and may be part of the royal propaganda of Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, king of Leinster (r. 1042-72), and the first of his lineage to hold the kingship of Leinster for centuries.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: "put in the mouth of Dubthach moccu Lugair"
records.Location of the narrative: Dubthach moccu Lugair; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, king of Leinster (r. 1042-72)

records.Title: Crimthann clothrí cóicid hÉrenn al. On Crimthann, king of Uí Chennselaig - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Crimthann clothrí cóicid hÉrenn Hectoir Elgga
records.Contents: An archaising poem (31st.) put in the mouth of Dubthach moccu Lugair, the ancient poet … on the battle triumphs of Crimthann son of Énna Cennselach, king of Leinster, noblest descendant (so the poet avers) of the legendary dynastic founder, Cathair Már ... The text reflects the rise of power of Uí Chennselaig under Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, king of Leinster (r. 1042-72) ... Crimthann's legendary victories ... echo Diarmait's campaigns against Munster.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: put in the mouth of Dubthach moccu Lugair
records.Location of the narrative: Dubthach moccu Lugair; Crimthann son of Énna Cennselach, king of Leinster; Cathair Már; Uí Chennselaig; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, king of Leinster (r. 1042-72)
records.info:: “a later date than the tenth century” (Van Hamel)

records.Title: Cath tucastar Crimthann - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Cath tucastar Crimthann do Láegaire línmar
records.Contents: A poem (23st.) attached, fictionally, to the famous poet Dubthach moccu Lugair …. The first part (st. 1-5) recounts clockwise Crimthann's victories over the kingdoms of Ireland; the second (st. 6-15) lists … victories of his father, Énna Cennselach, eponym of Uí Chennselaig; and the third (st. 16-23) tells of the large tribute paid Leinster by Uí Néill and Munster and the prosperity of Leinster in the reign of Énna. This vainglorious text may belong to the reign of Énna Mac Murchada, Uí Chennselaig king of Leinster (r. 1117-26).
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: put in the mouth of Dubthach moccu Lugair
records.Location of the narrative: Dubthach moccu Lugair; Crimthann son of Énna Cennselach, king of Leinster; Cathair Már; Uí Chennselaig; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, king of Leinster (r. 1042-72); Énna Mac Murchada, Uí Chennselaig king of Leinster (r. 1117-26)

records.Title: Flann mac Máel M'Áedóc (†979), Do chromramaib Laigen inso sís - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Éol dam i ndairib dréchta in midaig múaid móréchta
records.Contents: In this learned poem (43st.), opening with the remark that 'the relationship of the warriors of the Leinstermen … with the Ulaid, great Munster and red-sworded Leth Cuinn' was not peaceful. Flann mac Máel M'Áedóc, superior of the church of Glenn Uissen, rehearses in polished verse a dull litany of killings drawn from literature and early medieval history.

records.Title: Baile Moling - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: At-berim rib, a Laigniu
records.Contents: A part historicist, part pseudo-prophetic Leinster poem (47st.), from Tech Moling (St Mullins), in which Leinster kings are mostly indicated by references clearer to the poet than us. He is hostile to Osraige claims to the kingship of Leinster. The host of the Osraige king, Gilla Pátraic (1039-55), who plunder Tech Moling (St Mullins) ... The brave Diarmait mac Mael na mBó, king of Leinster (1042-72), is the 'warrior from Carn Cornáin who laid tribute on the Welsh' ... The poem ... may have been written in his reign. A great king, Flann Ginach al. Cinad, will reign when the Roth Rámach and the Scúab a Fánait will come over Ireland and Doomsday will be a hundred years after Flann.
records.Location of the narrative: Gilla Pátraic (1039-55); Diarmait mac Mael na mBó, king of Leinster (1042-72); Flann Ginach al. Cinad

records.Title: Legends of Fothairt - Poems of Leinster
records.Beginning lines: Fothairt for trebaib Con Corb (poem 1); Feidlimid athair Echach amra duine (poem 2)
records.Contents: Two poems … genealogical legends of the Leinster lineages called Fothairt, closely associated with the church of Kildare. The ancestral and eponymous Eochu Find Fuath nAirt is represented as son of Feidlimid Rechtaid and brother of Conn Cétchathach (ancestor of Uí Néill) and of Fiachu Suigde (ancestor of the Déissi). According to the first ill-ordered poem (19st.), Eochu is explled from Tara for outraging Art son of Conn ... The second (12 st.) describes the explusion of  ... Eochu Find Fuath nAirt from Tara with 700 men. He joined with Cú Chorb, ancestor of Laigin, and in seven battles, fought between noth Leinster and the sea at Waterford, drove the Munstermen out of Leinster.
records.Location of the narrative: Find Fuath nAirt son of Feidlimid Rechtaid and brother of Conn Cétchathach (ancestor of Uí Néill) and of Fiachu Suigde (ancestor of the Déissi); Art son of Conn; Eochu Find Fuath nAirt; Cú Chorb, ancestor of Laigin

records.Title: Do bunad imthechta Éoganachta - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Do-luid longes mór do ḟeraib hÉirenn a mbunad edón meic Éogain Taídlig
records.Contents: CODECS: It first relates how Éogan (the eponymous ancestor of the Éoganachta) and/or his sons arrive and settle in Ireland, how Éogan (the father or one of his sons) save the population from starvation, and how Éogan's son is chosen to be king. Their peaceful ascendancy is then contrasted with an origin tale of the Dál Cuinn (called children of the "second Míl Espáine"), who rule Ireland by the sword. In the north of the island, they alternately share the kingship with the Cruthin until Conn Cétchathach defeats them in a series of battles. The situation is reversed when Fíachu Araide, progenitor of the Dál Araide, expels Conn's grandson Cormac mac Airt from Tara. Cormac flees to Munster, where he becomes a vassal of Fíachu Muillethan, Éogan's great-grandson, in return for his assistance against Fíachu Araide. Fíachu Muillethan defeats the latter in battle. Cormac is thereby restored to the kingship and grants the lands settled by the Ciannachta to Fíachu Muillethan, who passes them on to Connla mac Taidg.
records.Location of the narrative: Éoganachta; Dál Cuinn; Cruthin; Conn Cétchathach; Fíachu Araide; Dál Araide; Cormac mac Airt; Fíachu Muillethan; Fíachu Araide
records.info:: “very likely, from the late ninth century or very early tenth” (Ó Corráin

records.Title: De causis torchi Corc' Óche - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Acuis torge Corc' Óche, ó Loch Echach a mbunad (prose); Ba mol Mídenn midlaige (verse); Rí Caisil do-rat fond & grian dóib (added text)
records.Contents: Origin legend, in prose and verse, with genealogies, of the Munster sub-kingdom of Corcu Óche (the barony of Glenquin, Co. Limerick), and of other petty kingdoms elsewhere called Corcu Óche … To this common core is added in MS i a tale that Corcu Óche fostered Corc, ancestor of the Éoganacht ... whose legendary king at Cashel is said to have granted them their lands. Éoganacht supported them whent heir neighbours, Uí Ḟidgeinte, oppressed them.
records.Location of the narrative: Corcu Óche; Corc, ancestor of the Éoganacht; Uí Ḟidgeinte

records.Title: West Munster synod - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Mac Ardæ mac Fidaig ba rí Ciarraigi Lúachra co muir
records.Contents: On the surface, an account of a sixth-century synod and of a covenant warranted by the oats of the greatest saints of Munster, representing the kingdoms whose patrons they are - Brendan of Clonfert, Brendan of Birr, Mochutu, Finn Cam, Nessán, Lugaid moccu Óche and others. By its terms, the kingdoms of west Munster secede from the overlordship of king of Éoganacht Locha Léin and transfer their loyalty to the king of Munster at Cashel ... Then follows an account of remarkably favourable conditions the king of Éoganacht Locha Léin concedes to his erstwhile subordinate, the king of Ciarraige Luachra ... ninth century, viz. the supremacy of the king of Cashel, the collapse of Éoganacht Locha Léin, and the rise of Ciarraige Luachra in alliance with Cashel. This is the voice of the court of Cashel and bishop Feidlimid (†847) mac Crimthainn was its king.
records.Location of the narrative: Éoganacht Locha Léin; Ciarraige Luachra; bishop Feidlimid (†847) mac Crimthainn

records.Title: Beir mo scíath scëo fri úath - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Beir mo scíath scëo fri úath breö fri brüach bruithnech bedgh
records.Contents: Formally a late Old Irish poem (25 st.) put in the mouth of Ailill Ólom, legendary king of Munster and ancestor of the Éoganacht dynasty. He laments the slaying of his seven sons (including the eponymous Éogan, anchestor of Éoganachta) in the battle of Mag Mucrama by Mac Con. The poem can be no earlier than c. AD 900, nor much later when Déis Tuaiscirt became 'Dál Cais' and were provided with a fictitious descent from Cormac Cas son of Ailill Ólom. Cormac Cas will rule 'from the esturary of Dublin to Tech nDuind' in south-west Munster. This is a historicist poem written in the interest of Dál Cais, staking their claim to rule Munster with the Éoganachta and linking them firmly to the royal lends of the Éoganachta.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: "put in the mouth of Ailill Ólom"
records.Location of the narrative: Ailill Ólom, legendary king of Munster and ancestor of the Éoganacht dynasty; Mac Con; Cormac Cas son of Ailill Ólom; Dál Cais
records.info:: early Middle Irish (O Daly)

records.Title: Nuallguba Ailella Óloim in ndiaid a chlainne al. The lamentation of Oilill Ólom - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Is annsin doríacht Anraigh gilla Oilella go sgélaib an chatha
records.Contents: A tale that derives from the poem 'Beir mo scíath scëo fri úath' and serves as an introduction to it. Anraigh, servant of Ailill Ólom, in reply to Ailill#s questions, lists those fallen in the battle of Mag Mucrama, and Ailill laments each.

records.Title: A maccáin ná cí - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: A maccáin ná cí ciasa dogra ara taí
records.Contents: ... verse monologue (46 st.) of Ailill Ólom, after the battle of Mag Mucrama, addressed to his orphaned grandson, Fiachu Muillethan mac Éogain, ancestor of the Éoganacht kings of Munster … is a historicist poem, by the author of Beir mo scíath scëo fri úath', written in the interest of Dál Cais, staking their claim to rule Munster with the Éoganachta and linking them firmly to the royal legends of the Éoganachta.
records.Location of the narrative: Ailill Ólom; Fiachu Muillethan mac Éogain, ancestor of the Éoganacht kings of Munster; Dál Cais
records.info:: early Middle Irish.

records.Title: Oilill Ólom amra in gein al. Senchas Aililla Óloim & Moga Nuadat - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Oilill Ólom amra in gein mac Moga Nuadat neimnig
records.Contents: A historicist poem, drawn from the genealogies (10st. With two later ones) … it is a list of the sons of Ailill Ólom and a gappy Munster king list. Kings of Éoganacht Locha Léin provenance are excluded. Its attribution to Cormac mac Cuilennáin (+908) is impossible. The aberrant Dub Ruis, nowhere attested in Munster king lists, occurs only in the later additions and is to be rejected.
records.Location of the narrative: sons of Ailill Ólom

records.Title: Clanna Ailella Úluim uill - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Clanna Ailella Úluim oill uas diagerbla dechardruing
records.Contents: A historicist geneaological poem (8 st.) on the twenty sons of Ailill Ólom, legendary ancestor of Éoganachta and other dynasties. It is legitimist in that it excludes all but three claims to descent from Ailill Ólom. Only Éogan (eponym Éoganachta), Cian (eponym of Cianachta), and Cormac Cas (eponym of Dál Cais) had offspring ... A prose version with more details ... occurs in the Book of Lecan ...
records.Location of the narrative: twenty sons of Ailill Ólom; Éogan (eponym Éoganachta), Cian (eponym of Cianachta), and Cormac Cas (eponym of Dál Cais)

records.Title: Noí meic déc Ailella Auloim - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Naí meic déc Aililla Úluim ad maisi 'ca rím
records.Contents: A … genealogical poem (54 st.), by an expert genealogist, on the offspring of many scions of Éoganacht and of two dynasties though related to them, Uí Ḟidgente and Uí Liatháin. The poet preserves important material, not found elsewhere, on Éoganacht Glendamnach.
records.Location of the narrative: Uí Ḟidgente; Uí Liatháin; Éoganacht Glendamnach

records.Title: Iarfaiged nech acaib al. Yew of the disputing sons - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Iarfaiged nech acaib dam cid dia tá in t-ibar iṅgnad
records.Contents: … scholastic poem (35 st.), attributed wrongly to Cormac mac Cuilennáin, king-bishop of Cashel (†908). It tells of one of the events leading ultimately to the battle of Mag Mucrama (1015), the quarrel between Éogan and Mac Con over the Otherworld musician come to avenge on Ailill Ólom his father's death and other offences. He was found in a yew tree and adjudged by Ailill Ólom to belong to his son Éogan - a judgement Mac Con regarded as false, and that led to violent conflict.
records.Location of the narrative: Éogan; Mac Con; Ailill Ólom

records.Title: Apair fri síl nÉogain Móir - Munster texts on Éoganacht and Ailill Ólom
records.Beginning lines: Apair fri síl nÉogain Móir daimet cóir din loṅgais duind
records.Contents: … poem (17st.), fathered on Senchán Torpéist, on the hostile relations between Ailill Ólom and Mac Con that led to the battle of Cenn Abrat (1005), Mac Con's exile, the battle of Mag Mucrama (1015), Mac Con's rule at Tara, and his loss at kingship.
records.Location of the narrative: Senchán Torpéist; Ailill Ólom; Mac Con
records.Characters in the narrative: Munster; battle of Cenn Abrat; battle of Mag Mucrama
records.info:: “The language of the Rule is Old Irish, though it contains a few Middle-Irish forms, such as gebes v. 1, geba v. 10, and the monosyllabic cóir v. 31 a, which are all fixed by the rhyme; the Middle-Irish plural mugada in 39 a is such a late form that it seems to point to some corruption in the text” (O Neill, p. 93).

records.Title: A fhir théit i mMag Medba - Connachta
records.Beginning lines: A ḟir théit i mMag Medba do scéla bar scothmebra
records.Contents: A poem (34 st.), listing the kings of Connacht from the fifth century Amalgaid mac Fiachrach to Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair, who became king in 1106 and ruled until 1156. The poem, by a retainer of Ua Conchobair, probably dates shortly after the death of Domnall (mac Ardgair) Mac Lochlainn, king of Ailech, and Ó Conchobair's great attack on Munster, both in 1121 ...
records.Location of the narrative: Amalgaid mac Fiachrach; Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair; Domnall (mac Ardgair) Mac Lochlainn, king of Ailech

records.Title: Néide Ó Maoil Chonaire (ascribed), Éol dam seiser cloinne Cuinn -  Connachta
records.Beginning lines: Eól dam seiser cloinne Cuinn - Maoin, Sáraid, Sadhb, Síl Úluim
records.Contents: This scholar's poem (50st.) traces the unbroken descent of Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair, king of Ireland (r. 1119-56), from the legendary Conn Cétchathach, and other dynastic heroes of a remote past. It is clearly and flatteringly refers to Tairdelbach as regnans ... reference to the family of Tigernán Ó Ruairc king of Breifne (r. 1124-72), Tairdelbach's ally since at least 1126 ... From st. 50 it appears that the poet was a son of Conaing Ó Maoil Chonaire, and they may be identical with Néidhe Ó Maoil Chonaire, the historian (†1136).
records.Location of the narrative: Tairdelbach Ó Conchobair, king of Ireland (r. 1119-56); Tigernán Ó Ruairc king of Breifne (r. 1124-72)
records.info:: apparently mid-twelfth century (Ó Cróinín)

records.Title: A fhir, ná suid ar in síd - Connachta
records.Beginning lines: A fhir ná suid ar in síd Síd nEochaill co n-ilar gním
records.Contents: A long historicist poem (49 st.), presented as an encounter between Cathal (+1010) son of Conchobar, king of Connacht, and two Otherworld figures, Áine who protects the dynasty of Connacht (Síl Muiredaig), and Aíbenn, tutelary goddess of Uí Briain (Dál Cais), their great rivals for kingly supremacy in Ireland in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. There will arise from Connacht an all-conquering champion who will reign gloriously over Ireland.

records.Title: Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib
records.Beginning lines: Bai docraite iongnadh adbalmór ar Eirinn uile go foirlethan ó geintibh gormglasa gusmara
records.Contents: … historicist account of the Viking wars, the career of Brian Bóraime, king of Ireland, and the battle of Clontarf (AD 1014), where he was killed. The text was written, in the interest of the dynasty, within a few years of 1100, in the reign of Brian's great-grandson, Muirchertach , king of Ireland. It is a response to the perceived crisis caused by the arrival in Ireland of Magnus Barelegs, king of Norway.
records.Location of the narrative: Brian Bóraime; Muirchertach , king of Ireland; Magnus Barelegs, king of Norway

records.Title: Leabhar oiris al. Leabhar oiris agus annála ar cogthaibh agus cathaibh Éireann
records.Beginning lines: Callann anno domini sé bliadhna seachtmhoghad ar naoi gcéad Maol Seachlainn mac Domhnaill do ghabháil ríghe hÉireann
records.Contents: A late text on the career of Brian Bóraime, a mix of annals and sagas … Most of the material originated in the late tenth to the early twelfth centuries; the date of compilation cannot be established without a critical edition.
records.Location of the narrative: Brian Bóraime
records.info:: Provenance - Munster (Best)

records.Title: Lament for Mael Sechnaill (†1022), king of Tara
records.Beginning lines: Mael Sechnlainn sinnser Gaeidhel cóir do chách a chommaeidhemh
records.Contents: A elegiac poem (17st.) Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill, king of Tara (†1022) and those seen as his centemporaries. The list is, in fact, closely connected with an inflated account of those who fell at the battle of Clontarf. King Brian and five of his sons are named (st. 16). The poem belongs to later legend-building about events in the early eleventh century.
records.Location of the narrative: Mael Sechnaill (†1022), king of Tara

records.Title: Dursan mar taí a Dhúin na Sciath al. Lament for Máel Sechnaill (†1022)
records.Beginning lines: Dursan mar taí a Dhún na Scieth dursan do thriath cen beith beó
records.Contents: A lament (8 st.) for Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill, king of Ireland (†1022). It is attributed to the famous poet Erard mac Coisse, but not regarded as his. It probably belongs to late medieval legend - building about Brian Bóraime and his contemporaries
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: attributed to Urard mac Coisse (†990), but not regarded as his
records.Location of the narrative: Máel Sechnaill (†1022)

records.Title: Dá mac déc Ceinnéidig cháid
records.Beginning lines: Dá mac déc Ceinnéidig cháid meic Lorcáin meic Lachtna láin
records.Contents: Attributed to Mac Liag in MS i, this short geneaological poem (8 st.), lists the deaths of the twelve sons of Cennétig (†951) mac Lorcáin, king of Dál Cais and father of Brian Bóraime (†1014). It is part of the late medieval growth of materials about Dál Cais and the battle of Clontarf in which Brian fell.
records.Location of the narrative: twelve sons of Cennétig (†951) mac Lorcáin, king of Dál Cais and father of Brian Bóraime (†1014)

records.Title: A mór Maigne Moige Síuil al. On the loss of a pet goose
records.Beginning lines: A Mór Maigne Moige Síuil bec a daimne esbaid n-éoin
records.Contents: … ironic poem ascribed by Meyer to Erard mac Coisse on Mór's mourning her pet goose … The lady is probably Mór (†986), daughter of king of Osraige and wife of Mael Sechnaill (†1022), king of Ireland … Whether contemporary or retrospective, this poem belongs to the literature created about great kings of the late tenth and early eleventh centuries.
records.Location of the narrative: Mór (†986), daughter of king of Osraige and wife of Mael Sechnaill (†1022)
records.info:: Late 10th or 11th century (Murphy); The poem is without ascription in the manuscript. Because of striking similarities to another Middle Irish poem, beg. Apair damsa re Der Fáil and attributed to the poet Erard mac Coise, Kuno Meyer suggested that the present text was written by the same author; Anonymous Middle Irish poem (11 qq) addressed to one ‘Mór of Maigen (Moyne) in Mag Siúil’, daughter of Donnchad, in which the speaker tells her not to lament the loss of her goose and lists the deaths of a number of famous kings and heroes of the Irish past.

records.Title: Bennacht a Bruin ar Brigit or In praise of Tadg Ua Cellaig (†1014)
records.Beginning lines: Bennacht a Bruin ar Brigit fuil am thig rim nach anait
records.Contents: Tadg Ua Cellaig, king of Uí Maine, fell at the battle of Clontarf in 1014. On that account he is known as Tadg catha Briain 'Tadg of Brian's battle'. This poem (34st.) is attributed to Mac Liag, poet of Brian Bóraime … praise poem in honour of Tadg …. When the poem is properly edited, the detailed references to people and places may help date it ... Conaing and Murchad (st. 23) are respectively nephew and son of Brian Bóraime, both fell at the battle of Clontarf. Thus, it belongs, like the others, to the literature created about the great personages of the late tenth and early eleventh centuries.
records.Location of the narrative: Tadg Ua Cellaig (†1014) king of Uí Maine, Conaing and Murchad nephew and son of Brian Bóraime (†1014)

records.Title: Sciath rígh Gæla glantar hí
records.Beginning lines: Sciath rígh Gæla glantar hí Cræba cailce for a clíu
records.Contents: This 'shield-song' (34st.), attributed to Mag Liag, opens with a shied of Tadg Ua Cellaig (†1014), king of Uí Maine … by which 181 shields have fallen … The poet boasts of Tadg's munificent gifts to him (st. 16-17). The imagined time is before the battle of Clontarf and the poet flatters Dál Cais extravagantly.
records.Location of the narrative: Tadg Ua Cellaig (†1014) king of Uí Maine,
records.info:: O'Curry sees the poem as a call to arms; Ó Lochlainn perceives Anglo-Norman heraldic influence and dates it to the mid fourteenth century.

records.Title: Leasg amleasg sind gu Áth Cliath al. Mac Liag's lament for Tadg Ua Cellaig (†1014), king of Uí Maine
records.Beginning lines: Leasg amleasg sing gu Áth Cliath co dún Amlaíb na n-órscíath
records.Contents: A text of literary cycle about Brian Bóraime and his contemporaries. Unhistorically, the poet Brian Bóraime (†1014), Áed ua Néill (†1004), king of Ailech, and Mael Sechnaill (†1022), king of Tara, assembled together at Dún Cattraige on the river Suck in Connacht, where there is a lovely exchange between their retainers.
records.Location of the narrative: Brian Bóraime (†1014); Áed ua Néill (†1004), king of Ailech; Mael Sechnaill (†1022), king of Tara
records.Characters in the narrative: Dún Cattraige on the river Suck in Connacht

records.Title: Marthain duit, a Ioraird fhéil
records.Beginning lines: Marthain duit, a Ioraird fhéil, a meic Coisi co ccaímchéill
records.Contents: A long poem (47st.) in the form of a competitive dialogue between the two poets, Mac Liac and Erard mac Coisse, about the lavish rewards and the high honours they are accorded by their respective royal patrons, Brian Bóraime (†1014) and Mael Sechnaill (†1022). The poem belongs to the literary legend-building about the kings of the late tenth and early eleventh centuries.
records.Location of the narrative: Mac Liag (†1015); Urard mac Coisse (†990); Brian Bóraime (†1014); Mael Sechnaill (†1022), king of Tara

records.Title: Áed Ailig inmain lim al. Lament for Áed, son of Domnall (†1004)
records.Beginning lines: Áed Ailig inmain lim hé dersan a Dé oided dó
records.Contents: A lament (9st.), by professional poet, for Áed (son of Domnall ua Néill), king of Ailech (r. 989-1004), who was killed at the battle of Cráeb Telcha (Crew Hill in the parish of Glenavy, Co. Antrim), fought between Ulaid and Cenél nÉogain. He was buried at Armagh (st. 8). Eochaid, his opponent (st. 9), is Eochaid mac Ardgair, king of Ulaid. The poem may belong to late medieval legend-building about king Brian Bóraime (†1014) and his contemporaries in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries.
records.Location of the narrative: Áed (son of Domnall ua Néill), king of Ailech (r. 989-1004); Eochaid mac Ardgair, king of Ulaid; Brian Bóraime (†1014)

records.Title: Caithréim Cellacháin Caisil al. Cathughudh Ceallachaín Chaisil re Lochlannaibh
records.Beginning lines: Airdri oirrdhirc airdmhenmnach ro-ghabhustar flaithius & forlamus for dhá coiged Muman
records.Contents: This text purports to be a historical account of the triumphs of Cellachán Caisil (†954), king of Munster, in his war against the Vikings. In fact, it is a historicist text, written between 1127 and 1134, in the interest of his descendant, Cormac Mac Carthaig (†1138), sole twelfth-century Éoganacht king of Munster (r. 1114-38). Its purpose is to provide his dynasty with as glorious a history in the peroid of the Viking wars as that claimed by his rivals, Dál Cais (Uí Briain).
records.Location of the narrative: Cellachán Caisil (†954), king of Munster; Cormac Mac Carthaig (†1138), sole twelfth-century Éoganacht king of Munster (r. 1114-38); Dál Cais (Uí Briain).
records.info:: Mid-12th century (Ó Corráin 1974)

records.Title: Mórthimchell Éireann uile
records.Beginning lines: A Mhuircheartaigh mhic Néill náir ro gabhais giallu Innse Fáil
records.Contents: A poem (64st.) attributed to one Cormacán mac Mael Brigte, purporting to be a contemporary account of the grand circuit of Ireland, made in the winter of 941/2, by Muirchertach mac Néill, king of Ailech (r. 938-43), who took the hostages of the king of Ireland. In fact, it is a historicist text, composed between 1157 and 1166, to glorify Muirchertach (mac Néill) Mac Lochlainn, king of Ireland (r. 1156-66), who, quite unhistorically, claimed Muirchertach (†943) as an illustrious ancestor and model.
records.Location of the narrative: Muirchertach mac Néill, king of Ailech (r. 938-43), who took the hostages of the king of Ireland. In fact, it is a historicist text, composed between 1157 and 1166, to glorify Muirchertach (mac Néill) Mac Lochlainn, king of Ireland (r. 1156-66)

records.Title: List of the kings of Ireland by Marianus Scottus the Chronicler
records.Beginning lines: Hi sunt flathi Hiberniae qui ex dimedia parte eius id est do Leth Chuinn regerunt o Chunn Cetchathach co Flann mac Mail Sechnaill
records.Contents: A list of 52 kings of Leth Cuinn … from the mythical Conn Cétchathach to Flann mac Máel Sechnaill (r. 879-916) … This is the oldest manuscript containing an Irish king list.
records.Location of the narrative: kings of Leth Cuinn; Conn Cétchathach ; Flann mac Máel Sechnaill (r. 879-916)

records.Title: Early medieval kings list in vernacular prose …
records.Beginning lines: O dilind co ragaib Parthalon hErind .cccxl (MS i)
records.Contents: Early medieval king lists, mostly loosely attached to Leabhar gabhála, some within the genealogies, MS i lists the prehistoric kings of Ireland; the king of Leinster … As a separate item within the genealogies, the same MS lists the kings of Munster … and MS iii have the same list of kings ... MS iii has a list of the kings of Ireland from prehistory to 1172 ... MS iv has an annotated list (compiled c. 1172) ... Most of these king lists are annotated, some heavily and independently of the extant annals - in fact, we perceived the beginning of a new type of historical text in which events are grouped under the reigns of kings, usually without the chronological criteria of the annals.

records.Title: Lebor Bretnach al. Irish version of Historia Britonum ascribed to Nennius
records.Contents: An Irish version of the now mostly lost mid eleventh-century 'Nennian recension' of Historia Britonum made probably in the second half of the eleventh century. It is attributed in MSS vi-vii … to Gilla Cóemáin … but this is doubted by Dumville and rejected by Thurneysen, Clancy and others.
records.Ascribed/Attributed to …: Gilla Cóemáin, but doubted by scholars

records.Title: The coarbs of Patrick al. Comarbada Pátraic
records.Contents: An annotated list of the rulers of Armagh (usually with years of office), in its longest form from the foundation of Armagh to the accession of archbishop Tomaltach Ó Conchobhair in 1181 … The early list may have come down to the rule of abbot Cú Dínaisc (†791) and was later filled retrospectively and unhistorically with the names of those believed to be early abbots of Armagh from the time of its foundation. It was then continued to Cellach (sed. 1105/6-29), and desultorily thereafter.
records.Location of the narrative: Tomaltach Ó Conchobhair in 1181; abbot Cú Dínaisc (†791); Cellach (sed. 1105/6-29)

records.Title: Mithigh techt tar mo thimna
records.Beginning lines: Mithig techt tar mo thimna cían as insa mé i mbáegul
records.Contents: A historicist ecclesiastical poem (13 st.). It is presented as the will of Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), king-bishop of Munster, by which he makes precious bequests to the saint-patrons of Emly, Cork, Lismore, Ardfert, Limerick and Lorrha, and he bequeaths his psalter to Cashel forever. This reflects the ecclesiastical arrangements of the reformed church of the later twelfth century and perhaps seek a special place for Lorrha in the favours of the archbishop of Cashel.
records.Location of the narrative: Cormac mac Cuilennáin (†908), king-bishop of Munster
records.info:: Cormac mac Cuilennáin identifies himself (as the speaker) in the last quatrain of version A. The Brussels MS 5100-5104 ascribes the poem to 'Corbmac', with a marginal note supplying ‘mac Cuileanain’. Erich Poppe Celtica 23 (1999): 300.; Version A is in later Middle Irish (Poppe).

records.Title: I cathraigh int oirdnide al. Kings buried at Clonmacnoise
records.Beginning lines: I cathraigh int oirdnide Ciarán cráibdig co ngrinde
records.Contents: Ascribed to Patrini who is identified in a marginal note in the MS as Máel Pátraic Ua Baeghaláin (†1028), priest of Clonmacnoise. This is a poem (17 st.) listing the royalty buried at the church of Clonmacnoise - fifty three names in all. There are members of Northern  Uí Néill, Southern Uí Néill, Uí Ḟiachrach, Uí Briúin, Airgialla and Uí Maine. Those named are too early to allow one to date the poem, but not too early to support unwarrented claims by Clonmacnoise to being the royal necropolis of Ireland. Its elergy could more safely claim the bones of ancient kings than those of the most recent, whose alleged burial in Clonmacnoise might be contested.
records.Location of the narrative: Northern Uí Néill, Southern Uí Néill, Uí Ḟiachrach, Uí Briúin, Airgialla and Uí Maine
records.info:: The poem is headed “Patriní cecinit”. A Latin note in another hand, which O'Keeffe suggests is probably that of John Colgan, identifies him as Máel Pátraic, a priest of Clonmacnoise who died in 1028 (Malpatric presybter Cluan qui obiit an. 1028).

records.Title: Cathair Chiaráin Cluain Mhac Nóis
records.Beginning lines: Cathair Chíarán Cluain Meic Nóis baile drúchtsholus deargróis
records.Contents: A poem (19 st.), doubtfully, to Enóg Ó Gilláin, in a final and added stanza. It promotes Clonmacnoise as a royal burial place by listing the dynasties whose nobel dead rest there. Reference to Mac Coise (st. 13) and Mac Lonáin (st. 14) indicates that the poem belongs to the cycle of later verse associated with them. On the promotion of Clonmacnoise as a sacred necropolis see further 1254-5
records.info:: Codecs "Early Modern Irish?"

records.Title: Finghala Chlainne Tantail
records.Beginning lines: Pealoip mac Tantail is dó tuc a lesmáthair grádh dearmhair .i. Moesia ingen Aiax
records.Contents: A tale of the kin-murders of the descendants of Tantalus, especially the House of Atreus … This is a text carefully compiled from the Latin commentators, especially Servius, and may have served as a text book and reference work in the twelfth-century Irish schools, whose language it reflects. For example, there are no borrowings from Latin or elsewhere - the terminology for war and institutions is purely Irish.

records.Title: Imthechta Áeníasa al. Irish Aeneid
records.Beginning lines: O thairnic tra do Grécaib slad & inrad & díthláithriugud ríg-chathrach na Frigia .i. in Træ
records.Contents: This is the first version of Virgil in a Western vernacular. It is in prose, the normal medium for Irish narrative. In style, the text is within the narrative conventions and language preferences of the eleventh and twelfth centuries. An adaptation, rather than a translation ...
records.info:: Irish vernacular adaptation of Vergil’s Aeneid, produced perhaps in the 12th century.

records.Title: In cath catharda
records.Beginning lines: Sé histudha flatha ro gabhustar flaithius & forlámhus ar críchaibh & ar cennadhchaibh na cruinne domhanta a llos neirt & niachais
records.Contents: A very competent medieval Irish adaptation  of the first seven books of the classical Latin poem Pharsalia al. Bellum civile by M. Annaeus Lucanus (AD 39-65) … In the matter of language, Old Norse borrowings are common … borrowings from Romance are scarce ...

records.Title: In tres Troí .i. Troí Astinactes
records.Beginning lines: Atá sund scél ingnáthach anaithnigh arna tharraing & arna thinól a diamraibh & a deiridibh na scriptúire diagha & domanda
records.Contents: The history of Troy and its people after its destruction by the Greeks. Its author/translator gives the sources: 'Bede, Servius [Danielis], Orosius, Augustine and Varro are the authors from whom this story has been compiled. Flannacán turned it into Irish' ... Flannacán may be identical with bishop Flannagán Ó Dubthaigh (†1168), scholar and historican, but this is uncertain.
records.info:: “Late Middle Irish at the earliest” (Miles)

records.Title: Romul & Remul
records.Beginning lines: Ceist cia cétna ro-ordaig míssu hi tossach?
records.Contents: A scholar's brief narrative of the story of the birth of Romulus and Remus compiled from works of reference.

records.Title: Scél an Mínaduir al. Senchas in Minaduir & a oidhedh al. Story of the Minotaur
records.Beginning lines: Baí rí amra oiregda i nInis Creit .i. Minosa a ainm-sidhein
records.Contents: This brief text tells the tales of Minos and Pasiphae, the killing of the Minotaur by Theseus, and the story of Daedalus and Icarus.

records.Title: Scéla Alaxandair al. Iomthúsa Alexandair Móir do réir an Sdair Laidne Justin bodéin & na ríg ro gaib ríge roime san nGréig Móir
records.Beginning lines: Cóic prímflaithiusa ro bátar for in domun ria flaithius Rómhán
records.Contents: … this is not a translation or adaptation of a pre-existing Latin text. It is the artistic creation of a scholarly Latinist and a well-read author … It tells us much of the sources available in Irish schools of the tenth century. The work belongs to the Insular tradition of Alexander, shared with Anglo-Saxon England, and is earlier than the continental European one. It opens with synchronisms drawing on indigenous Irish scholarship, and elsewhere its creator depends on the historical works of the Irish schools.

records.Title: Statius, Togail na Tebe al. Irish Thebaid: the Thebaid of Statius
records.Beginning lines: Aroile righ uasal oirmuidnech rogabh forlambhus & ferandus ar an ardcathraigh n-aibind n-alaind .i. Teibh isin nGreic
records.Contents: Togail na Tebe is a prose translation of the whole of the Thebaid … The translation is not literal … is the most faithful of all the Irish classical translations …

records.Title: Riss in mundtuirc
records.Beginning lines: Mundtorc do-rindi Ulcan do Eirmione .i. do seitcid Chaithim
records.Contents: The tale of the misfortunes visited on the royal house of Thebes, this text is based on Statius, Thebaid III and on the account of Theban history in Ovid Metamorphoses IX.

records.Title: Togail Troí: the destruction of Troy
records.Beginning lines: Do-rigni Iason innisin tria druidhecht Mediae .i. cethardam Ulcain do thabairt a hiffrind (recension 1); Ro gab rí uasal ordnide rigi in domain .i. Satuirn mac Polluir meic Phic meic Trois meic Esrom meic Chaim meic Noe (recension2); Ro bui forbairt for clandaib Ádaimh ria ndilinn (recension 3); Luid Iasón ina luing lóir co cathraig na gColach gcóir (recension 4)
records.Contents: … Medieval writers knew the story of Troy from Latin texts: De excidio Trojae was one of the most important … Latin original used as a framework … Irish literary creation … recension 1 belongs to first half of eleventh century. Recension 2 shares common source with recension 1 and is expanded. Thurneysen ... thinks it later than the first quarter of the twelfth century. Recension 3 has additional material and is later than recension 1. Recension 4, dated by Mac Eoin ..., to the first quarter of the twelfth century appears to derive from an independent prose version.

records.Title: Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica al. Stair Béid
records.Beginning lines: Augtar inna healathan sa Béid huasalsacart ecnaid fer ratha Dé i n-ecna & i crábud (praef.); Britania insola occiani cui quondam Albion nomen erat ocht cét míle chémend ina fot (text)
records.Contents: A very free and much abbreviated translation of the first two books of Bede's Historia Ecclesiastica. The text ends abruptly and the copy appears to be imperfect. Glossing and annotations for Irish readers have been absorbed into the text. The whole reflects Irish concerns and sensitivities.

records.Title: The Middle Irish version of Bede, De locis sanctis
records.Beginning lines: Tindscanad inso tuaruscbala na locc filet isin doman airtherach im Ierusalem
records.Contents: A paraphrase rather than a translation, with additional material from unknown sources.

records.Title: Iartaige na hingine colaige
records.Beginning lines: Baí rí amra do Grécaib i ndúnad fecht and. Dúnad dano lasna rígu
records.Contents: This tale was very widespread in the East and in the West in the middle ages. Krappe … thinks that the text depends on a Latin archetype, and that the extant versions are mostly thirteenth century or later. The Irish rendering is much earlier … transposed seamlessly into its Irish milieu.

records.Title: Bretha crólige
records.Beginning lines: Cis lir ro suidiged crolige la Fene? Co direnaiter?
records.Contents: An Old-Irish medico-legal tract … It contains much information on the classification of injuries, diet, and the social arrangements that attend criminal wounding and covalescence.

records.Title: Bretha Déin Chécht
records.Beginning lines: Bretha Dein Checht o legib. duine-diglaim a nnae ngrainnib gaibtir
records.Contents: An Old-Irish medico-legal tract that treats, in detail, of injuries, the fines and compensation payable (this forms a large part of the tract), and the fees of the physician. The tract reveals the expertise of early Irish doctors in anatomy, and physiology, notably in trauma ... and in dentistry.

records.Title: Airg & fir & mná
records.Beginning lines: Airg & fir & mná & ferdomun, a fuile, a mbánbéimenn
records.Contents: A succinct tract on compensations. Injuries are carefully classified by degree of trauma.

records.Title: Segar slicht otrusa
records.Beginning lines: Segar slicht otrusa urgnaiter manib i nindtech
records.Contents: An imperfect fragment of an Old-Irish medico-legal tract on sick maintenance.

records.Title: Cidh tré comraite, cidh tre anfót
records.Beginning lines: Cidh tré comraite, cidh tre anfót, cid tre hespa, cid tre indeithbhire
records.Contents: A late medieval legal commentary of uncertain date. Despite, what the text says, the institution of sick-maintenance that it describes was long obsolete by its time, but its concern for physician's fees, especially those paid by the upper classes, has the ring of truth.

records.Title: Materia Medica I
records.Beginning lines: … postea ollam de fornace … asinio lacte restringe
records.Contents: A mutilated fragment. It contains a Latin text on materia medica (herbal and otherwise) and a fragment of a calendarium diaeteticum with one Old-Irish gloss and many Old-Breton ones.

records.Title: Materia Medica II: two texts
records.Beginning lines: … a naighe ait ocus tinnis béil in gaile prémha mése do bruith (text 1); Circa presens negocium in simplicibus medicinis (text 2)
records.Contents: Text 1 is a list of materia medica - animal, mineral and vegetable - that draws (so the author avers) on Aristotle, Avicenna, Galen, Isaac &cc. Text 2 is another Latin and Irish parmacological tract on other materia medica.

records.Title: Medical glossaries
records.Beginning lines: Aculus adon soileasdar (glossary A); Arnaglosa plantago linga arietis .i. an cruach Patraic (glossary B); Pastinaca .i. athair liath .i. copog .i. ragum (glossary C).
